7:FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 show a vibration device 10 in use. A covering element 36, which may be a ceramic or porcelain tile, a stone slab, a large-format panel or a similar rigid covering element, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material that is plastic when the covering element 36 is laid and hardens afterwards. The substrate 42 may be a floor screed, a wall, a backer board or any other surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the proportion of the underside of the covering element 36 that is wetted by the bonding material 40, and seats the covering element 36 to the intended height.
15:The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22. An extraction opening 30 passes through the base 12 from the second side 16 to the first side 14 and places the chamber 22 in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20 through a duct 32. In the embodiment of FIG. 1, FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 there is a single extraction opening 30 at the centre of the second side 16, with the duct 32 standing over it at the centre of the first side 14 and the vibration motor 18 set toward one end of the base 12; two or more extraction openings 30 distributed over the second side 16 may be used instead, which evens out the pressure across a chamber 22 of large plan area.
19:The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12. It is mounted directly against the first side 14 and fixed to it by fasteners 54 spaced around its foot, so that no resilient mount, rubber bush or foam pad is interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. The fasteners 54 are shown in FIG. 1. That direct mounting is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.
21:The vibration motor 18 may be of any type that produces mechanical vibration in the base 12, including an electric motor driving an eccentric mass, a pneumatic vibrator, and a linear oscillator. In the embodiment of FIG. 1 the vibration motor 18 is a housing standing directly on the base 12, wider along the long edge of the base 12 than it is tall. What matters to the arrangement described here is not the mechanism by which the vibration is generated but the path by which it leaves the vibration device 10, which is dealt with below.
29:An electrical supply 50 provides power to the vibration motor 18 and, where the air-extraction mechanism 20 is electrically driven, to the air-extraction mechanism 20. In the embodiment of FIG. 1 the electrical supply 50 is a flexible cord leaving the air-extraction mechanism 20 and running to a mains or site supply; a battery carried on the base 12 may be used instead. The vibration motor 18 and the air-extraction mechanism 20 may be switched together or independently of one another.
33:A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 near its perimeter. In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a continuous closed loop, unbroken at the corners, standing a little inboard of the outer edge of the base 12 so that a plain margin of the second side 16 lies outside the loop, as seen in the bottom plan view. The loop may equally run at the very edge of the base 12, its outer side coinciding with that edge and leaving no such margin. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly fixed to the base 12 by fasteners, or is formed integrally with the base 12 as one piece; either way the joint between them is rigid and carries vibration across itself without loss.
35:The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The bearing face 26 is a low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials. In the embodiment of FIG. 4, the perimeter member 24 is a metal loop carrying a low-friction facing 28 of PTFE bonded or mechanically fixed to its end, and the exposed surface of the low-friction facing 28 forms the bearing face 26; the low-friction facing 28 is thin and hard, and being a rigid plastic rather than an elastomer it does not act as a spring in the vibration path. In another embodiment the perimeter member 24 is made in one piece of a low-friction rigid plastic, and the bearing face 26 is simply the end face of that member. The bearing face 26 lies in a single plane, so that the vibration device 10 sits flat on a planar exposed face 38 and the load is shared around the whole loop.
41:Because the perimeter member 24 is rigid and the exposed face 38 is neither perfectly flat nor perfectly clean, in that it carries dust, grains of bonding material 40 and its own surface texture, and the covering element 36 itself may be slightly bowed, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is far too small to be drawn to scale, and so are the departures from flatness of the exposed face 38 that give rise to it. FIG. 2 accordingly shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 without any gap, at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 appears only in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4, where it is drawn many times its true height. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22, and does so by presenting a long, narrow, high-resistance path around the whole loop, without closing that path.
75:In the embodiment of FIG. 1 the handle 44 is a single bail standing on the base 12 clear of the vibration motor 18 and the air-extraction mechanism 20. Two side grips, one at each side of the base 12, may be used instead.
79:FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10 at an attachment formation 48 on the base 12. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.
83:In the embodiment of FIG. 5 the attachment formation 48 is placed low on the base 12, close to the plane of the bearing face 26, so that the line of the applied tension lies near that plane and produces little moment tending to tilt the vibration device 10 about the leading edge of the perimeter member 24. More than one attachment formation 48 may be provided, for instance one at each end of the base 12, so that the vibration device 10 can be drawn in either direction without being turned about.
89:The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. It may instead be divided into two or more chambers 22 by rigid walls standing on the second side 16, each of the chambers 22 being in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20. Dividing the chamber 22 in this way keeps the pressure differential more uniform beneath a base 12 of large plan area, because each of the chambers 22 is fed by its own extraction opening 30 and the pressure in it does not depend on flow travelling the whole width of the base 12. Rigid walls used in this way also stiffen the base 12 against the alternating force from the vibration motor 18, and, standing on the second side 16 with their lower ends in the plane of the bearing face 26, they add further rigid contact area through which vibration passes into the covering element 36.
91:The perimeter member 24 is shown as a rectangular loop in FIG. 3. It may equally be circular, oval or any other closed shape.

    extra = body - set(nums)
    if extra:
        print('   mentioned-not-listed:', sorted(extra))
print('unused table numerals:', sorted(tbl - used))
print('fig numerals not in table:', sorted(used - tbl))

# FIG. 1 - Perspective view of the vibration device in use

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, onto one large plain tile. Outline line work, no shading, no hatching. Every body except the cable has flat faces, straight edges and square corners. No text of any kind appears: no word, letter, digit, number, nameplate, dial, screen, button, logo or marking on any body or on the tile, and no border. Every drawn face is blank. No circle, ring, roundel, disc, hole, ellipse or pair of closed curves appears anywhere on the sheet, on the tile or on any face of any body.

**Geometry to be drawn**

A large plain tile fills the lower part of the sheet, with no joint line and no other tile, and carries no numeral. Only one cable appears on the sheet, and nothing at all leaves the motor block.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole shallow rectangular assembly standing on the middle of that tile. Identified on the outer silhouette of the assembly, along the upright outer edge line at the left end of the lowest slab.
- The base 12 is that lowest slab, a flat rectangle on which every other body stands. Its thickness is clearly visible, so its near front side face is a band of plain paper tall enough to take a point well inside it. Identified well inside that front side face, clear of both of its long edges.
- The vibration motor 18 is a rectangular block of flat faces standing on the slab at its left end. Identified well inside its flat front face.
- The duct 32 is an upright rectangular column of square section rising from the middle of the slab. Identified well inside its flat front face.
- The air-extraction mechanism 20 is a further rectangular block resting on the flat top of that column, lifted clear of the slab and touching it nowhere. Identified well inside its flat right-hand face.
- The fasteners 54 are a row of square bolt heads standing proud of the slab in front of the motor block, each drawn large enough to hold a point well inside it. Identified well inside the leftmost head of that row.
- The handle 44 is a bail of three straight members at the right end of the slab, clear of both blocks and the column: an upright on each long edge and a cross bar joining their tops at square corners. It has no other member, and the space beneath the cross bar is open paper down to the slab. Identified on the cross bar, clear of both uprights.
- The electrical supply 50 is the one flexible cable on the sheet, slender and of even width, and the only curved line drawn. It leaves the rear face of the upper block, runs rearward and to the left behind the assembly, and passes off the left edge of the sheet above the motor block. It stays in the left part of the sheet and never crosses the handle. Identified on the drawn cable in its run to the left of the column, clear of the upper block and of the left edge of the sheet.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 10, 12, 18, 20, 32, 44, 50, 54

47	The pressure at which the chamber 22 settles is the working pressure difference, and it is what the air-extraction mechanism 20 is sized to reach. The vibration device 10 is designed for a working pressure difference that produces a holding force adequate to hold it against the covering element 36, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 is then chosen so that the rate it delivers at that working pressure difference is at least equal to the rate at which ambient air passes through the clearance 34 at the same pressure difference. Both rates are taken at the same pressure difference, so the comparison is between like and like, and meeting it places the crossing point of the two curves at or beyond the intended working pressure difference, which is what draws the chamber 22 down at least that far.
48	
49	The rate an air-extraction mechanism 20 delivers against a pressure difference is not always to hand, whereas its free-air displacement, the volumetric rate it delivers with no pressure difference across it, is a figure commonly quoted for pumps, fans and blowers. Free-air displacement may therefore be used to make a first selection, provided a margin is allowed for the fall in delivered rate with rising pressure difference, and the choice is then confirmed against the delivered rate at the working pressure difference.
50

All flagged figure briefs are repaired. Summary of what changed and why:

**Titles cut off at the 60-character label limit** (preflight): FIG. 2, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 headings ended mid-word ("cha", "membe", "pulli"). Shortened to "Vertical section through the chamber", "Enlarged section of the perimeter member end", and "Second embodiment with a pulling element", and renamed the three files to match. The Brief Description of the Drawings already describes each view in its own sentences and still matches, so no text section changed.

**Arbitrary endpoint targets**: removed "in its left-hand part" / "in its right-hand part" / "well below its top edge line" style depth and part-fraction instructions from FIG. 2 numerals 12, 22, 36 and FIG. 4 numerals 36, 40, 42, replacing each with a broad interior ("well inside the hatching of the upper band, clear of its upper and lower edge lines"). FIG. 4's clearance 34 lost its "low down, nearer the top edge" instruction and now reads as the open gap clear of the two bounding lines.

**The two failed endpoints**: FIG. 2 numeral 30 landed on a slab boundary line instead of inside the channel, so the channel is now specified to be drawn broad with plain white paper running the full depth of the slab, and the target excludes both bounding lines and both slab edges. FIG. 4 numeral 38 landed one pixel inside the hatching, so its target is now the whole top edge line of the upper band ("anywhere along that top edge line"), and bearing face 26 was narrowed to its own foot line only so 26, 34 and 38 cannot be confused with one another.

**FIG. 1 OCR "unexpected 00"**: the sheet now forbids any circle, ring, roundel, disc, hole or ellipse anywhere, which removes the only plausible source of a digit-like read on an otherwise blank flat-faced assembly. Trimming was needed to keep the brief under the 2800-character cap after that addition; the trimmed wording is redundancy, not geometry.

**Ordinal shape references**: "a second rectangular block", "no second tile", "no fourth member", "no second circle" became "further"/"other" so no numeral target or geometry constraint depends on an ordinal whose direction could be read two ways. FIG. 4's bands are now "upper, middle, lower" rather than "uppermost".

Nothing in the application text, claims, numeral table or figure membership changed: all 22 numerals are still defined once and still distributed 8/6/3/8/4 across FIG. 1 to FIG. 5, and every brief is at or below 2800 characters. I could not run the render, OCR, semantic, coordinate, topology or cross-provider gates myself; this workspace contains only the patent lookup tool, so those gates run in the pipeline against the repaired briefs.

input.summary: Repaired the five figure briefs against the new preflight: completed three figure labels that were truncated mid-word at 60 characters (and renamed those files), removed every arbitrary part-fraction and exact-depth endpoint instruction, rewrote the two endpoints that the marked-endpoint review rejected (FIG. 2 extraction opening 30, FIG. 4 exposed face 38) as broad interiors or full boundaries, banned circles on FIG. 1 to kill the "unexpected 00" OCR read, and replaced ambiguous shape ordinals with stable names. No application section, claim, numeral definition or figure membership was touched.
reasoning: The two rejected endpoints were not renderer noise but under-specified targets, so I fixed the specification rather than asking for a re-render of the same brief. FIG. 2 numeral 30 kept landing on the slab's top boundary because the channel was only said to be 'drawn broad'; it now must show plain white paper running the whole depth of the slab between its two lines, and the target explicitly excludes both bounding lines and both slab edge lines.

FIG. 4 numeral 38 was rejected at one pixel inside the hatching. Rather than tighten the tolerance, I made the target the entire boundary line ('anywhere along that top edge line'), which the request endorses as a full-boundary target. That created a possible overlap with bearing face 26 and clearance 34, both of which live near the same gap, so I split the three cleanly: 26 is the column foot line only, 34 is the open white gap clear of both lines, 38 is the band top edge line. Each point now falls to exactly one numeral.

The preflight flagged 'in its left-hand part' and 'well below its top edge line' as arbitrary exact targets. I removed that whole family of phrasing from FIG. 2 (12, 22, 36) and FIG. 4 (36, 40, 42) and replaced it with broad interiors keyed to a named part, which is what the request asked for. I kept 'right-hand leg' in FIG. 2 and 'upper/middle/lower band' in FIG. 4 because those are stable part names, not positions within one part.

The 'unexpected 00' OCR failure on FIG. 1 has no text source in the brief, which already forbids all lettering, so the likely source is drawn circular geometry (bolt heads, bosses, cable end) reading as a pair of zeros. I added an absolute prohibition on any circle, ring, roundel, disc, hole or ellipse on that sheet. FIG. 3 keeps its single circle because the extraction opening is the disclosed geometry there and that sheet's OCR passed.

Adding the circle prohibition pushed FIG. 1 over the 2800-character cap, so I cut redundant wording only: 'of flat faces' on a block already stated to have flat faces, 'of square section' on the duct column, 'above the motor block' on a cable already constrained to the left part of the sheet. No geometry constraint, relationship or numeral target was lost.

I renamed the FIG. 2, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 files as well as their headings, because the slug and the label both truncate at 60 characters and a fixed heading over an old slug would have left the same cut-off label in the pipeline. FIG. 5 was not on the reviewer's list but its label was cut at 'pulli', so I fixed it in the same pass rather than let it fail the next run.

I changed nothing in the nine application sections. The Brief Description of the Drawings describes each view in its own full sentences and never quotes the figure-file titles, so the shortened titles left it accurate; the Detailed Description references figures only by number. Rewriting either would have been churn the review did not ask for.

I could not execute the render, OCR, semantic, coordinate, topology or cross-provider gates: this workspace exposes only tools/patent_lookup.py, and the drawing pipeline runs outside it. I verified by hand what is checkable here, namely brief lengths (all at or below 2800), eight-numeral-per-sheet limits (8/6/3/8/4), the 22-numeral table matching the union of the five sheets exactly, and the absence of banned endpoint vocabulary and human-directed wording.

figures/FIG-4-ENLARGED-FRAGMENTARY-SECTION-OF-THE-PERIMETER-MEMBE.md renamed to figures/FIG-4-ENLARGED-SECTION-OF-THE-PERIMETER-MEMBER-END.md, heading completed
figures/FIG-5-SECOND-EMBODIMENT-DEVICE-DRAWN-BY-A-FLEXIBLE-PULLI.md renamed to figures/FIG-5-SECOND-EMBODIMENT-WITH-A-PULLING-ELEMENT.md, heading completed
FIG. 2: extraction opening 30 now requires a channel showing plain white paper the whole depth of the slab, with the endpoint clear of both bounding lines and both slab edge lines

FIG. 2: base 12, chamber 22, covering element 36 and first side 14 endpoint targets rewritten as broad interiors or a full boundary line, dropping 'left-hand part', 'right-hand part', 'right-hand run' and 'well below its top edge line'

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged this turn. The claims, specification and numeral definitions were preserved exactly, so the existing distinction stands: claim 1 recites a rigid perimeter member terminating in a low-friction bearing face that deliberately does not seal, together with an air-extraction mechanism sized to exceed the leakage rate through the resulting clearance at the working pressure difference, so the device is held down by the pressure differential while remaining free to slide, and vibration passes to the covering element through an all-rigid path with no resilient mount anywhere between motor and bearing face. The prior_art references teach sealing suction attachment or compliant pads, not a deliberately leaking rigid low-friction skirt whose leakage is the design parameter the extraction rate is chosen against. Ambiguous shape ordinals were replaced with stable names throughout. The nine application sections, the claims, all 22 numeral definitions and the five-figure numeral assignment are byte-for-byte unchanged. The device is drawn large in the frame and the slab has clearly visible thickness, so its near left side face is a band of plain paper tall enough to take a point well inside it. # FIG. 4 - Enlarged section of the perimeter member end

**View:** Greatly enlarged fragmentary section through the lower end of a perimeter member shown in FIG. 2, where the clearance is present, with the bedded layers beneath. Outline line work, hatching on cut material. No word, digit or label appears, and no border.

**Geometry to be drawn**

One upright hatched column hangs from a fragment of hatched slab at the top of the sheet. That fragment carries no numeral. The column is bounded by one vertical line at each side. One horizontal line crosses the column above its lower end, dividing it into a tall upper part and a short lower part.

Three hatched bands lie one above another across the lower part of the sheet, each spanning the full width and drawn deep, separated by one horizontal line. They are the upper band, the middle band and the lower band.

The white gap between the column and the upper band is drawn very tall, so the short foot line closing the bottom of the column lies far above the top edge line of the upper band, which runs the full width of the sheet.

- The perimeter member 24 is the tall upper part of the column. Identified well inside the hatching of that upper part.
- The low-friction facing 28 is the short lower part of the column, below the dividing line. Identified well inside the hatching of that lower part.
- The bearing face 26 is the short horizontal line at the foot of the column, where the hatching of the column stops and the white gap begins. Identified anywhere along that short foot line, at the underside of the column hatching, and never on the top edge line of the upper band across the gap.
- The clearance 34 is the open white gap between the foot of the column and the top edge of the upper band, drawn taller than the short lower part of the column, so that column and band nowhere touch. Identified in the open white paper of that gap beneath the column, clear of the foot line above it and of the top edge of the upper band below it.
- The covering element 36 is the upper band. Identified well inside the hatching of the upper band, clear of its upper and lower edge lines.
- The exposed face 38 is the top edge of the upper band, the line where the white gap above meets the hatching below. Identified anywhere along that top edge line, in the run clear of the column, and never inside the hatching beneath it.
- The bonding material 40 is the middle band. Identified well inside the hatching of the middle band, clear of the lines above and below it.
- The substrate 42 is the lower band. Identified well inside the hatching of the lower band, clear of the line above it and of its lower edge.

# FIG. 5 - Second embodiment with a pulling element

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, as FIG. 1 but from further off, so several laid tiles are in frame. Outline line work. The sheet contains only the parts listed. No word, letter, digit or label appears, no border, bar, band or filled area, and nothing is drawn below the floor.

**Geometry to be drawn**

- The covering element 36 is a flat floor of a few large square tiles in perspective filling the lower part of the sheet, joined edge to edge in one plane with a straight joint line between neighbours. The floor is otherwise plain. One tile in the lower right of the sheet, in front of the device and well away from the cord, is drawn large, with no cord crossing it and no joint line within it. Identified well inside the open surface of that lower right tile, clear of the device, of every joint line and of the cord.
- The vibration device 10 is a shallow rectangular assembly standing on a tile at the middle right of the floor, drawn as on FIG. 1: a flat slab carrying a rectangular motor housing at its left end, and at the middle of the slab an upright rectangular column with a rectangular pump housing on its top, held clear of the slab. The slab has clearly visible thickness, so its near left side face is a band of plain paper deep enough to take a point. Identified well inside that side face, clear of both its long edges, and not on the floor, the cord, the ring or either housing.
- The attachment formation 48 is one simple closed ring projecting from the left end of the slab, low on that end and touching it: a single loop of one continuous outline enclosing one opening. It is a single ring, not a chain and not a knot, and no other ring, loop or hook appears anywhere. It is drawn large, so its opening is plainly visible. Identified on the outline of that ring, and not on the slab, the cord or the floor.
- The flexible pulling element 46 is a slack cord running from that ring away to the left, sagging gently and passing off the left edge of the sheet in one unbroken sweep, without doubling back or looping. It stays in the left part of the sheet. It is drawn as one bold continuous line of even width broad enough to carry a point on the line itself, with no core line. It runs across one tile of the floor in which no joint line is drawn, so that a long stretch of the cord has plain paper on both sides of it and no other line touches or crosses it. No block, connector or arrowhead appears along it. Identified on that open stretch of the cord, where no other line touches it, clear of the ring and of the left edge of the sheet, and not on the ring, the slab, a joint line or the floor.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 10, 36, 46, 48

- 10

# FIG. 5 - Second embodiment with a pulling element

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, as FIG. 1 but from further off, so several laid tiles are in frame. Outline line work. The sheet contains only the parts listed. No word, letter, digit or label appears, no border, bar, band or filled area, and nothing is drawn below the floor.

**Geometry to be drawn**

- The covering element 36 is a flat floor of a few large square tiles in perspective filling the lower part of the sheet, joined edge to edge in one plane with a straight joint line between neighbours. The floor is otherwise plain. One tile in the lower right of the sheet, in front of the device, away from the cord, is drawn large, with no cord crossing it and no joint line within it. Identified well inside the open surface of that lower right tile, clear of the device, of every joint line and of the cord.
- The vibration device 10 is a shallow rectangular assembly standing on a tile at the middle right of the floor, drawn as on FIG. 1: a flat slab carrying a rectangular motor housing at its left end, and at the middle of the slab an upright rectangular column with a rectangular pump housing on its top, held clear of the slab. The slab has clearly visible thickness, so its near left side face is a band of plain paper deep enough to take a point. Identified well inside that side face, clear of both its long edges, and not on the floor, the cord, the ring or either housing.
- The attachment formation 48 is one simple closed ring projecting from the left end of the slab, low on that end and touching it: a single loop of one continuous outline enclosing one opening. It is a single ring, not a chain and not a knot, and no other ring, loop or hook appears. It is drawn large, so its opening is plainly visible. Identified on the outline of that ring, and not on the slab, the cord or the floor.
- The flexible pulling element 46 is a slack cord running from that ring away to the left, sagging gently and passing off the left edge of the sheet in one unbroken sweep, without doubling back or looping. It stays in the left part of the sheet. It is drawn as one bold continuous line of even width broad enough to carry a point on the line itself, with no core line. It runs across one tile of the floor in which no joint line is drawn, so that a long stretch of the cord has plain paper on both sides of it and no other line touches or crosses it. No block, connector or arrowhead appears along it. Identified on that open stretch of the cord, where no other line touches it, clear of the ring and of the left edge of the sheet, and not on the ring, the slab, a joint line or the floor.

All five sheets' briefs are repaired and every brief is back under the 2800-character cap.

**FIG. 1** (numerals 10, 12, 50, 54 misplaced; leader 50 had no terminal dot): the root cause was that numeral 10, the assembly as a whole, and numeral 12, the slab that forms part of that same assembly, competed for the same silhouette. Endpoint reviewers read the two dots as pointing at "the assembly's slab" versus "some other main base", and the 10 dot drifted onto a fastener head at the crowded left end. Numeral 10 now sits only on FIG. 5, where it labels the same assembly on a sheet with no competing part numerals and where it already passed. FIG. 1 keeps the assembly in its geometry, and base 12 is now stated to be the one slab on the sheet with no other slab, plate or panel drawn. Fastener 54 targets the broad flat top of the leftmost head. The cable is specified as a bold continuous line broad enough to carry a point, crossing no other line, with the dot on an open run where nothing touches it.

**FIG. 2** (14 ambiguous against 30): the two dots were at nearly the same horizontal position, one on the slab's upper edge and one in the channel below it. First side 14 is now confined to the run of the upper edge line to the right of the channel, and the brief states the two points lie far apart.

**FIG. 3** (24 in a rejected cluster): the band between the middle and innermost rectangles is now specified as a broad corridor of even width on every side of the loop, and 24's target is the open white paper of that band along the right side, with explicit exclusion of the innermost rectangle and of the margin outside the middle rectangle.

**FIG. 4** (26 landed on the band's top edge, which is 38): the brief now states the gap is drawn very tall, that the foot line is short and runs only across the column while the band's top edge runs the full sheet width, and 26's target excludes the band's top edge across the gap.

**FIG. 5** (46 had no terminal dot and landed on a cord/joint-line intersection): the cord is now a bold continuous line broad enough to carry a point, running across a tile in which no joint line is drawn, and the dot must lie on that open stretch where no other line touches it, explicitly not on a joint line.

Trimming to stay under the cap removed only redundant rendering constraints ("every drawn face is blank", duplicate depth assurances, the circle prohibition on FIG. 4, which never had an OCR finding). No claim, description, numeral definition or disclosed embodiment changed; all 22 numerals remain defined once and distributed 7/6/3/8/4 across the five sheets.

I reinforced base 12 against the same misreading by stating that the slab is the only slab, plate or panel on the sheet and that it rests directly on the tile. That removes the imagined second base the reviewers were reaching for without altering the disclosed structure.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged. # FIG. 1 - Perspective view of the vibration device in use

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, onto one large plain tile. Outline line work, no shading, no hatching. Every body except the cable has flat faces, straight edges and square corners. No text of any kind appears: no word, letter, digit, nameplate, dial, screen, button, logo or marking, and no border. No circle, ring, roundel, disc, hole or ellipse appears anywhere on the sheet.

**Geometry to be drawn**

A large plain tile fills the lower part of the sheet, with no joint line and no other tile, and carries no numeral. A shallow rectangular assembly of a slab and the bodies standing on it rests on that tile. Only one cable appears on the sheet, and nothing at all leaves the motor block.

- The base 12 is the one slab on the sheet, a flat rectangle resting on the tile, on which every other body stands; no other slab, plate or panel is drawn. Its thickness is clearly visible, so its near front side face is a band of plain paper deep enough to take a point. Identified well inside that front side face, clear of both of its long edges.
- The vibration motor 18 is a rectangular block standing on the slab at its left end. Identified well inside its flat front face.
- The duct 32 is an upright rectangular column rising from the middle of the slab. Identified well inside its flat front face.
- The air-extraction mechanism 20 is a further rectangular block resting on the flat top of that column, lifted clear of the slab and touching it nowhere. Identified well inside its flat right-hand face.
- The fasteners 54 are a row of square bolt heads standing on the top of the slab in front of the motor block, each drawn large. Identified well inside the flat top of the leftmost head of that row.
- The handle 44 is a bail of three straight members at the right end of the slab, clear of both blocks and the column: an upright on each long edge and a cross bar joining their tops. It has no other member, and the space beneath the cross bar is open paper. Identified on the cross bar, clear of both uprights.
- The electrical supply 50 is the one flexible cable on the sheet, the only curved line drawn, a bold continuous line of even width, broad enough to carry a point on the line itself. It leaves the rear face of the upper block, runs to the left behind the assembly, and passes off the left edge of the sheet. It crosses no other line and never crosses the handle. Identified on the drawn cable along its open run to the left of the assembly, where no other line touches it, and clear of the upper block and of the left edge of the sheet.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 12, 18, 20, 32, 44, 50, 54

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10

reasoning: The preflight failure was a declaration mismatch on FIG. 1: the sheet list carried numeral 10 while the declaration line did not. Restoring 10 to both places is the fix, and it also restores the figure plan the pipeline expects, so the earlier redistribution is fully reversed.

The two numerals now target features of different kinds on the same body: 10 on the lower boundary line where the assembly meets the tile, 12 on the broad interior of the front side face above it. A point is on a line or inside a face, never both, so the reviewer has a decidable rule.

The endpoint reviewers previously rejected 12 on the theory that the slab under the assembly was something other than the base. I met that head on by stating in the brief that the slab belongs to the assembly and that the outline it stands on is the outline of the assembly itself, and by repeating that no other slab, plate or panel is drawn. That removes the imagined second object without adding structure to the invention.

I kept fastener 54 on the flat top of the leftmost bolt head, which is on the top of the slab and well away from the lower front outline, so the numeral 10 dot has no nearby competitor of the sort that captured it before.

The restored bullet pushed FIG. 1 to 2827 characters, so I cut only rendering redundancy: the enumerated list of forbidden text objects, which the shorter blanket prohibition already covers, 'square corners' on bodies already specified as flat-faced, and the duplicated statement that the cable never crosses the handle, which the crossing prohibition already covers. Disclosed geometry and every relationship are intact at 2782 characters.

The distinction remains the rigid perimeter member ending in a low-friction bearing face that deliberately does not seal, combined with an air-extraction mechanism whose delivered rate at the working pressure difference is at least the leakage rate through the resulting clearance at that same pressure difference, giving a device held by pressure differential yet free to slide, with an all-rigid vibration path and no resilient mount between motor and bearing face. **View:** Plan view of the underside of the plate, with the tile removed. Outline line work only: no hatching, shading, stippling, dashed or double line, every outline one thin line. The whole sheet contains four outlines and nothing else: from the outside inward, a large outermost rectangle with square corners, a middle rectangle within it, an innermost rectangle within that, and one circle standing clear of the sides of the innermost rectangle. Each is drawn once, as one closed line. # FIG. 3 - Bottom plan view of the vibration device

**View:** Plan view of the underside of the plate, with the tile removed. Outline line work only: no hatching, shading, stippling, dashed or double line, every outline one thin line. No word, digit or label appears, and no border. Each point lies well inside a surface, away from every outline and from every corner, and the three points are far apart.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The whole sheet contains four outlines and nothing else: from the outside inward, a large outermost rectangle with square corners, a middle rectangle within it, an innermost rectangle within that, and one circle standing clear of the sides of the innermost rectangle. Each is drawn once, as one closed line. There are three rectangles and no more: no further rectangle outside the outermost, inside the innermost or alongside any of them, and no frame surrounds the drawing. The circle is one thin closed curve with plain white paper inside it, not a ring, an annulus or a hole with a wall, and no other circle appears.

Those outlines enclose four surfaces: the margin between the outermost and middle rectangles, the band between the middle and innermost rectangles, the area inside the innermost rectangle around the circle, and the inside of the circle. The circle is drawn large in relation to the innermost rectangle, so a point sits easily inside it.

The margin and the band are each drawn as a broad corridor of open white paper of even width. The margin is the widest open run on the sheet, drawn wider than the band inside it, and the band is wide on every side of the loop, so that in either corridor a point sits with clear white paper on both sides of it, touching neither line that bounds that corridor.

- The extraction opening 30 is the circle. Identified well inside that circle, clear of its curve.
- The perimeter member 24 is the band between the middle and innermost rectangles, the loop seen end on. Identified in the open white paper of that band along the right side of the sheet, between the middle rectangle and the innermost rectangle, clear of both of those lines and of the corners; the point is not inside the innermost rectangle, and not inside the margin outside the middle rectangle.
- The second side 16 is the underside surface outside the loop, the margin between the outermost and middle rectangles, wide enough to read as a surface. Identified in the open white paper of that margin along the bottom of the sheet, with clear white paper both above and below the point, touching neither the outermost rectangle nor the middle rectangle; the point is not inside the band, not inside the innermost rectangle, and not outside the outermost rectangle.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 16, 24, 30

- 16
- 24
- 30

# FIG. 5 - Second embodiment with a pulling element

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, as FIG. 1 but from further off, so several laid tiles are in frame. Outline line work. The sheet contains only the parts listed. No word, letter, digit or label appears, no border, bar, band or filled area, and nothing is drawn below the floor.

**Geometry to be drawn**

- The covering element 36 is a flat floor of a few large square tiles in perspective filling the lower part of the sheet, joined edge to edge in one plane with a straight joint line between neighbours. The floor is otherwise plain. One tile in the lower right of the sheet, in front of the device and away from the cord, is drawn large and plain, the widest open expanse on the sheet, with no joint line within it and nothing drawn across it. Identified well inside that open expanse, far from every line, and not on the device, a joint line, the ring or the cord.
- The vibration device 10 is a shallow rectangular assembly standing on a tile at the middle right of the floor, drawn as on FIG. 1: a flat slab carrying a rectangular motor housing at its left end, and at the middle of the slab an upright rectangular column with a rectangular pump housing on its top, held clear of the slab. The slab has clearly visible thickness, so its near left side face is a band of plain paper deep enough to take a point. Identified well inside that side face, clear of both its long edges, and not on the floor, the cord, the ring or either housing.
- The attachment formation 48 is one simple closed ring projecting from the left end of the slab, low on that end and touching it: a single loop of one continuous outline enclosing one opening. It is a single ring, not a chain and not a knot, and no other ring, loop or hook appears. It is drawn large, so its opening is plainly visible. Identified on the outline of that ring, and not on the slab, the cord or the floor.
- The flexible pulling element 46 is a slack cord running from that ring away to the left, sagging gently and passing off the left edge of the sheet in one unbroken sweep, without doubling back or looping. It stays in the left part of the sheet. It is drawn as one bold continuous line of even width broad enough to carry a point on the line itself, with no core line. It runs across one tile of the floor in which no joint line is drawn, so that a long stretch of the cord has plain paper on both sides of it and no other line touches or crosses it. No block, connector or arrowhead appears along it. Identified on that open stretch of the cord, where no other line touches it, clear of the ring and of the left edge of the sheet, and not on the ring, the slab, a joint line or the floor.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 10, 36, 46, 48

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10
- 36
- 46
- 48

One tile in the lower right of the sheet, in front of the device and away from the cord, is drawn large and plain, the widest open expanse on the sheet, with no joint line within it and nothing drawn across it. Identified well inside that open expanse, far from every line, and not on the device, a joint line, the ring or the cord.

# FIG. 3 - Bottom plan view of the vibration device

**View:** Plan view of the underside of the plate, with the tile removed. Outline line work only: no hatching, shading, stippling, dashed or double line, every outline one thin line. No word, digit or label appears, and no border. Each point lies well inside a surface, away from every outline and corner, and the three points are far apart.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The whole sheet contains four outlines and nothing else: from the outside inward, a large outermost rectangle with square corners, a middle rectangle within it, an innermost rectangle within that, and one circle standing clear of the sides of the innermost rectangle. Each is drawn once, as one closed line. There are three rectangles and no more: no further rectangle outside the outermost, inside the innermost or alongside any of them, and no frame surrounds the drawing. The circle is one thin closed curve with plain white paper inside it, not a ring, an annulus or a hole with a wall, and no other circle appears.

Those outlines enclose four surfaces: the margin between the outermost and middle rectangles, the band between the middle and innermost rectangles, the area inside the innermost rectangle around the circle, and the inside of the circle. The circle is drawn large in relation to the innermost rectangle, so a point sits easily inside it.

The margin and the band are each drawn as a broad corridor of open white paper of even width. The margin is the widest open run on the sheet, drawn wider than the band inside it, and the band is wide on every side of the loop, so that in either corridor a point sits with clear white paper on both sides of it, touching neither line that bounds that corridor.

Identified in the open white paper of that band along the right side of the sheet, between the middle rectangle and the innermost rectangle, clear of both of those lines and of the corners; the point is not inside the innermost rectangle nor in the margin outside the middle rectangle.
- The second side 16 is the underside surface outside the loop, the margin between the outermost and middle rectangles, wide enough to read as a surface. Identified in the open white paper of that margin along the bottom of the sheet, with clear white paper both above and below the point, touching neither the outermost rectangle nor the middle rectangle; the point is not inside the band, not inside the innermost rectangle, and not outside the outermost rectangle.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 16, 24, 30

- 16

All five sheets are addressed, and every brief is under the cap (2798, 2730, 2793, 2775, 2762).

The two "no terminal dot" failures (FIG. 1 numeral 50, FIG. 2 numeral 14) and the two rejected endpoints (FIG. 3 numeral 16, FIG. 4 numeral 26) share one cause: those four targets were drawn lines, and a dot placed on a line merges into it or slides onto a neighbouring line. Each is now an area target:

- **FIG. 1 numeral 50**: the cable is now drawn as a cord of visible thickness bounded by two lines, so the electrical supply has an interior, and the point sits well inside it between those lines rather than on a single stroke.
- **FIG. 2 numeral 14**: the first side is now marked in the open white paper directly above the slab's upper edge line, in the run to the right of the channel, so the point is in clear space and still far from the point inside the channel.
- **FIG. 3 numeral 16**: the margin between the outermost and middle rectangles is now specified as the widest open run on the sheet, and the point must have clear white paper both above and below it, touching neither rectangle.
- **FIG. 4 numeral 26**: the bearing face is now marked in the open white paper immediately below the column's foot line and directly beneath the column, with the upper band's top edge excluded by name. Clearance 34 moved to the lower reach of the same very tall gap, so the two sit in well-separated strips and neither needs a line target.
- **FIG. 5 numeral 36**: the lower right tile is now specified as the widest open expanse on the sheet with nothing drawn across it, and the covering element point sits well inside that expanse, far from every line.

I left numeral 38 in FIG. 4 and numeral 46 in FIG. 5 alone; both passed this round, so I did not disturb them. Trimming to stay under 2800 removed only wording redundancy, no geometry or relationships. The numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description and claims are unchanged, all five declarations match their sheet lists, and the 22 numerals remain distributed 8/6/3/8/4.

input.summary: Converted the four failing line-based numeral targets into broad area targets: the FIG. 1 cable is now a cord of visible thickness with an interior, FIG. 2 numeral 14 marks the open paper above the slab's upper edge, FIG. 3 numeral 16 sits in a widened margin corridor with white paper on both sides, and FIG. 4 numeral 26 sits in the open gap immediately beneath the column foot with clearance 34 moved to the lower reach of the same tall gap. FIG. 5 numeral 36 now targets the widest open tile expanse on the sheet. No application text, claim, numeral definition or figure membership changed, and every brief is under 2800 characters.
reasoning: The four findings on FIG. 1, FIG. 2, FIG. 3 and FIG. 4 are one failure mode. Every one of those targets was a drawn line: the cable stroke, the slab's upper edge, and the column foot line, with numeral 16 landing on a rectangle line. A terminal dot placed on a line either merges into the line, which reads as no dot at all, or slips onto the nearest parallel line, which is exactly what put numeral 26 on the band's top edge. So I gave each of them an area.

For the electrical supply 50 the area had to be created: the cable is now drawn as a cord of visible thickness bounded by two curved lines, which is ordinary drafting practice for a flexible lead and gives the numeral an interior to sit in. The cord is still the only curved element on the sheet, so the OCR constraint that cleared the earlier 'unexpected 00' finding is intact.

For first side 14 the face is genuinely edge on in a section and cannot be given an interior without inventing structure, so the point moved into the open white paper directly above that edge line. That keeps it pointing at the upper face while giving the dot clear space, and the run to the right of the channel keeps it far from the point inside the channel, which was the earlier ambiguity finding on this sheet.

For bearing face 26 the same reasoning applies, but the open space beneath the column already belonged to clearance 34. Rather than let the two compete, I split the very tall gap into two well-separated strips: 26 immediately below the column foot, 34 in the lower reach just above the upper band. Both points stay physically within the region the enlarged detail exists to show, and neither depends on a line.

For second side 16 the fix was width, not wording alone. The margin is now specified as the widest open run on the sheet and the point must have clear white paper above and below it, so a dot that drifts still lands in the margin rather than on the middle rectangle.

For covering element 36 on FIG. 5 the rejected cluster came from a tile surface that was competing with joint lines, the device and the cord. The lower right tile is now the widest open expanse on the sheet with nothing drawn across it, which gives the annotator a large unambiguous region.

I deliberately left numeral 38 on FIG. 4 and numeral 46 on FIG. 5 as line targets, because both were accepted in this round. Rewriting passing items risks new findings, and the evidence shows a dot can sit on a line when the line is long and isolated, which is true of the band's top edge and the cord.

Every addition was paid for by cutting wording redundancy so all five briefs stay at or below 2800 characters: duplicated exclusions, 'plain paper' where 'band' suffices, and repeated statements that a line is not crossed. No disclosed geometry or required relationship was removed, including that the column and band nowhere touch.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged. No claim, specification sentence or numeral definition was altered this turn. The distinction remains the rigid perimeter member ending in a low-friction bearing face that deliberately does not seal, together with an air-extraction mechanism whose delivered rate at the working pressure difference is at least the leakage rate through the resulting clearance at that same pressure difference, so the device is held by pressure differential yet free to slide, with an all-rigid vibration path and no resilient mount between motor and bearing face. The references teach sealing suction attachment or compliant interfaces, not a deliberately leaking rigid low-friction skirt whose leakage sets the extraction sizing. All repairs were confined to drawing geometry instructions and endpoint targets.

content.text:
All five findings are addressed, and every brief now sits well under the cap (2724, 2694, 2680, 2746, 2746).

**FIG. 1 semantic (two cords from three lines)**: the "bounded by two curved lines" wording invited the renderer to draw a second cord. The electrical supply is now specified as a single narrow strip of even width with plain paper inside it, one cord only and never a pair or a bundle, the only curving element on the sheet. It keeps an interior for the terminal dot without telling the renderer to draw a line count.

**FIG. 2 numeral 14**: the dot landed at y≈22, at the very top of the sheet, because there was almost no white paper above the slab to aim at. The three bodies are now drawn well down the sheet, leaving a broad expanse of empty paper above the slab, and the target is that expanse well clear of the upper edge line and to the right of the channel, rather than the sliver directly above the line.

**FIG. 3 semantic (margin versus band width)**: the requirement that the margin be wider than the band was an invented rendering constraint the sheet did not honour. It is removed. Both corridors are simply broad and of even width, which is all the endpoint targets need.

**FIG. 4 numeral 26**: the dot kept settling at the upper band's top edge. Rather than describe 26 by its distance below the foot line, 26 and 34 now divide the tall gap by a single complementary rule: 26 is nearer the foot of the column, 34 is nearer the top edge of the upper band, both directly beneath the column and touching no line. Each point is checkable against its own sentence and neither satisfies the other's.

**FIG. 5 numeral 36**: the lower right of the floor is now one plain tile surface, the largest unbroken area on the sheet, with no joint line, cord or other line within it, and the brief states plainly that this tile surface is part of the covering element, so a point there cannot be read as pointing at something else.

The numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description and claims are untouched; all five declarations match their sheet lists; the 22 numerals remain distributed 8/6/3/8/4.

input.summary: Repaired all five sheets in the figure briefs: removed the line-count wording that made FIG. 1 render two cords, opened a broad expanse of white paper above the slab so FIG. 2 numeral 14 has somewhere to land, dropped the unsatisfied margin-wider-than-band constraint on FIG. 3, replaced FIG. 4's distance-based wording for numerals 26 and 34 with a complementary nearer-to rule that divides the tall gap, and made the FIG. 5 lower right floor one unbroken tile surface stated to be part of the covering element. No application text, claim, numeral definition or figure membership changed; all briefs are between 2680 and 2746 characters.
reasoning: FIG. 1's semantic failure came from my own fix last turn: telling the renderer the cord was 'bounded by two curved lines' is a line-count instruction, and the image model duly produced three lines and two parallel cords. The cord still needs an interior so its leader can end in a dot, so I specified the result rather than the construction: a single narrow strip of even width with plain paper inside it, one cord only and never a pair or a bundle. That preserves the dot target and removes the instruction that caused the artifact.

FIG. 2's endpoint was at y=22, hard against the top of the sheet, which tells me the slab was drawn so high that the white paper above it was a sliver. Widening the target alone would not have helped, so I changed the composition: the three bodies sit well down the sheet with a broad expanse of empty paper above the slab, and numeral 14 now aims into that expanse well clear of the edge line rather than immediately above it.

FIG. 3's finding was a mismatch between an invented constraint and the pixels. The requirement that the margin be wider than the band served nothing: both corridors only need to be wide enough to hold a point clear of their lines. I deleted the comparison rather than fight the renderer over a proportion that no part of the disclosure calls for.

FIG. 4 numeral 26 has now failed three times with the dot at the upper band's top edge, whether the target was the foot line itself or the paper immediately below it. Both of those formulations describe a position by its small distance from a line, which is precisely what the placement engine gets wrong. So 26 and 34 now partition the whole gap by one comparative rule, 26 nearer the column foot and 34 nearer the band top edge, both beneath the column. Every point in the gap belongs to exactly one of the two, the rule is checkable by eye, and neither numeral depends on hugging a line.

FIG. 5 numeral 36's cluster kept being rejected, and the likeliest reading is that the point was landing on or beside joint lines in a floor made of several tiles. The lower right of the floor is now a single plain tile surface with no line of any kind within it, the largest unbroken area on the sheet. I also stated that this tile surface is part of the covering element, because a reviewer that treats 'a tile' and 'the covering element' as different things would reject an otherwise correct point.

All five briefs lost length rather than gained it, because the fixes replaced construction instructions with result statements. That leaves headroom under the 2800-character cap for future repairs without further trimming of disclosed geometry.

FIG. 4: bearing face 26 and clearance 34 now divide the tall gap by a complementary rule, 26 nearer the column foot and 34 nearer the upper band's top edge, both directly beneath the column and touching no line

content.text:
All flagged endpoint instructions are repaired. Summary of what changed and what I could not do myself:

**Repairs (figure briefs only, no body text touched):**
- FIG. 2, numeral 14: the disconnected target that floated the numeral in empty paper above the slab now lands on the part's own boundary, the straight upper edge line of the slab. The geometry paragraph no longer reserves deep white space above the slab for that point.
- FIG. 3, numerals 24 and 16: the sheet-coordinate targets ("along the right side of the sheet", "along the bottom of the sheet", plus the multi-clause exclusion lists) are replaced with broad interior targets, "well inside that band" and "well inside that margin", each keeping only the two bounding-line exclusions that distinguish the corridor from its neighbours. The view note's "the three points are far apart" constraint went with them.
- FIG. 4, numerals 26, 34, 38 (not flagged, same defect class, fixed pre-emptively): the "nearer the foot of the column than the top edge of the band" / "nearer the top edge than the foot" pair was arbitrary relative placement inside one white gap. Numeral 26 now sits on the short line closing the bottom of the column, which is the bearing face itself seen edge on; numeral 34 sits well inside the clearance gap, which is the part itself. Numeral 38 sits on the top edge line of the upper band with the hatching exclusion kept.

FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 needed nothing: their "middle of the slab" and "middle right of the floor" phrases describe where a body sits in the drawn geometry, not where a numeral endpoint goes, and "leftmost", "outermost", "middle", "innermost" and "right-hand" are the stable position names the request asks for.

**What I did not run:** rendering, OCR, coordinate, topology, and cross-provider gates are pipeline stages, not something I can execute from this workspace. content.content:
/home/nimrod_rotem/patent-search-pilot/data/draft_workspaces/p8/input/disclosure.md:17:The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.
/home/nimrod_rotem/patent-search-pilot/data/draft_workspaces/p8/draft/07-detailed-description.md:29:An electrical supply 50 provides power to the vibration motor 18 and, where the air-extraction mechanism 20 is electrically driven, to the air-extraction mechanism 20. In the embodiment of FIG. 1 the electrical supply 50 is a flexible cord leaving the air-extraction mechanism 20 and running to a mains or site supply; a battery carried on the base 12 may be used instead. The vibration motor 18 and the air-extraction mechanism 20 may be switched together or independently of one another.
/home/nimrod_rotem/patent-search-pilot/data/draft_workspaces/p8/draft/07-detailed-description.md:41:Because the perimeter member 24 is rigid and the exposed face 38 is neither perfectly flat nor perfectly clean, in that it carries dust, grains of bonding material 40 and its own surface texture, and the covering element 36 itself may be slightly bowed, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is far too small to be drawn to scale, and so are the departures from flatness of the exposed face 38 that give rise to it. FIG. 2 accordingly shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 without any gap, at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 appears only in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4, where it is drawn many times its true height. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22, and does so by presenting a long, narrow, high-resistance path around the whole loop, without closing that path.
/home/nimrod_rotem/patent-search-pilot/data/draft_workspaces/p8/draft/07-detailed-description.md:55:Two properties of this arrangement should be noted, because they are what the arrangement is for.
/home/nimrod_rotem/patent-search-pilot/data/draft_workspaces/p8/draft/07-detailed-description.md:77:Embodiment with a flexible pulling element
/home/nimrod_rotem/patent-search-pilot/data/draft_workspaces/p8/draft/07-detailed-description.md:79:FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10 at an attachment formation 48 on the base 12. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.
/home/nimrod_rotem/patent-search-pilot/data/draft_workspaces/p8/draft/07-detailed-description.md:81:This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 can transmit force only along its own length and, being flexible, cannot transmit compression at all. It therefore cannot press the vibration device 10 down against the covering element 36, whatever the operator does with it. Because the attachment formation 48 is placed low, as described below, the line along which the tension acts lies close to the plane of the exposed face 38. The flexible pulling element 46 is thus incapable of transmitting compression to the vibration device 10, and is arranged to apply to the vibration device 10 a pulling force substantially in the plane of the exposed face 38. # FIG. 4 - Enlarged section of the perimeter member end

**View:** Greatly enlarged fragmentary section through the lower end of a perimeter member shown in FIG. 2, where the clearance is present, with the bedded layers beneath. Outline line work, hatching on cut material. No word, digit or label appears, and no border.

**Geometry to be drawn**

One upright hatched column hangs from a fragment of hatched slab spanning the top of the sheet. That fragment carries no numeral. The column stands in the right part of the sheet, with open white paper to the left of it. Its two side lines are straight, parallel and unbroken from the slab fragment down to a short horizontal line closing its bottom, so the column keeps one even width throughout and is nowhere stepped, widened or flanged. One horizontal line crosses the column between the slab fragment and its bottom, dividing it into a tall upper part and a short lower part. The column thus has three horizontal lines, of which the short bottom line is the lowest and lies far below the other two.

Three hatched bands lie one above another across the lower part of the sheet, each spanning the full width and drawn deep, separated by one horizontal line: the upper band, the middle band and the lower band. The white gap between the column and the upper band is drawn very tall, so the bottom line of the column lies far above the top edge line of the upper band, and that top edge line has a long open run across the left part of the sheet with no column above it.

- The perimeter member 24 is the tall upper part of the column. Identified well inside the hatching of that upper part.
- The low-friction facing 28 is the short lower part of the column, below the dividing line. Identified well inside the hatching of that lower part.
- The bearing face 26 is the flat lower end face of the column, seen edge on as the short line closing the bottom of the column. Identified on that bottom line of the column, the lowest line of the column, which has open white paper directly below it, and not on either horizontal line higher up.
- The clearance 34 is the open white gap between the bottom of the column and the top edge of the upper band, so tall that column and band nowhere touch. Identified well inside that gap, touching no line.
- The covering element 36 is the upper band. Identified well inside its hatching, clear of its edge lines.
- The exposed face 38 is the top edge line of the upper band, where the white gap above meets the hatching below. Identified on that top edge line in its open run to the left of the column, and never inside the hatching beneath it.
- The bonding material 40 is the middle band. Identified well inside its hatching, clear of the lines above and below it.
- The substrate 42 is the lower band. Identified well inside its hatching, clear of both of its edge lines.

- The covering element 36 is a flat floor of a few large square tiles in perspective filling the lower part of the sheet, joined edge to edge in one plane with a straight joint line between neighbours. The floor is otherwise plain. The lower right part of the floor, in front of the device and away from the cord, is one plain tile surface: the largest unbroken area on the sheet, with no joint line, cord or other line anywhere within it. That tile surface is part of the covering element itself. Identified well inside that unbroken area, far from every line and from the device.
- The vibration device 10 is a shallow rectangular assembly standing on a tile at the middle right of the floor, drawn as on FIG. 1: a flat slab carrying a rectangular motor housing at its left end, and at the middle of the slab an upright rectangular column with a rectangular pump housing on its top, held clear of the slab. The slab has clearly visible thickness, so its near left side face is a band deep enough to take a point. Identified well inside that side face, clear of both its long edges, and not on the floor, the cord, the ring or either housing.
- The attachment formation 48 is one simple closed ring projecting from the left end of the slab, low on that end and touching it: a single loop of one continuous outline enclosing one opening. Identified on the outline of that ring, and not on the slab, the cord or the floor.

Identified well inside that strip, in its open stretch clear of the ring and of the left edge of the sheet, and not on the slab, a joint line or the floor.

import re, glob, os

os.chdir(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), '..'))
tbl = {}
for line in open('draft/numerals.md'):
    m = re.match(r'\|\s*(\d+)\s*\|\s*(.+?)\s*\|', line)
    if m:
        tbl[m.group(1)] = m.group(2)
used = set()
for f in sorted(glob.glob('figures/*.md')):
    txt = open(f).read()
    lst = re.search(r'\*\*Numerals appearing on this figure:\*\*(.*)', txt).group(1)
    nums = set(re.findall(r'\d+', lst))
    head = txt.split('**Numerals appearing')[0]
    bullets = set(re.findall(r'\b(\d{2})\b', head))
    tail = set(re.findall(r'-\s*(\d+)', txt.split('## Numerals shown on this figure')[1]))
    used |= nums
    print(os.path.basename(f)[:12], len(txt), sorted(nums, key=int),
          'body diff:', sorted(bullets ^ nums, key=int), 'tail diff:', sorted(tail ^ nums, key=int))
print('in table, on no sheet:', sorted(set(tbl) - used, key=int))
print('on a sheet, not in table:', sorted(used - set(tbl), key=int))
desc = open('draft/07-detailed-description.md').read()
print('table numerals missing from description:',
      sorted([n for n in tbl if not re.search(r'\b%s\b' % n, desc)], key=int))

content.text:
All five flagged sheets are repaired at the brief level, and every brief is back under the length limit.

**FIG. 1** (semantic: cable drawn with three parallel lines, cord leaving the wrong face): the cord is now specified as a strip bounded by exactly two lines with plain white paper between them and no third line along or inside it, so a two-conductor rendering is ruled out. The "rear face" exit was an invented rendering constraint, not something the description requires; §07 says only that the cord leaves the air-extraction mechanism. The brief now has it leave the left-hand face of the upper block, which is visible in this view and is what the leader can reach.

**FIG. 2** (numeral 14 anchor 10 units from the sheet boundary): the slab now stops well short of the left and right sheet edges, so its whole upper edge line sits well inside the drawing area, and the endpoint for the first side is on that line clear of both of its ends.

**FIG. 3** (numeral 16 in a rejected coordinate cluster): the margin between the outermost and middle rectangles is now the wider of the two corridors, the outermost rectangle stops short of the sheet edges, and the endpoint is a broad interior target described by which side of each bounding rectangle it falls on.

**FIG. 4** (numeral 26 landing on the flange/web line of a T-shaped column, numeral 38 converging with it): the column is now specified with parallel unbroken side lines and one even width, nowhere stepped, widened or flanged, so no T forms below the slab fragment. Numeral 26 targets the lowest line of the column, the one with open white paper directly below it, and explicitly not either horizontal line higher up. The column stands in the right part of the sheet, giving the upper band's top edge a long open run to the left where numeral 38 lands, away from the column foot.

**FIG. 5** (numeral 46 leader with no terminal dot): the pulling element was a single bold stroke with no interior. It is now a strip bounded by two lines with white paper between them, broad enough for the endpoint to sit well inside it.

To fit the 2800-character limit after these additions I removed redundant wording only, not geometry or relationships: FIG. 4 lost a sentence restating the three-line count that its numeral 26 bullet already carries, and FIG. 5 lost a duplicate exclusion list on numeral 46.

Unchanged: the claims, the detailed description, the drawing descriptions, the numeral table, and the numeral list on every sheet. The union of the five sheets still covers all 22 table entries exactly.

input.summary: Repaired all five sheets flagged by the geometry, leader, and OCR gate, working only in the figure briefs. FIG. 1: the electrical supply is now specified as a strip bounded by exactly two lines with plain white paper between them and no third line along or inside it, which rules out the two-conductor cable the renderer drew, and the cord now leaves the left-hand face of the upper block instead of the rear face, since the detailed description requires only that it leave the air-extraction mechanism and the rear face is not visible in this view. FIG. 2: the slab now stops well short of the left and right sheet edges so the whole upper edge line lies well inside the drawing area, and numeral 14 is placed on that line clear of both ends, which cures the ungrounded anchor 10 units from the boundary. FIG. 3: the margin is now the wider of the two corridors, the outermost rectangle stops short of the sheet edges, and numeral 16 has a broad interior target defined by which side of each bounding rectangle it falls on. FIG. 4: the column is specified with straight parallel unbroken side lines and one even width, nowhere stepped, widened or flanged, so it forms no T shape whose flange line could capture numeral 26; numeral 26 now targets the lowest line of the column, the one with open white paper directly below it, and expressly not either horizontal line higher up; the column stands in the right part of the sheet so the upper band top edge has a long open run to the left where numeral 38 lands, away from the column foot. FIG. 5: the pulling element is now a strip bounded by two lines with white paper between them, broad enough for a terminal dot to sit well inside it, replacing the single bold stroke that gave the leader nothing to terminate in. All five briefs were then trimmed back under the 2800 character limit by removing redundant wording only. The claims, detailed description, drawing descriptions, numeral table, and per sheet numeral lists are unchanged, and the five sheets still cover all 22 table entries exactly.
reasoning: The FIG. 1 cable finding had two halves and they needed opposite treatments. The three-parallel-lines rendering was a real drawing defect, so I tightened the brief to bound the cord with exactly two lines and forbid any third line along or inside it, which is the same construction FIG. 1 already used successfully elsewhere. The rear-face exit, by contrast, was a constraint the brief had invented: the detailed description says only that the cord leaves the air-extraction mechanism and runs to a mains or site supply, and in a view taken from above and to the front left the rear face is hidden, so demanding it there could only ever produce a defect. I moved the exit to a visible face rather than fight the renderer over a detail the specification does not fix.

FIG. 2's anchor was ungrounded because the slab ran nearly the full sheet width, so the upper edge line reached the paper edge and the endpoint had nowhere to sit inside the drawing area. The cure belongs in the composition, not the endpoint: the slab now stops short of both side edges. That keeps numeral 14 on the part's own boundary, which is what the first side is, rather than pushing it back into open paper.

FIG. 4 was the substantive one. The reviewer's coordinates showed the leader landing on the line between what it read as a flange and a web, which is the junction where the slab fragment meets the column, so the renderer was producing an inverted T and the brief never forbade it. I fixed the geometry rather than the label: parallel unbroken side lines, one even width, nowhere stepped or flanged. Numeral 26 is then identified by a property no other line on the column has, being the lowest line with open white paper directly below it, which is exactly what a bearing face facing a gap is.

For the 38 and 26 convergence I re-added a disambiguator I had removed last turn. The rule permits a locating modifier where it is necessary to tell the intended part from another visible part, and here two horizontal lines separated only by the exaggerated clearance were being resolved to the same anchor. Putting the column in the right part of the sheet gives the upper band top edge a long run with nothing above it, so numeral 38 has somewhere unambiguous to land without touching the clearance or the column foot.

FIG. 5's missing terminal dot was a consequence of drawing the cord as one bold stroke with no interior, so there was no enclosed area for the endpoint marker. Giving the cord two bounding lines and white paper between them is ordinary patent draughting for a rope or cable and matches how FIG. 1 already draws the electrical supply, so it costs nothing in accuracy. The disclosure calls the pulling element a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible element, none of which is contradicted by showing its thickness.

Three briefs went over the 2800 character limit once the new constraints were in, so I cut only redundancy: a sentence in FIG. 4 that restated the three-line count already carried in the numeral 26 bullet, a duplicate exclusion list on FIG. 5's numeral 46 whose work is done by 'well inside that strip', and a few doubled phrasings. No geometry, relationship, or numeral was dropped to make room, and no numeral moved between sheets, so the drawing descriptions and the numeral table needed no edit.
