input.summary: Four sheets are repaired and one focused sheet was added. FIG. 1 had five ungrounded anchors because a perspective overview carrying eight numerals gives small bodies and thin faces to point into. Rather than delete any part or numeral, the equipment labels were redistributed to a new FIG. 6, a side elevation of the vibration motor, the fasteners, the duct and the air-extraction mechanism drawn as large plain rectangles with broad empty interiors. FIG. 1 keeps the whole machine drawn large, with the slab, the motor housing, the column and the pump housing still drawn but unnumbered there, and now carries only the vibration device 10 on its outer silhouette, the handle 44 on its cross bar, and the electrical supply 50 inside its cord, all targets that have grounded before. FIG. 3: the requirement that the band be of even width was contradicted by the rendered corridors, so that invented constraint is gone; both corridors are now required to be deep across the top and the bottom of the drawing, and the two labels are taken to the upper run of the band for 24 and the lower run of the margin for 16, which keeps them far apart as well as inside wide paper. FIG. 4: numeral 26 is a face seen edge on, so the sheet was rebuilt around it. The column is drawn very broad so its bottom line is long, the upper and lower parts of it are drawn deep and hatched in opposite directions as different materials, and the bearing face is described as the long line closing the bottom with the lower hatching directly above and the open gap directly below. FIG. 5: numeral 46 is now taken to the upper of the two long lines of the cord, which is a line target of the kind that has grounded on other sheets, and the cord is required to be a broad strip. The device 10 target on that sheet was also moved from the thin slab side face to the assembly silhouette, the same target that works on FIG. 1, since the thin-band anchor is what failed on FIG. 1. Everything outside figures/ was changed only to stay in step: FIG. 6 was added to the Brief Description of the Drawings, and the four sentences that attributed the fasteners, the motor housing, the duct or the pump to FIG. 1 now cite FIG. 6, with the handle and cord sentences reworded so each figure reference names only parts that sheet lists. No claim, no numeral definition, and no embodiment changed. All twenty-two numerals remain covered, no sheet carries more than eight, and every brief is between 2002 and 2713 characters.
reasoning: The FIG. 1 failures were a density problem, not a wording problem: five of eight anchors had between 1.1 and 16.2 units of clearance, which no rephrasing of an endpoint can cure when the underlying faces are small. Redistribution is the sanctioned remedy, so the equipment labels moved to a sheet whose whole purpose is to show those four parts at a size that gives each a broad interior.

A side elevation was chosen for the new sheet rather than another perspective because elevation projects each housing as a plain rectangle with a large empty interior, which is the geometry the grounding check wants. The bodies are specified as standing clear of one another with open paper between, so no anchor sits near a neighbouring outline.

Nothing was deleted to achieve this. The motor, duct, pump and bolt heads are still drawn on FIG. 1; they simply carry their numerals on FIG. 6 now. Every part, numeral definition, and paragraph of the description survives, which is what the coverage rule requires.

FIG. 6 is drawn to obey the description rather than the other way round: because the specification says the vibration motor housing is wider along the long edge of the base than it is tall, the motor rectangle is specified as wider than tall, and because the duct is described as an upright column carrying the pump on its upper end, the duct rectangle is taller than wide with the pump resting on its top.

The FIG. 3 finding was that the band's top and bottom runs are wider than its left and right runs, which contradicted the even-width wording. Even width was an invented rendering constraint, so it went, and the endpoints followed the geometry that the renderer actually produces: the upper run of the band and the lower run of the margin are the deep stretches, and choosing one of each also preserves the wide separation that fixed the earlier convergence failure between these same two numerals.

For numeral 26 on FIG. 4 the target cannot honestly move, since the bearing face is the surface that contacts the exposed face and appears in section as a line. So the geometry around it was changed instead: a very broad column makes that line long, deep upper and lower parts move the neighbouring dividing line away, and opposed hatching directions, which is ordinary practice for two different materials and is supported by the description of a PTFE facing on a metal loop, give the line a high-contrast boundary on the hatched side and the tall open clearance on the other.

On FIG. 5 the cord interior kept being rejected, so the anchor moved to one of the cord's own long lines. Line anchors on this application have grounded reliably, on the handle cross bar, the assembly silhouette, and the band edges in FIG. 4, so this is the target type with the best record here.

The device 10 anchor on FIG. 5 was changed although it was not flagged, because it is the same thin slab side face that failed with 1.1 units on FIG. 1. Fixing it now avoids spending a cycle on a defect already demonstrated on the other sheet.

The description edits were kept to the minimum needed to obey the rule that a part described as visible in a figure must be listed on that figure. Four figure citations moved from FIG. 1 to FIG. 6, and two sentences that mentioned the motor and the pump as landmarks in FIG. 1 were reworded to name only parts that FIG. 1 still lists. No substantive statement about the invention changed.

structured_output.summary: Four sheets are repaired and one focused sheet was added. FIG. 1 had five ungrounded anchors because a perspective overview carrying eight numerals gives small bodies and thin faces to point into. Rather than delete any part or numeral, the equipment labels were redistributed to a new FIG. 6, a side elevation of the vibration motor, the fasteners, the duct and the air-extraction mechanism drawn as large plain rectangles with broad empty interiors. FIG. 1 keeps the whole machine drawn large, with the slab, the motor housing, the column and the pump housing still drawn but unnumbered there, and now carries only the vibration device 10 on its outer silhouette, the handle 44 on its cross bar, and the electrical supply 50 inside its cord, all targets that have grounded before. FIG. 3: the requirement that the band be of even width was contradicted by the rendered corridors, so that invented constraint is gone; both corridors are now required to be deep across the top and the bottom of the drawing, and the two labels are taken to the upper run of the band for 24 and the lower run of the margin for 16, which keeps them far apart as well as inside wide paper. FIG. 4: numeral 26 is a face seen edge on, so the sheet was rebuilt around it. The column is drawn very broad so its bottom line is long, the upper and lower parts of it are drawn deep and hatched in opposite directions as different materials, and the bearing face is described as the long line closing the bottom with the lower hatching directly above and the open gap directly below. FIG. 5: numeral 46 is now taken to the upper of the two long lines of the cord, which is a line target of the kind that has grounded on other sheets, and the cord is required to be a broad strip. The device 10 target on that sheet was also moved from the thin slab side face to the assembly silhouette, the same target that works on FIG. 1, since the thin-band anchor is what failed on FIG. 1. Everything outside figures/ was changed only to stay in step: FIG. 6 was added to the Brief Description of the Drawings, and the four sentences that attributed the fasteners, the motor housing, the duct or the pump to FIG. 1 now cite FIG. 6, with the handle and cord sentences reworded so each figure reference names only parts that sheet lists. No claim, no numeral definition, and no embodiment changed. All twenty-two numerals remain covered, no sheet carries more than eight, and every brief is between 2002 and 2713 characters.
reasoning: The FIG. 1 failures were a density problem, not a wording problem: five of eight anchors had between 1.1 and 16.2 units of clearance, which no rephrasing of an endpoint can cure when the underlying faces are small. Redistribution is the sanctioned remedy, so the equipment labels moved to a sheet whose whole purpose is to show those four parts at a size that gives each a broad interior.

A side elevation was chosen for the new sheet rather than another perspective because elevation projects each housing as a plain rectangle with a large empty interior, which is the geometry the grounding check wants. The bodies are specified as standing clear of one another with open paper between, so no anchor sits near a neighbouring outline.

Nothing was deleted to achieve this. The motor, duct, pump and bolt heads are still drawn on FIG. 1; they simply carry their numerals on FIG. 6 now. Every part, numeral definition, and paragraph of the description survives, which is what the coverage rule requires.

FIG. 6 is drawn to obey the description rather than the other way round: because the specification says the vibration motor housing is wider along the long edge of the base than it is tall, the motor rectangle is specified as wider than tall, and because the duct is described as an upright column carrying the pump on its upper end, the duct rectangle is taller than wide with the pump resting on its top.

The FIG. 3 finding was that the band's top and bottom runs are wider than its left and right runs, which contradicted the even-width wording. Even width was an invented rendering constraint, so it went, and the endpoints followed the geometry that the renderer actually produces: the upper run of the band and the lower run of the margin are the deep stretches, and choosing one of each also preserves the wide separation that fixed the earlier convergence failure between these same two numerals.

For numeral 26 on FIG. 4 the target cannot honestly move, since the bearing face is the surface that contacts the exposed face and appears in section as a line. So the geometry around it was changed instead: a very broad column makes that line long, deep upper and lower parts move the neighbouring dividing line away, and opposed hatching directions, which is ordinary practice for two different materials and is supported by the description of a PTFE facing on a metal loop, give the line a high-contrast boundary on the hatched side and the tall open clearance on the other.

On FIG. 5 the cord interior kept being rejected, so the anchor moved to one of the cord's own long lines. Line anchors on this application have grounded reliably, on the handle cross bar, the assembly silhouette, and the band edges in FIG. 4, so this is the target type with the best record here.

The device 10 anchor on FIG. 5 was changed although it was not flagged, because it is the same thin slab side face that failed with 1.1 units on FIG. 1. Fixing it now avoids spending a cycle on a defect already demonstrated on the other sheet.

The description edits were kept to the minimum needed to obey the rule that a part described as visible in a figure must be listed on that figure. Four figure citations moved from FIG. 1 to FIG. 6, and two sentences that mentioned the motor and the pump as landmarks in FIG. 1 were reworded to name only parts that FIG. 1 still lists. No substantive statement about the invention changed.

# FIG. 1 - Perspective view of the vibration device in use

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, onto one large plain tile. Outline line work, no shading or hatching. Every body except the cord has flat faces and straight edges. No text of any kind appears, and no border. No circle, ring, disc, hole or ellipse appears anywhere on the sheet.

**Geometry to be drawn**

A large plain tile fills the lower part of the sheet, with no joint line and no other tile, and carries no numeral. The machine standing on it is drawn large, filling much of the sheet, and each of its bodies is drawn large, with plain faces and open white paper between neighbours.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole machine, the slab together with every body standing on it, drawn with one continuous outer silhouette. Identified on that continuous outer silhouette.
- The base 12 is the flat slab the other bodies stand on, and the only slab of the machine, the tile beneath being the surface it rests on. It is drawn deep in thickness, so its near front side face is a tall band running the whole length of the machine, with nothing standing in front of it. Identified well inside that front side face.
- The vibration motor 18 is a large rectangular housing standing on the slab at its left end. Identified well inside its flat front face.
- The fasteners 54 are square bolt heads standing on the top of the slab along the near foot of the motor housing, spaced apart, each drawn large with a broad flat front face. Identified well inside the front face of the leftmost head.
- The duct 32 is an upright rectangular column rising from the slab at the right of the motor housing, drawn broad, with open paper between it and that housing. Identified well inside its flat front face.
- The air-extraction mechanism 20 is a large rectangular housing resting on the flat top of that column, wider than the column and touching the slab nowhere. Identified well inside its flat front face.
- The handle 44 is a bail at the right end of the slab, clear of both housings and the column: an upright on each long edge and a cross bar joining their tops, open paper beneath. Identified on the cross bar, clear of both uprights.
- The electrical supply 50 is the one flexible cord on the sheet: a strip of even width bounded by two long lines with plain white paper between them, so that it reads as one cord. It is the only curving element drawn. It leaves the left-hand face of the upper housing and runs away to the left, clear of the machine and off the left edge of the sheet. Identified well inside that strip, clear of both of its long lines.

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, onto one large plain tile. Outline line work, no shading or hatching. Every body except the cord has flat faces and straight edges. input.summary: The check reported that FIG. 1's numeral declaration was missing 12, 18, 20, 32 and 54 relative to that sheet's numeral list. The workspace state confirms the five-sheet plan with those eight numerals on FIG. 1: the sixth sheet added last turn is no longer present in figures/, FIG. 1's sheet list carries all eight numerals, and the Brief Description of the Drawings and the detailed description again reference only FIG. 1 through FIG. 5. FIG. 1's brief is rewritten to that plan. Its declaration and its sheet list both read 10, 12, 18, 20, 32, 44, 50, 54, and the geometry now gives every one of those eight a named target: the vibration device 10 on the continuous outer silhouette, the base 12 well inside a front side face that is specified as a tall band running the whole length of the machine with nothing standing in front of it, the vibration motor 18 and the air-extraction mechanism 20 well inside the flat front faces of large rectangular housings, the duct 32 well inside the flat front face of a broad upright column separated from the motor housing by open paper, the fasteners 54 well inside the broad flat front face of the leftmost bolt head, the handle 44 on the cross bar, and the electrical supply 50 well inside its cord. The sheet is also specified to draw the machine and each of its bodies large with open white paper between neighbours, which is what gives those anchors room. The brief is 2702 characters. Nothing else changed: the numeral table, the claims, the detailed description, the drawing descriptions, and the briefs for FIG. 2 through FIG. 5 are as they stand, with the repairs from earlier turns intact, including the opposed hatching and tall clearance on FIG. 4, the upper-run and lower-run separation on FIG. 3, and the cord line anchor and silhouette anchor on FIG. 5. All twenty-two numerals are covered across the five sheets, and no sheet carries more than eight.
reasoning: The mismatch was between the two numeral sections of one file, so it could be resolved in either direction. I resolved it toward the eight-numeral sheet list because that is the plan the workspace holds: the sixth sheet is gone from figures/, and the specification text in the workspace cites only five figures. Declaring three numerals against a sheet list of eight would have left the same file inconsistent.

Because the equipment numerals are back on FIG. 1, each of them needed a target sentence again; a declared numeral with no described target leaves the annotation step with nowhere to point. So every one of the eight has an explicit target on a named part.

The targets were chosen to give the anchors as much room as this view allows, since the earlier grounding trouble on this sheet came from small faces. The bodies are specified as large with open paper between them, the base's front side face is specified as a tall band running the whole length with nothing in front of it, the duct is broad and separated from the motor housing, and the bolt heads are large with broad front faces.

1	# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)
2	
3	This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.
4	
5	The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.
6	
7	Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.
8	
9	Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.
10	
11	The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.
12	
13	Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.
14	
15	Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.
16	
17	The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)

This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.

The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.

Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.

Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.

The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.

Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.

The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

# FIG. 1 - Perspective view of the vibration device in use

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, onto one large plain tile. Outline line work, no shading or hatching. Every body except the cord has flat faces and straight edges. No text of any kind appears, and no border. No circle, ring, disc, hole or ellipse appears anywhere on the sheet.

**Geometry to be drawn**

A large plain tile fills the lower part of the sheet, with no joint line and no other tile, and carries no numeral. The machine standing on it is drawn large, and so is each of its bodies, with open white paper between neighbours.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole machine, the slab together with every body standing on it, drawn with one continuous outer silhouette. Identified on that continuous outer silhouette.
- The base 12 is the flat slab the other bodies stand on, and the only slab of the machine; the tile beneath is the surface it rests on. It is drawn deep in thickness, so its near front side face is a tall band running the whole length of the machine, with nothing in front of it. Identified well inside that front side face.
- The vibration motor 18 is a large rectangular housing standing on the slab at its left end. Identified well inside its flat front face.
- The fasteners 54 are square bolt heads standing on the top of the slab along the near foot of the motor housing, spaced apart, each drawn large with a broad flat front face. Identified well inside the front face of the leftmost head.
- The duct 32 is an upright rectangular column rising from the slab at the right of the motor housing, drawn broad, with open paper between it and that housing. Identified well inside its flat front face.
- The air-extraction mechanism 20 is a large rectangular housing resting on the flat top of that column, wider than the column and touching the slab nowhere. Identified well inside its flat front face.
- The handle 44 is a bail at the right end of the slab, clear of both housings and the column: an upright on each long edge and a cross bar joining their tops, open paper beneath. Identified on the cross bar, clear of both uprights.
- The electrical supply 50 is the one flexible cord on the sheet: a strip of even width bounded by two long lines with plain white paper between them, so that it reads as one cord. It is the only curving element drawn. It leaves the left-hand face of the upper housing and runs off the left edge of the sheet, clear of the machine. Identified well inside that strip, clear of both of its long lines.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 10, 12, 18, 20, 32, 44, 50, 54

input.summary: Repaired the figure briefs the preflight flagged (FIG. 1, FIG. 2, FIG. 5), replacing blanket shape exclusions, background-control instructions, and stroke-count wording with positive, disclosure-grounded geometry, and moving the two stroke-count-based numeral endpoints to broad interiors. The nine application sections, the claims, the 22-entry numeral table, the five-figure plan, and FIG. 3 and FIG. 4 (which the preflight passed) are unchanged. I cannot myself execute the rendering, OCR, coordinate, topology, cross-provider, or publish stages of the pipeline; those run on the returned turn. What I can verify from the files is done: every brief is under 2800 characters, each brief's listed numerals match those used in its body, the union across the five sheets is exactly the 22 table entries, no sheet carries more than eight numerals, and draft/ and figures/ contain no note, placeholder, question, or person-directed instruction.
reasoning: The preflight objection to FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 was blanket shape exclusion ('No circle, ring, disc, hole or ellipse appears anywhere on the sheet'). Deleting it outright would have let the renderer round off bodies that the specification describes as flat-faced, so I replaced it with the positive equivalent already implied by the disclosure: in FIG. 1 the existing sentence that every body except the cord has flat faces and straight edges now carries that work alone, and in FIG. 2 I added the same positive statement. The constraint survives; the blanket negative does not.

FIG. 1's tile carried an arbitrary background exclusion ('with no joint line and no other tile'). The single-tile framing is what the brief needs, so the sentence now states it positively as one large plain tile surface filling the lower part of the sheet, and the exclusion of joint lines and neighbouring tiles is gone. FIG. 5 still shows several tiles with joint lines, which is what its own brief requires, so nothing there had to move.

The stroke-count wording ('bounded by two long lines') appeared in FIG. 1 for the electrical supply 50, in FIG. 2 for the extraction opening 30, and in FIG. 5 for the flexible pulling element 46. In each place the point was that the part reads as a body with open interior rather than a single stroke, so the briefs now say the cord is a strip of even width with plain white paper along its interior reading as a single cord, and the channel has straight parallel upright sides with white paper running the whole depth of the slab within it. No line count is dictated.

Two numeral endpoints depended on that line count and are now broad interiors: electrical supply 50 in FIG. 1 was 'clear of both of its long lines' and is now simply well inside the strip; flexible pulling element 46 in FIG. 5 was 'on the upper of the two long lines of that cord' and is now well inside the strip, clear of the ring. The ring disambiguation is kept because the cord and the attachment formation 48 touch, so an endpoint near the join could land on the wrong part.

FIG. 5 also placed the vibration device 10 'at the middle right of the floor' with the column 'at the middle of the slab'. The column position is not a disclosed proportion, so it is now stated the way FIG. 1 already states it, on the slab to the right of the motor housing, and the device stands in the right part of the floor. This removes a mid-width constraint without changing any depicted relationship.

I removed two further same-class negatives from FIG. 5 that the preflight had not yet reached but that would fail the same rules on the next pass: 'no border, bar, band or filled area, and nothing is drawn below the floor' in the view line, and 'not a chain or knot, and no other ring or hook appears' for the attachment formation 48. Both parts keep their positive identity: outline line work with no shading or hatching, and one single closed loop of continuous outline enclosing one opening, drawn large enough that the opening is visible.

I deliberately left FIG. 3 and FIG. 4 alone. FIG. 3's 'not a ring, an annulus or a hole with a wall, and no other circle appears' is scoped to the one drawn circle and states what the extraction opening 30 is, not a sheet-wide prohibition, and it is the only thing preventing the opening from rendering as an annulus that a leader could land in the wall of. FIG. 3's outermost, middle and innermost rectangle naming and FIG. 4's bearing-face endpoint on the full bottom boundary line already satisfy this turn's requirements. Both sheets passed the preflight, so rewriting them would risk certified geometry for nothing.
No finding in the review was mistaken and none was left unaddressed. The review reported only the preflight failure, and every item it listed is now gone from the briefs.

Nothing in the specification changed, so no claim support moved. The specification's use of 'centre' in the detailed description of the extraction opening 30 is descriptive text about the embodiment, not a numeral endpoint instruction in a figure brief, and the request's prohibition is directed at the latter.
changes: figures/FIG-1-PERSPECTIVE-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE-IN-USE.md: removed the sheet-wide 'No circle, ring, disc, hole or ellipse' exclusion from the view line, leaving the positive flat-face statement to carry it.
figures/FIG-1-PERSPECTIVE-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE-IN-USE.md: replaced 'with no joint line and no other tile' with a positive single plain tile surface filling the lower part of the sheet.

figures/FIG-1-PERSPECTIVE-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE-IN-USE.md: electrical supply 50 is now a slender strip of even width with plain white paper along its interior, and its endpoint is well inside that strip rather than clear of two named lines.

figures/FIG-2-VERTICAL-SECTION-THROUGH-THE-CHAMBER.md: replaced the sheet-wide 'No circle, ring, roundel or ellipse' exclusion with the positive statement that every body is drawn with straight edges and flat faces.

figures/FIG-2-VERTICAL-SECTION-THROUGH-THE-CHAMBER.md: the channel through the slab now reads as a broad run of open white paper within the hatching, and extraction opening 30 is described by its straight parallel upright sides rather than by two bounding lines.

figures/FIG-5-SECOND-EMBODIMENT-WITH-A-PULLING-ELEMENT.md: view line simplified to outline line work with no shading or hatching, no text and no border, dropping the bar, band, filled area and below-the-floor exclusions.

figures/FIG-5-SECOND-EMBODIMENT-WITH-A-PULLING-ELEMENT.md: vibration device 10 stands in the right part of the floor with the column on the slab to the right of the motor housing, replacing the two mid-width placements.
figures/FIG-5-SECOND-EMBODIMENT-WITH-A-PULLING-ELEMENT.md: attachment formation 48 keeps its single closed loop description without the chain, knot, ring and hook exclusions.

figures/FIG-5-SECOND-EMBODIMENT-WITH-A-PULLING-ELEMENT.md: flexible pulling element 46 is a broad strip of even width with plain white paper along its interior, joint lines stop at the side of the cord, and its endpoint is well inside the strip, clear of the ring.
input.prior_art_strategy: No claim was touched this turn, so the standing position is unchanged. Claim 1 rests on a combination none of the five references discloses: a rigid perimeter member that deliberately does not seal, leaving a clearance along at least part of its length through which ambient air keeps entering, with the air-extraction mechanism sized to hold the chamber below atmospheric pressure against that continuing inflow, so the bearing face stays slidable over the covering element while the pressure differential holds. The vacuum gripping references, [REF:US-11408462-B2], [REF:US-11247858-B2] and [REF:DE-202021002652-U1], all work toward a sealed or flexible-sealed attachment that fixes the device at one place, which is the opposite of the sliding, leaking interface recited here; [REF:US-10001245-B2] couples an end effector to a structure rather than driving vibration through the contact; and [REF:US-4934475-A] moves along a wall by suction adhesion using its own traction arrangement, not by a low-friction rigid rim left free to slide. The second limitation that carries the claim is the all-rigid vibration transmission path from motor through base and perimeter member to the bearing face with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed, which is what makes the deliberate leak worth having, and which the suction-cup and flexible-seal art teaches away from because its seals are the very compliant elements excluded. The Background sets out the technical problem, damping by flexible seals and the operator pressure that stronger coupling demands, before it is needed.

The three stroke-count descriptions are gone: the electrical supply 50, the extraction opening 30 and the flexible pulling element 46 are each described by their own positive geometry, a strip or channel of even width with plain white paper along its interior. The two endpoints that hung on those line counts now sit in broad interiors, and the two mid-width placements in FIG. 5 are restated as left and right relationships that match FIG. 1. I also cleared the same class of negative wording from FIG. 5's view line and from the attachment formation 48, since it would fail the same rules on the next pass. FIG. 3 and FIG. 4 passed the preflight and are untouched; FIG. 3's statement that the extraction opening is a plain closed curve and not an annulus is scoped to that one part and is what keeps a leader from landing in a wall that should not exist, so removing it would trade a passing sheet for a new defect. The invention, all nine sections, the claims, the numeral table and the five-figure plan are unchanged. Rendering and the OCR, coordinate, topology and cross-provider gates run outside these files; from the files themselves, every brief is under 2800 characters, each sheet's listed numerals match its body and stay within eight, the five sheets together use exactly the 22 table entries, and draft/ and figures/ contain no note, placeholder, question or instruction to a person.

1	# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)
2	
3	This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.
4	
5	The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.
6	
7	Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.
8	
9	Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.
10	
11	The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.
12	
13	Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.
14	
15	Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.
16	
17	The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.

The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.

Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.

The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

input.summary: Repaired the two figure briefs the preflight flagged (FIG. 1 and FIG. 5), which both defined a flexible cord as a white-interior strip of even width, the exact multi-stroke construction the cord check rejects. Each is now specified as one single curved path of even thickness, and the numeral endpoint targets that path rather than a strip interior. No other figure brief, and no part of the application text, needed a change: a scan of all five briefs for the endpoint patterns listed in the request (center/centre, midpoint, mid-height, mid-width, mid-depth, halfway, quarter, topmost, near-end, toward-end, ambiguous shape ordinals) found only the canonical part names "first side 14" and "second side 16" and the FIG. 5 title word "second", none of which is a shape ordinal or an endpoint coordinate, so those were left alone. All existing endpoints already use broad interiors ("well inside its hatching"), full boundaries ("on that upper edge line"), or stable position names (leftmost, outermost, middle, innermost, upper run, lower run). Verified after editing: all nine draft sections intact, cross-reference still reads "Not applicable.", every numeral used in text or on a sheet appears exactly once in draft/numerals.md, no sheet lists more than eight numerals, every brief is under the 2800 character limit, all five citation keys match prior_art/INDEX.md and appear only in the Background, and no placeholder, note, question, or em dash appears anywhere in draft/ or figures/. I could not execute the render, OCR, semantic, coordinate, topology, or cross-provider gates or the publish step from here: this workspace exposes only tools/patent_lookup.py, so the pipeline has to run those passes; the briefs are in the state those gates require.
reasoning: The preflight failure was a drawing-specification defect, not a substantive one, so the invention, claims, numeral table, and all nine sections were left untouched. A cord described as 'a slender strip of even width with plain white paper along its interior' asks the geometry model for two outline strokes with fill between them, which is why the check called it an ambiguous multi-stroke cord; the fix is to specify the cord as a single curved path, which is one stroke by construction.

FIG. 1: the electrical supply 50 is now 'a single curved path of even thickness and the only curving element on the sheet', leaving the left-hand face of the upper housing in one unbroken curve off the left edge. Its endpoint targets the curved path where it runs over open paper clear of the machine, which is a broad stretch of the part rather than a coordinate.

FIG. 5: the flexible pulling element 46 is likewise one curved path, sagging gently from the attachment formation ring off the left edge without doubling back or crossing itself. The occlusion instruction was kept because it is what makes the cord read as lying on the floor rather than under it, but it now speaks of joint lines stopping at the side of the path, not at the side of a strip. Its endpoint targets the path over the floor, clear of the ring, so the numeral cannot land on the attachment formation 48 next to it.

Left deliberately in place: the FIG. 1 endpoint 'on the cross bar, clear of both uprights' for the handle 44 and the FIG. 3 'upper run' and 'lower run' endpoints. These are not arbitrary aesthetic coordinates; the handle qualifier is needed to keep the numeral off the uprights of the same bail, and the run names are stable positions of the two corridors that distinguish the perimeter member 24 band from the second side 16 margin.

Left alone as a false positive risk rather than editing good text: 'first side 14' and 'second side 16' are the canonical part names carried through the specification and claims. Renaming them in the briefs to dodge a word match would break numeral-to-part consistency across the drawings, the Detailed Description, and draft/numerals.md, which is a real defect in exchange for a cosmetic one.

figures/FIG-5-SECOND-EMBODIMENT-WITH-A-PULLING-ELEMENT.md: the flexible pulling element 46 is respecified as one single curved path of even thickness instead of a broad strip with a white interior, the occlusion instruction now refers to the path rather than the strip, and its numeral endpoint targets that path over the floor clear of the ring.
input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged this turn: no claim, description, or citation was touched. The claims continue to rest on the rigid, deliberately non-sealing perimeter member whose low-friction bearing face slides on the covering element while the air-extraction mechanism continuously exhausts the air drawn in under that perimeter, so a pressure differential holds the device down while it remains free to translate. That combination of a rigid, leak-tolerant perimeter and continuous extraction sustaining the hold during sliding is what separates the claims from the compliant suction-cup and sealed-gripper teachings in prior_art/, which all depend on a flexible periphery achieving and keeping a seal at one fixed location. All five INDEX keys remain cited in the Background only.

2

5	The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.
6	
7	Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.
8	
9	Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.
10	
11	The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.
12	
13	Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.
14	
15	Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.
16	
17	The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)

This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.

The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.

Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.

Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.

The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.

Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.

The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.
