content.text:
All four flagged sheets are repaired. Here's the state of each fix:

**FIG. 1 (numeral 54 rejected cluster):** the fasteners were specified as "square bolt heads" with the endpoint aimed at "the broad flat top face" of one head, a small perspective facet the marker kept missing. They are now two large upright bolt-head blocks standing on the open top face of the slab in front of the motor housing, each touching only the slab and clear of the motor housing and the column, with the endpoint aimed broadly at the interior of the left-hand block rather than at one facet of it.

**FIG. 3 (numeral 16 rejected cluster):** the second side was being targeted in the narrow margin corridor outside the loop, wedged between two rectangle outlines. It is now identified in the broad open field inside the innermost rectangle around the extraction opening, which is the same surface (the underside face of the base, seen both inside and outside the loop) but a large unambiguous region. The margin outside the loop is still drawn, so the description's statement that a plain margin lies outside the loop remains supported.

**FIG. 4 (semantic failure and stroke count):** the reviewer saw a stepped component with a cutout at the left, which was the L-shaped read of the slab fragment plus the column hanging from its right. The slab fragment is gone; the column is now a plain broken-off rectangle running from the top edge of the sheet, explicitly with no step, notch, flange or cutout, its parallel sides running unbroken through the material boundary. The flagged "separated by one horizontal line" is replaced by "each meeting the next along a straight horizontal boundary", and the parallel phrase inside the column paragraph got the same treatment. Trimmed to stay inside the length cap.

**FIG. 5 (numeral 36 rejected cluster):** the covering element endpoint competed with the device, which sat in the same right-hand part of the floor. The device now stands on a tile farther back, and the foreground tile at the lower right is left entirely bare, so the endpoint lands on an unbroken stretch of tile with no body or cord on it.

Text sections, claims, the numeral table, and FIG. 2 are untouched; no numeral was added to or removed from any sheet.

input.summary: Repaired the four figure briefs the preflight and drawing review flagged, leaving the nine application sections, the claims and the numeral table unchanged. FIG. 1: the fasteners 54 are respecified as two large upright bolt-head blocks on the open top face of the slab, targeted broadly inside the left-hand block instead of at one small top facet. FIG. 3: the second side 16 is now identified in the broad open field inside the innermost rectangle around the extraction opening rather than in the narrow margin corridor between two outlines; the margin outside the loop is still drawn, so the description's plain-margin statement stays supported. FIG. 4: the slab fragment that made the upper body read as a stepped part with a left-hand cutout is removed, so the column is a plain broken-off rectangle with explicitly unstepped parallel sides, and both stroke-count phrases ("separated by one horizontal line", "One horizontal line crosses the column") are replaced by boundary relationships; the brief was trimmed back under the length cap. FIG. 5: the device is moved farther back in the view and the foreground tile at the lower right is left entirely bare, giving numeral 36 an unambiguous broad target. No banned endpoint wording (centre, midpoint, mid-height, halfway, quarter, topmost, near-end, toward-end, ordinal shape references) appears in any brief; the only ordinals remaining are the canonical part names first side 14 and second side 16 and the title phrase "second embodiment". A temporary consistency-check script created during the pass was deleted, so the workspace holds only draft, figures and inputs.
reasoning: The two coordinate-cluster failures on FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 had the same root cause: an endpoint aimed at a small or contested surface. Rather than nudge coordinates, which the brief must never do, I enlarged the target. Numeral 54 now points into the whole interior of a large bolt-head block that touches only the slab, and numeral 36 points into a foreground tile that is expressly bare of the device, the ring and the cord. Both are still the same disclosed parts, only drawn with room around them.

FIG. 3's numeral 16 was the harder one, because widening the margin corridor would have meant asserting a proportion the disclosure does not give: the specification says the loop stands 'a little inboard' of the base edge. Instead of inventing a wide margin, I moved the endpoint to the other part of the same surface. The second side is the whole underside of the base, and the field inside the loop around the extraction opening is that same face, so the numeral is still correct and now sits in a large open region. The margin outside the loop remains in the drawing so the sentence in the detailed description about a plain margin outside the loop keeps its figure support.

The FIG. 4 semantic failure was a reading of two bodies as one: a hatched slab fragment spanning the top with a broad column hanging from its right end forms an L, which the reviewer described as a stepped component with a left-hand cutout. The base is not part of what FIG. 4 is for (the Brief Description scopes it to the perimeter member end, the facing, the clearance and the bedded layers), so deleting the fragment removes the ambiguity without losing any disclosed structure, and the column now runs off the top edge as an ordinary broken-off fragmentary section. I also stated positively that the column has no step, notch, flange or cutout and that its sides run on through the material boundary, so the same misread cannot recur.

Both stroke-count phrases in FIG. 4 were replaced with relationships rather than deleted outright, because the boundaries carry real information: the material change between the perimeter member and the low-friction facing, and the three bedded layers of the covering element, the bonding material and the substrate. 'Each meeting the next along a straight horizontal boundary' states the topology the section needs without dictating how many strokes the renderer draws.

Removing the slab fragment cost about a hundred characters of new text, which pushed FIG. 4 over the length cap, so I compressed the column paragraph and one endpoint sentence rather than dropping any geometry. Nothing describing a listed part was cut.

Nothing in the invention, the claims or the description needed to move for any of this. The only body removed from a sheet was unnumbered context, and no numeral changed sheets, so the numeral table and the Brief Description of the Drawings are still in step with the figures.
changes: figures/FIG-1-PERSPECTIVE-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE-IN-USE.md: fasteners 54 respecified as two large upright bolt-head blocks standing on the open top face of the slab in front of the motor housing, each clear of the motor housing and the column with plain slab surface all round it; endpoint changed from the block's top facet to the broad interior of the left-hand block.

figures/FIG-3-BOTTOM-PLAN-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE.md: second side 16 endpoint moved from the margin corridor outside the loop to the broad open field inside the innermost rectangle around the circle, with the bullet stating that the underside face shows both inside and outside the loop; the circle is specified to stand well away from all four sides of the innermost rectangle so that field is broad.

figures/FIG-4-ENLARGED-SECTION-OF-THE-PERIMETER-MEMBER-END.md: the hatched slab fragment across the top is removed and the column now runs broken off from the top edge of the sheet, expressly a plain upright rectangle with no step, notch, flange or cutout and with sides running on through the material boundary without step or offset.

figures/FIG-4-ENLARGED-SECTION-OF-THE-PERIMETER-MEMBER-END.md: 'separated by one horizontal line' replaced by 'each meeting the next along a straight horizontal boundary', and 'One horizontal line crosses the column' replaced by a division of the column across its full width along a straight horizontal boundary; the two bullets that referred to 'the dividing line' now refer to that horizontal boundary.
figures/FIG-4-ENLARGED-SECTION-OF-THE-PERIMETER-MEMBER-END.md: column paragraph and the bearing face endpoint sentence compressed to keep the brief within the length cap.

figures/FIG-5-SECOND-EMBODIMENT-WITH-A-PULLING-ELEMENT.md: the vibration device 10 is placed on a tile farther back in the view, and the tile at the lower right is left entirely bare with nothing standing on it and no line crossing it, so covering element 36 is identified on an unbroken stretch of plain tile clear of every other body.
input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged this turn. The independent claims still turn on the combination the references do not show: a rigid, deliberately non-sealing perimeter member with a low-friction bearing face that leaves a clearance to the covering element, through which ambient air is drawn continuously while the air-extraction mechanism holds a below-atmospheric chamber, so the device is held down without operator pressure and can still slide, with the whole vibration path from motor to covering element free of any resilient member. The vacuum-handling and suction-gripper references rely on a compliant sealing lip and an achieved seal, and the tile-vibrator references rely on downward hand pressure or a flexible suction cup in the vibration path, which is the damping the specification explains this arrangement exists to avoid. The figure repairs touched only how the disclosed structure is drawn: no structure, relationship or claim was added or widened to suit a rendered sheet.

FIG. 4's stepped-component misread came from a slab fragment that the figure did not need, and it is deleted, leaving a plain broken-off column with its no-step geometry stated positively. structured_output.summary: Repaired the four figure briefs the preflight and drawing review flagged, leaving the nine application sections, the claims and the numeral table unchanged. FIG. 1: the fasteners 54 are respecified as two large upright bolt-head blocks on the open top face of the slab, targeted broadly inside the left-hand block instead of at one small top facet. FIG. 3: the second side 16 is now identified in the broad open field inside the innermost rectangle around the extraction opening rather than in the narrow margin corridor between two outlines; the margin outside the loop is still drawn, so the description's plain-margin statement stays supported. FIG. 4: the slab fragment that made the upper body read as a stepped part with a left-hand cutout is removed, so the column is a plain broken-off rectangle with explicitly unstepped parallel sides, and both stroke-count phrases ("separated by one horizontal line", "One horizontal line crosses the column") are replaced by boundary relationships; the brief was trimmed back under the length cap. FIG. 5: the device is moved farther back in the view and the foreground tile at the lower right is left entirely bare, giving numeral 36 an unambiguous broad target. No banned endpoint wording (centre, midpoint, mid-height, halfway, quarter, topmost, near-end, toward-end, ordinal shape references) appears in any brief; the only ordinals remaining are the canonical part names first side 14 and second side 16 and the title phrase "second embodiment". A temporary consistency-check script created during the pass was deleted, so the workspace holds only draft, figures and inputs.
reasoning: The two coordinate-cluster failures on FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 had the same root cause: an endpoint aimed at a small or contested surface. Rather than nudge coordinates, which the brief must never do, I enlarged the target. Numeral 54 now points into the whole interior of a large bolt-head block that touches only the slab, and numeral 36 points into a foreground tile that is expressly bare of the device, the ring and the cord. Both are still the same disclosed parts, only drawn with room around them.

FIG. 3's numeral 16 was the harder one, because widening the margin corridor would have meant asserting a proportion the disclosure does not give: the specification says the loop stands 'a little inboard' of the base edge. Instead of inventing a wide margin, I moved the endpoint to the other part of the same surface. The second side is the whole underside of the base, and the field inside the loop around the extraction opening is that same face, so the numeral is still correct and now sits in a large open region. The margin outside the loop remains in the drawing so the sentence in the detailed description about a plain margin outside the loop keeps its figure support.

The FIG. 4 semantic failure was a reading of two bodies as one: a hatched slab fragment spanning the top with a broad column hanging from its right end forms an L, which the reviewer described as a stepped component with a left-hand cutout. The base is not part of what FIG. 4 is for (the Brief Description scopes it to the perimeter member end, the facing, the clearance and the bedded layers), so deleting the fragment removes the ambiguity without losing any disclosed structure, and the column now runs off the top edge as an ordinary broken-off fragmentary section. I also stated positively that the column has no step, notch, flange or cutout and that its sides run on through the material boundary, so the same misread cannot recur.

Both stroke-count phrases in FIG. 4 were replaced with relationships rather than deleted outright, because the boundaries carry real information: the material change between the perimeter member and the low-friction facing, and the three bedded layers of the covering element, the bonding material and the substrate. 'Each meeting the next along a straight horizontal boundary' states the topology the section needs without dictating how many strokes the renderer draws.

Removing the slab fragment cost about a hundred characters of new text, which pushed FIG. 4 over the length cap, so I compressed the column paragraph and one endpoint sentence rather than dropping any geometry. Nothing describing a listed part was cut.

Nothing in the invention, the claims or the description needed to move for any of this. The only body removed from a sheet was unnumbered context, and no numeral changed sheets, so the numeral table and the Brief Description of the Drawings are still in step with the figures.

Overview

FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 show a vibration device 10 in use. A covering element 36, which may be a ceramic or porcelain tile, a stone slab, a large-format panel or a similar rigid covering element, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material that is plastic when the covering element 36 is laid and hardens afterwards. The substrate 42 may be a floor screed, a wall, a backer board or any other surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the proportion of the underside of the covering element 36 that is wetted by the bonding material 40, and seats the covering element 36 to the intended height.

The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

The base 12 is a rigid plate. It is rigid in the sense that matters here: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 does not deflect enough to absorb an appreciable fraction of the vibration energy, and it transmits that energy to the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished. Suitable materials are metals such as aluminium alloy or steel, and rigid engineering plastics. The base 12 is shown as a flat plate of constant thickness; it may equally be ribbed, dished or box-sectioned on the first side 14 to raise its stiffness without adding mass.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22. An extraction opening 30 passes through the base 12 from the second side 16 to the first side 14 and places the chamber 22 in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20 through a duct 32. In the embodiment of FIG. 1, FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 there is a single extraction opening 30 at the centre of the second side 16, with the duct 32 standing over it at the centre of the first side 14 and the vibration motor 18 set toward one end of the base 12; two or more extraction openings 30 distributed over the second side 16 may be used instead, which evens out the pressure across a chamber 22 of large plan area.

The vibration motor

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12. It is mounted directly against the first side 14 and fixed to it by fasteners 54 spaced around its foot, so that no resilient mount, rubber bush or foam pad is interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. The fasteners 54 are shown in FIG. 1. That direct mounting is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 may be of any type that produces mechanical vibration in the base 12, including an electric motor driving an eccentric mass, a pneumatic vibrator, and a linear oscillator. In the embodiment of FIG. 1 the vibration motor 18 is a housing standing directly on the base 12, wider along the long edge of the base 12 than it is tall. What matters to the arrangement described here is not the mechanism by which the vibration is generated but the path by which it leaves the vibration device 10, which is dealt with below.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22 through the duct 32 and the extraction opening 30, discharging it to atmosphere through an exhaust outlet on the pump housing. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12, so that the vibration device 10 is self-contained and no hose runs back to a separate machine. The duct 32 is an upright hollow column open at both ends that stands on the first side 14 over the extraction opening 30 and carries the air-extraction mechanism 20 on its upper end, so that the column is interposed between the pump and the base 12 and the whole of the withdrawn air passes up through it from the chamber 22 into the pump. Other air-extraction mechanisms 20 that withdraw air from the chamber 22 may be used, including a fan or blower, or an ejector supplied with compressed air.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is devoid of a valve operable to close the chamber 22 to atmosphere, and there is nothing in which a vacuum could be held. As explained below, the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

An electrical supply 50 provides power to the vibration motor 18 and, where the air-extraction mechanism 20 is electrically driven, to the air-extraction mechanism 20. In the embodiment of FIG. 1 the electrical supply 50 is a flexible cord leaving the air-extraction mechanism 20 and running to a mains or site supply; a battery carried on the base 12 may be used instead. The vibration motor 18 and the air-extraction mechanism 20 may be switched together or independently of one another.

The substrate 42 may be a floor screed, a wall, a backer board or any other surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the proportion of the underside of the covering element 36 that is wetted by the bonding material 40, and seats the covering element 36 to the intended height.

The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

The base 12 is a rigid plate. It is rigid in the sense that matters here: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 does not deflect enough to absorb an appreciable fraction of the vibration energy, and it transmits that energy to the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished. Suitable materials are metals such as aluminium alloy or steel, and rigid engineering plastics. The base 12 is shown as a flat plate of constant thickness; it may equally be ribbed, dished or box-sectioned on the first side 14 to raise its stiffness without adding mass.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22. An extraction opening 30 passes through the base 12 from the second side 16 to the first side 14 and places the chamber 22 in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20 through a duct 32. In the embodiment of FIG. 1, FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 there is a single extraction opening 30 at the centre of the second side 16, with the duct 32 standing over it at the centre of the first side 14 and the vibration motor 18 set toward one end of the base 12; two or more extraction openings 30 distributed over the second side 16 may be used instead, which evens out the pressure across a chamber 22 of large plan area.

The vibration motor

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12. It is mounted directly against the first side 14 and fixed to it by fasteners 54 spaced around its foot, so that no resilient mount, rubber bush or foam pad is interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. The fasteners 54 are shown in FIG. 1. That direct mounting is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 may be of any type that produces mechanical vibration in the base 12, including an electric motor driving an eccentric mass, a pneumatic vibrator, and a linear oscillator. In the embodiment of FIG. 1 the vibration motor 18 is a housing standing directly on the base 12, wider along the long edge of the base 12 than it is tall. What matters to the arrangement described here is not the mechanism by which the vibration is generated but the path by which it leaves the vibration device 10, which is dealt with below.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22 through the duct 32 and the extraction opening 30, discharging it to atmosphere through an exhaust outlet on the pump housing. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12, so that the vibration device 10 is self-contained and no hose runs back to a separate machine. The duct 32 is an upright hollow column open at both ends that stands on the first side 14 over the extraction opening 30 and carries the air-extraction mechanism 20 on its upper end, so that the column is interposed between the pump and the base 12 and the whole of the withdrawn air passes up through it from the chamber 22 into the pump. Other air-extraction mechanisms 20 that withdraw air from the chamber 22 may be used, including a fan or blower, or an ejector supplied with compressed air.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is devoid of a valve operable to close the chamber 22 to atmosphere, and there is nothing in which a vacuum could be held. As explained below, the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

An electrical supply 50 provides power to the vibration motor 18 and, where the air-extraction mechanism 20 is electrically driven, to the air-extraction mechanism 20. In the embodiment of FIG. 1 the electrical supply 50 is a flexible cord leaving the air-extraction mechanism 20 and running to a mains or site supply; a battery carried on the base 12 may be used instead. The vibration motor 18 and the air-extraction mechanism 20 may be switched together or independently of one another.

1	# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)
2	
3	This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.
4	
5	The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.
6	
7	Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.
8	
9	Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.
10	
11	The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.
12	
13	Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.
14	
15	Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.
16	
17	The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)

This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.

The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.

Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.

Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.

The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.

Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.

The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

# FIG. 1 - Perspective view of the vibration device in use

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, onto one large plain tile. Outline line work, no shading or hatching. Every body except the cord has flat faces and straight edges. No text of any kind appears, and no border.

**Geometry to be drawn**

One large plain tile surface fills the lower part of the sheet and carries no numeral. The machine standing on it is drawn large, and so is each of its bodies.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole machine, the slab together with every body standing on it, drawn with one continuous outer silhouette. Identified on that continuous outer silhouette.
- The base 12 is the flat slab the other bodies stand on, and the only slab of the machine; the tile beneath is the surface it rests on. It is drawn thick, so its near front side face reads as a broad band running the whole length of the machine, with nothing in front of it. Identified anywhere well inside that broad front side band of the slab.

**View:** Plan view of the underside of the plate, with the tile removed. Outline line work only: no hatching, shading, stippling, dashed or double line, every outline one thin line. No word, digit or label appears, and no border.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The whole sheet contains three nested rectangles with square corners and a circle within them, and nothing else. From the outside inward they are a large outermost rectangle, a middle rectangle standing just inside it, and an innermost rectangle standing well inside the middle rectangle. The circle lies within the innermost rectangle and stands clear of its sides. Each outline is drawn as one closed thin line, and no frame surrounds the drawing. The circle has plain white paper inside it, and is not a ring, an annulus or a hole with a wall.

Those outlines enclose four surfaces: the narrow margin between the outermost and middle rectangles, the band between the middle and innermost rectangles, the field inside the innermost rectangle around the circle, and the inside of the circle.

The band between the middle and innermost rectangles is the widest open corridor in the drawing. The margin outside the band, between the outermost and middle rectangles, is by contrast a narrow border, and it is plainly narrower than the band everywhere.

The circle stands well away from all four sides of the innermost rectangle, so that the field inside the innermost rectangle around the circle is a broad open surface on every side of the circle, and the circle itself is drawn large enough that a point sits easily inside it.

The outermost rectangle stops well short of the edges of the sheet, so empty white paper surrounds the whole drawing.

- The extraction opening 30 is the circle. Identified well inside that circle, clear of its curve.

draft/07-detailed-description.md:49:The rate an air-extraction mechanism 20 delivers against a pressure difference is not always to hand, whereas its free-air displacement, the volumetric rate it delivers with no pressure difference across it, is a figure commonly quoted for pumps, fans and blowers. Free-air displacement may therefore be used to make a first selection, provided a margin is allowed for the fall in delivered rate with rising pressure difference, and the choice is then confirmed against the delivered rate at the working pressure difference.
draft/04-background.md:9:An example of the vibrating suction-cup approach applied to tiling is described in [REF:DE-202021002652-U1], which discloses a device provided with a handle for lifting and laying slabs, in particular tiles, having two shafts slidably connected in the handle, at least one electrically operated pump for generating a negative pressure in suction cups at the free ends of the shafts, and at least one electric motor for generating vibration of the shafts, the suction cup being formed by a rubber-elastic apron. The negative pressure in that device is developed inside a rubber-elastic cup. A head shell is connected at the free end of each vibrated shaft and carries that cup on its underside, so that the member presented to the tile is a compliant cup.
draft/04-background.md:11:Attaching a body to a surface by reducing the pressure in a space bounded by a compliant peripheral wall is also known outside the tiling field. [REF:US-11408462-B2] describes an adhesion device that defines a decompression space between a wall surface and the device, in which the peripheral wall of the decompression space is formed by elastic partitions, the wall-surface-side end of the partition nearest the wall surface contacting the wall surface, together with a restricting member of higher rigidity placed on that partition to restrict it from being deformed into the decompression space as the space becomes negatively pressured. The rigidity there is added to keep a compliant partition in shape; the member that meets the wall surface remains an elastic one. [REF:US-4934475-A] describes a device for moving along a wall surface having a main body, a seal member, a pressure reduction space defined by the seal in cooperation with the wall surface, vacuum creating means for discharging fluid from that space, and vibration generating means; there, the vibration generating means imparts a lifting force to the main body in a direction away from the wall surface so as to reduce the suction-adhering force, and imparts a moving force that moves the body along the wall.
draft/04-background.md:13:Vacuum handling equipment for sheet goods holds the workpiece through a suction surface applied flat against it. [REF:US-11247858-B2] describes a vacuum plate lifting system having a substantially horizontal suction plate with a perforated suction lifting surface, an airflow suction system for conveying vacuum air pressure to that surface, and an elongate bar carrying nozzles that is movable between a raised orientation and a lowered orientation so that a suction airflow sweeps dust or debris from the surface beneath. [REF:US-10001245-B2] describes a base assembly having a cup-shaped portion that defines a cavity on its second side and a pneumatic generator in flow communication with the cavity, the pneumatic generator being operable in a suction mode and a blower mode: in the suction mode the second side is securely coupleable to the surface by vacuum force, and in the blower mode the second side is movable substantially frictionlessly across the surface on an air cushion. Holding and moving are alternative states of that apparatus, which holds when it is not sliding and slides when it is not holding, and a control is provided to switch between them.

[REF:US-10001245-B2] describes a base assembly having a cup-shaped portion that defines a cavity on its second side and a pneumatic generator in flow communication with the cavity, the pneumatic generator being operable in a suction mode and a blower mode: in the suction mode the second side is securely coupleable to the surface by vacuum force, and in the blower mode the second side is movable substantially frictionlessly across the surface on an air cushion. Holding and moving are alternative states of that apparatus, which holds when it is not sliding and slides when it is not holding, and a control is provided to switch between them.

# FIG. 4 - Enlarged section of the perimeter member end

**View:** Greatly enlarged fragmentary section through the lower end of a perimeter member shown in FIG. 2, where the clearance is present, with the bedded layers beneath. Outline line work, hatching on cut material. No word, digit or label appears, and no border.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The sheet shows one upright hatched column and three hatched bands beneath it, and nothing else. The column is a plain upright rectangle in outline, with no step, notch, flange or cutout, standing in the right part of the sheet. It is drawn very broad, its straight parallel sides running unbroken from the top edge of the sheet, where the column is broken off, down to the horizontal line that closes its bottom. A straight horizontal boundary crosses its full width, dividing it into a deep upper part and a deep lower part, the sides running on through that boundary without step or offset. The upper part is hatched with lines sloping one way and the lower part with lines sloping the other, the two being different materials.

Three hatched bands lie one above another across the lower part of the sheet, each spanning the full width and drawn deep, each meeting the next along a straight horizontal boundary: the upper, middle and lower bands. Because the view is greatly enlarged, the gap between the column and the upper band is a tall open space, the bottom line of the column standing well above the unbroken top edge line of the upper band.

- The perimeter member 24 is the upper part of the column, above the horizontal boundary that crosses it. Identified well inside the hatching of that upper part.
- The low-friction facing 28 is the lower part of the column, below that horizontal boundary. Identified well inside the hatching of that lower part.
- The bearing face 26 is the flat lower end face of the column, seen edge on as the horizontal line that closes the bottom of the column and bounds the tall open gap from above. Identified on that bottom line, anywhere along its length.
- The clearance 34 is the open white gap between the bottom of the column and the top edge of the upper band, the two nowhere touching. Identified well inside that gap, clear of the lines bounding it.
- The covering element 36 is the upper band. Identified well inside its hatching.
- The exposed face 38 is the upper face of the upper band, seen edge on as its top edge line, which runs unbroken across the full width of the sheet. Identified on that top edge line, anywhere along its length.
- The bonding material 40 is the middle band. Identified well inside its hatching.
- The substrate 42 is the lower band. Identified well inside its hatching.

<!-- Claims - body text only, no heading line. -->

1. A vibration device for bedding a covering element into a bonding material, the vibration device comprising:

a base that is rigid and has a first side and a second side opposite the first side;

a vibration motor coupled to the first side;

a perimeter member extending from the second side and surrounding a chamber located on the second side, the perimeter member being rigid and terminating, remote from the base, in a bearing face of a low-friction material, the chamber being bounded by the second side, the perimeter member and, when the bearing face is placed in contact with an exposed face of the covering element, by the exposed face, and a clearance remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member, between the bearing face and the exposed face, through which clearance ambient air enters the chamber; and

an air-extraction mechanism coupled to the first side and in fluid communication with the chamber, the air-extraction mechanism being operable to withdraw air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while the ambient air continues to enter the chamber through the clearance, a resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device against the covering element;

wherein a vibration transmission path from the vibration motor to the bearing face passes through the base and the perimeter member, each member of the vibration transmission path is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed in the vibration transmission path; and

wherein the bearing face is slidable over the exposed face while the pressure differential is maintained.

2. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the perimeter member is a continuous closed loop that runs unbroken around the chamber near a perimeter of the second side, and the bearing face lies in a single plane.

3. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the low-friction material of the bearing face is plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials.

4. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the perimeter member comprises a low-friction facing of polytetrafluoroethylene fixed to an end of the perimeter member remote from the base, an exposed surface of the low-friction facing forming the bearing face.

5. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the perimeter member is free of rubber, elastomer and foam, and makes rigid contact with the exposed face.

6. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the pressure differential produces a holding force sufficient to hold the vibration device against the exposed face without a downward force being applied by an operator.

7. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the chamber is devoid of a valve operable to close the chamber to atmosphere, such that the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism withdraws air from the chamber, and wherein the air-extraction mechanism is operable to withdraw air from the chamber continuously while the vibration motor operates.

8. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein, at a working pressure difference at which the pressure differential holds the vibration device against the covering element, the rate at which the air-extraction mechanism withdraws air from the chamber is at least equal to the rate at which the ambient air passes through the clearance at that same working pressure difference, such that the chamber falls below atmospheric pressure and settles at a pressure at which the rate at which the ambient air enters the chamber through the clearance equals the volumetric extraction rate.

content.text:
Repairs are done and confined to the figure briefs; no application text, claim, or numeral changed.

**What I changed**

- **FIG. 1, base 12** (review: rejected coordinate cluster): the target was a "tall band" on a narrow front side face. It is now a broad unbroken front band of the slab, with the endpoint stated as anywhere well inside that band rather than a depth-constrained spot.
- **FIG. 1, air-extraction mechanism 20** (review: rejected cluster; the brief had also acquired the banned word "topmost"): the housing is now identified by a stable structural relationship, the only body of the machine touching the slab nowhere, carried on the column and wider than it, with the endpoint anywhere well inside its broad front face. The cord bullet was updated to call the same body "that raised housing" so the sheet uses one name for it.
- **FIG. 3, perimeter member 24** (review: rejected cluster): the endpoint no longer requires the upper run of the loop. All four runs of the band are now specified as the widest open corridor in the drawing, and the numeral may land anywhere well inside that corridor clear of the two rectangles bounding it.
- **FIG. 4, bearing face 26** (review: rejected cluster): kept as a full-boundary target, tightened so the bottom line is identified by what it does (closes the column, bounds the tall gap from above) and the endpoint is anywhere along its length.
- **Line-type targets made uniform**: first side 14 (FIG. 2) and exposed face 38 (FIG. 4) now read "anywhere along its length" on their full boundary line, matching the full-boundary rule the request sets out.
- **Length gate**: FIG. 1 (2848) and FIG. 4 (3084, after the endpoint wording grew) were over the 2800-character limit. Both are now under it (2781 and 2790) by condensing prose, not by dropping geometry or relationships.

**What I deliberately left alone**

- "first side 14", "second side 16" and the FIG. 5 caption "Second embodiment" keep their wording. These are numeral-table part names and a standard caption, not ambiguous shape ordinals; renaming them would break the claims, the numeral table and the detailed description.
- The banned endpoint vocabulary (center/centre, midpoint, mid-height/width/depth, halfway, quarter, near-end, toward-end, shape ordinals) does not otherwise appear in any brief; a scan confirms this.

**One thing to flag:** `input/conversation.md` contains two later user messages describing a source-fidelity repair that would delete or generalize numbered parts such as the duct 32, fasteners 54, attachment formation 48, electrical supply 50 and the PTFE facing. This turn's request in `input/request.md` says the opposite, to preserve the numeral table, claims and disclosed geometry, so I did not act on those messages. If that narrowing is wanted, it is a substantial text-and-figure rework and should be the explicit request for a turn.

input.summary: Repaired the four figure briefs the preflight and the previous review flagged, without touching the invention text. FIG. 1 base 12 now targets a broad front band of the slab instead of a narrow face; FIG. 1 air-extraction mechanism 20 is identified by the stable relationship "the only body touching the slab nowhere, carried on the column" and the banned word "topmost" was removed; FIG. 3 perimeter member 24 may now land anywhere in the loop corridor, which is specified as broad on all four runs, instead of only the upper run; FIG. 4 bearing face 26 stays a full-boundary target and is now tied to what the line does rather than to an exact spot. Line-type targets 14 and 38 were made uniform with "anywhere along its length". FIG. 1 and FIG. 4 were over the 2800-character brief limit (2848 and 3084) and are now 2781 and 2790, trimmed by condensing prose only. No claim, specification section, numeral definition, or disclosed geometry changed. Two later messages in conversation.md call for a source-fidelity narrowing that contradicts this turn's request to preserve the claims and numeral table; I did not act on them and flagged that in the answer.
reasoning: The review's three failures were all rejected endpoint clusters, which is a symptom of a target region that is too thin or not uniquely identifiable in pixels, not of wrong subject matter. So every repair widened the target region or anchored it to a relationship no other body on the sheet shares, rather than moving the numeral to a different part.

FIG. 1 base 12 failed because the front side face of the slab is the thinnest region on a crowded sheet. I specified the slab as drawn thick so the front face reads as a broad unbroken band along the whole machine, and dropped the 'clear of its upper and lower edge lines' squeeze, so any interior point of that band satisfies the brief.

FIG. 1 numeral 20 sits on one of three similar rectangular housings, which is why its cluster kept getting rejected. Rather than adding an arbitrary coordinate, I gave it the one structural property that separates it from motor housing 18 and duct column 32: it is the only body of the machine that touches the slab nowhere. That is a relationship already in the drawn geometry, not a new invention detail. The brief the file had picked up also used 'topmost', which this turn's request bans, so that had to go regardless.

FIG. 3 numeral 24 was pinned to the upper run of the loop band, which made a single horizontal stretch carry the whole endpoint. I moved the width requirement onto all four runs and let the endpoint fall anywhere in the corridor, which multiplies the acceptable area roughly fourfold while keeping the loop unambiguously distinct from the narrow outer margin.

FIG. 4 numeral 26 is a line, so no interior exists. Under the request's 'full boundaries' allowance I kept it on the bottom line but identified that line functionally (it closes the column and bounds the tall gap from above), which lets any point along it be checked as correct. I applied the same 'anywhere along its length' phrasing to the other two line targets, 14 and 38, so a passing rule is used consistently rather than only where a failure was reported.

FIG. 1 at 2848 characters and FIG. 4 at 3084 both breached the 2800 limit, FIG. 4 partly because the endpoint sentences had grown. I recovered the space by condensing prose (removing 'where the clearance is present' from the FIG. 4 view line, collapsing the column description) and not by deleting geometry, so every listed numeral still has its identifying structure.

I left 'first side 14', 'second side 16', and the FIG. 5 caption 'Second embodiment' untouched. A regex for shape ordinals may flag them, but they are numeral-table part names and a standard caption; renaming them to satisfy a check would desynchronize the claims, numeral table, and detailed description, which is exactly the trade the instructions say not to make.

input.prior_art_strategy: No claim or specification text was altered this turn, so the existing positioning stands. Claim 1 rests on a perimeter member that is rigid and deliberately does not seal: a clearance remains along at least part of the bearing face through which ambient air keeps entering, while the extraction mechanism withdraws air fast enough to hold the chamber below atmosphere, and the whole vibration path from motor to bearing face is rigid with no elastomer, foam, or resilient mount in it, the bearing face remaining slidable while the differential is maintained. That leakage-tolerant rigid interface is what carries the claim past DE-202021002652-U1 and US-11408462-B2, whose pressure spaces are bounded by a rubber-elastic apron and by elastic partitions respectively, so their vibration path runs through a compliant member. It also separates the claim from US-10001245-B2, where holding by vacuum and sliding on an air cushion are alternative switched states rather than simultaneous, and from US-4934475-A, where vibration is used to reduce the suction-adhering force and move the body rather than to be delivered into the workpiece through a rigid path. The figure repairs kept FIG. 4, the sheet that shows the clearance, the low-friction facing, and the bearing face standing off the exposed face, intact as the drawing support for that distinction.
