33	The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.
34	
35	Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is far too small to be drawn to scale. FIG. 2 accordingly shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 without any gap, at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 appears only in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4, where it is drawn many times its true height. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.
36	
37	The pressure differential that holds the device down
38	
39	The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.
40	
41	The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. In use the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load.
42	
43	A property of this arrangement should be noted, because it is what the arrangement is for.
44	
45	The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.
46	
47	The vibration transmission path
48	
49	The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 through the rigid joint at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.
50	
51	The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38 throughout each vibration cycle. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.
52	
53	The clearance 34 does not stand between the bearing face 26 and the covering element 36 in the way that a film of air stands between a pressed-on sliding base and the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and makes hard, direct contact with it over the remainder of the loop, and it is that contact, not the clearance 34, that carries the vibration. The clearance 34 admits air into the chamber 22 alongside the contact rather than lying between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38: air passes along it, edgewise, into the chamber 22, and the vibration passes across the contact beside it. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is far too small to be drawn to scale. FIG. 2 accordingly shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 without any gap, at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 appears only in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4, where it is drawn many times its true height. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. In use the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load.

A property of this arrangement should be noted, because it is what the arrangement is for.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 through the rigid joint at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38 throughout each vibration cycle. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not stand between the bearing face 26 and the covering element 36 in the way that a film of air stands between a pressed-on sliding base and the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and makes hard, direct contact with it over the remainder of the loop, and it is that contact, not the clearance 34, that carries the vibration. The clearance 34 admits air into the chamber 22 alongside the contact rather than lying between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38: air passes along it, edgewise, into the chamber 22, and the vibration passes across the contact beside it. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

input.summary: Applied every listed finding. Six passages of untraced technical substance were removed or replaced with disclosure-grounded wording in the detailed description, the "incapable of transmitting compression" limitation was struck from claim 10 and the description, and the four drawing contradictions were resolved: FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 now show the perimeter member as the member touching the tile, FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 no longer negate a route through the base, FIG. 3 places the loop at the perimeter as two nested rectangles, and numeral 36 now means the single tile the device stands on across all sheets.
reasoning: The untraced explanatory material in the description was cut to what the disclosure actually says. The cause of the clearance is now the disclosed fact that the perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, rather than invented surface-condition and flatness facts. The restriction mechanism is now simply that the perimeter member restricts the flow without closing the path, with no length, width or resistance characterization. The bonding material is named without a cure property. The sliding paragraph drops the quantified resistance, the air-cushion comparison and the full-amplitude absolute, keeping the disclosed contrast that intensity no longer falls away with distance from a fixed attachment point. The consistency claim ends at the working area. The interface paragraph keeps the disclosed damping statement and describes the clearance as admitting air alongside the contact rather than lying between the faces, dropping the parallel/series model and the energy-storage assertion.

Claim 10 lost its negative capability limitation. What now distinguishes the system claim is the decoupled-control relationship that the disclosure states affirmatively: position is set by tension on the flexible pulling element while the holding force is supplied independently and continuously by the pressure differential. That relationship, together with the non-sealing rigid perimeter and the all-rigid transmission path carried into the claim body, is what the claim rests on. The description paragraph was reduced in the same way, so claim and description use the same words.

The FIG. 1 defect was the most serious drawing finding, because the sole in-use perspective showed the base sitting on the tile with the only member that actually touches the tile invisible. FIG. 1 now carries the perimeter member 24 as a shallow band running round the underside of the slab at its edge, holding the slab clear of the tile, and the base's front band is described with the perimeter member below it and plain tile below that. Numeral 24 is on the sheet, six numerals in total, within the cap. I made the same correction in FIG. 5 and numbered the band there too, so no depicted body is left unidentified.

The through-base negation was a contradiction between the briefs and the claims, not a missing structure. Since the corrective turn removed the extraction opening and duct as unsupported, the repair is silence rather than an added route: FIG. 2 no longer says the slab has no opening anywhere, FIG. 3 no longer says no shape appears inside the loop, both briefs state that the route of communication is not depicted in that view, and the Brief Description of FIG. 2 says the same. Nothing was added to the invention to excuse the drawing.

FIG. 3 was reduced from three nested rectangles to two, so the outer edge of the loop coincides with the outline of the underside of the plate. That removes the inboard margin the reviewer flagged and makes the drawing agree with claim 2 and with the description, which both put the loop at the perimeter of the second side. FIG. 2's legs now stand at the ends of the slab, and the description's internal contradiction between 'near its perimeter' and 'at its perimeter' is resolved in favour of the perimeter.

Numeral 36 now denotes one thing everywhere: the covering element the device is working on. In FIG. 5 the multi-tile floor is drawn as unnumbered context and 36 is anchored to the tile the machine stands on, with that tile drawn much larger than the machine so a broad bare stretch of its surface is available for the leader. The pulling element is called a flexible line rather than a cord, so numeral 46 carries one vocabulary across the table, the claims, the description and the briefs.

Layout assertions that read as structural relationships were removed from FIG. 1 and FIG. 5. Neither brief now says the bodies touch one another nowhere; they say only that three bodies stand on the slab spaced apart so each presents a clear surface for its numeral. Left and right survive purely as drawing positions for leader disambiguation, with no functional ordering asserted, and the handle is described as a grip carried on the machine rather than fixed to the base, matching the description's amended statement that the device may include one or more handles.

Two smaller text fixes complete the set: the joint between the perimeter member and the base now carries vibration substantially undiminished, matching the qualified language used everywhere else and in the disclosure, and the overview now says FIG. 1 shows the device in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers, which is what those sheets actually depict.

After the changes the ledger still closes: all 16 tabled numerals appear in the text and on at least one sheet, no sheet carries more than seven, every brief is well under the character limit, and no note, placeholder, question, bracketed token or em dash remains in draft/ or figures/.

input.prior_art_strategy: "Claim 1 is untouched and continues to rest on the combination the disclosure supplies: a chamber that is never closed, a rigid perimeter member ending in a low-friction bearing face that leaves a clearance through which ambient air enters continuously, extraction sufficient to hold the chamber below atmosphere despite that ingress, an all-rigid transmission path with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed, and a bearing face that slides while the differential is maintained. That non-sealing rigid perimeter is what separates the claim from vacuum-attachment apparatus that closes a space against atmosphere through a compliant sealing member, which necessarily puts compliance in the load path this invention keeps rigid, and the simultaneous holding and sliding separates it from apparatus whose holding and moving are alternative states. Claim 10 now rests on the disclosed decoupled-control relationship rather than on the struck compression limitation: position set by tension on the flexible pulling element while the holding force is supplied independently and continuously by the pressure differential. The supporting explanation of why the deliberately non-sealing rigid perimeter solves the coupling-versus-damping problem remains in the detailed description, now stated in the disclosure's own qualified terms. Consistent with the previous review, the background carries no reference characterizations and no citation tokens."

# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)

This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.

The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.

Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.

Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.

The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.

Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.

The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

# Conversation so far

### USER

Here is my invention.

The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.

Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.

Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.

The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.

Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.

The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

1	<!-- Detailed Description - body text only, no heading line. -->
2	
3	In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.
4	
5	Overview
6	
7	FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the proportion of the underside of the covering element 36 that is wetted by the bonding material 40, and improves the contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40.
8	
9	The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.
10	
11	The base
12	
13	The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 does not deflect enough to absorb an appreciable fraction of the vibration energy, and it transmits that energy to the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.
14	
15	The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22, and the chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.
16	
17	The vibration motor
18	
19	The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no resilient mount, rubber bush or foam pad interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.
20	
21	The vibration motor 18 may be of any type that produces mechanical vibration in the base 12. What matters to the arrangement described here is not the mechanism by which the vibration is generated but the path by which it leaves the vibration device 10, which is dealt with below.
22	
23	The air-extraction mechanism
24	
25	The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.
26	
27	The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.
28	
29	The perimeter member and the chamber
30	
31	A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The joint between the perimeter member 24 and the base 12 is rigid and carries vibration across itself substantially undiminished.
32	
33	The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The bearing face 26 is a low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member.
34	
35	The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.
36	
37	Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is far too small to be drawn to scale. FIG. 2 accordingly shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 without any gap, at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 appears only in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4, where it is drawn many times its true height. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.
38	
39	The pressure differential that holds the device down
40	
41	The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.
42	
43	The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. In use the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load.
44	
45	A property of this arrangement should be noted, because it is what the arrangement is for.
46	
47	The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.
48	
49	The vibration transmission path
50	
51	The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 through the rigid joint at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.
52	
53	The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38 throughout each vibration cycle. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.
54	
55	The clearance 34 does not stand between the bearing face 26 and the covering element 36 in the way that a film of air stands between a pressed-on sliding base and the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and makes hard, direct contact with it over the remainder of the loop, and it is that contact, not the clearance 34, that carries the vibration. The clearance 34 admits air into the chamber 22 alongside the contact rather than lying between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38: air passes along it, edgewise, into the chamber 22, and the vibration passes across the contact beside it. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.
56	
57	The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the only force the operator supplies is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because the operator applies no downward force, there is no loaded path from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.
58	
59	Handles
60	
61	The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. It is not used to press the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36, and it need not be dimensioned or damped as though it were, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.
62	
63	Embodiment with a flexible pulling element
64	
65	FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.
66	
67	This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls.
68	
69	Method of use
70	
71	A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought into contact with the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without downward force applied by an operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12, the perimeter member 24 and the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.
72

In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.

A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 does not deflect enough to absorb an appreciable fraction of the vibration energy, and it transmits that energy to the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22, and the chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no resilient mount, rubber bush or foam pad interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 may be of any type that produces mechanical vibration in the base 12. What matters to the arrangement described here is not the mechanism by which the vibration is generated but the path by which it leaves the vibration device 10, which is dealt with below.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

The perimeter member and the chamber

A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The joint between the perimeter member 24 and the base 12 is rigid and carries vibration across itself substantially undiminished.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The bearing face 26 is a low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is far too small to be drawn to scale. FIG. 2 accordingly shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 without any gap, at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 appears only in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4, where it is drawn many times its true height. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. In use the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load.

A property of this arrangement should be noted, because it is what the arrangement is for.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 through the rigid joint at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38 throughout each vibration cycle. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not stand between the bearing face 26 and the covering element 36 in the way that a film of air stands between a pressed-on sliding base and the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and makes hard, direct contact with it over the remainder of the loop, and it is that contact, not the clearance 34, that carries the vibration. The clearance 34 admits air into the chamber 22 alongside the contact rather than lying between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38: air passes along it, edgewise, into the chamber 22, and the vibration passes across the contact beside it. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the only force the operator supplies is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because the operator applies no downward force, there is no loaded path from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. It is not used to press the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36, and it need not be dimensioned or damped as though it were, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought into contact with the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without downward force applied by an operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12, the perimeter member 24 and the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.

<!-- Title - body text only, no heading line. -->

VIBRATION DEVICE FOR BEDDING COVERING ELEMENTS, HELD BY A SUSTAINED PRESSURE DIFFERENTIAL ACROSS A RIGID LOW-FRICTION PERIMETER
<!-- Cross-Reference to Related Applications - body text only, no heading line. -->

Not applicable.
<!-- Field of the Disclosure - body text only, no heading line. -->

The present disclosure relates to power tools for installing tiles and other covering elements, whether guided by hand or drawn across the work by a flexible pulling element, and more particularly to a vibration device that transmits mechanical vibration into a covering element that has been placed on a bed of thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material, in order to release trapped air, distribute the bonding material and improve the contact between the covering element and the bonding material.
<!-- Background - body text only, no heading line. -->

When a tile or similar covering element is laid onto a bed of thinset, mortar or adhesive, air is trapped between the covering element and the bonding material and the bonding material is unevenly distributed beneath the covering element. Mechanical vibration applied to the exposed face of the covering element after it is laid drives the trapped air out, spreads the bonding material into a more uniform layer, increases the area over which the bonding material actually touches the covering element, and thereby improves the strength of the completed bond. Hand-guided vibration devices are used for this purpose.

Such devices generally comprise a vibration motor carried on a handle together with one of two arrangements for putting the vibration into the covering element: a smooth sliding base that the operator presses down onto the exposed face, or a flexible suction cup that grips the exposed face at one place.

Both arrangements couple the vibration into the covering element poorly. A smooth sliding base has to be pressed hard against the covering element by the operator, and even under that pressure a thin film of air can remain between the base and the covering element and damp the vibration crossing the interface. A flexible suction cup makes a firmer connection, but the rubber or foam wall that forms the cup is compliant, and a compliant member placed in the path between the motor and the covering element absorbs and dissipates part of the vibration instead of delivering it. A device gripped by such a cup is also anchored at one place on the covering element: it cannot be slid to another area without first releasing the grip, and the vibration amplitude reaching areas remote from the point of attachment falls off with distance from that point.

The second problem with existing tile vibration devices concerns the operator rather than the tile. Because contact has to be maintained by hand, the operator applies substantial and continuous downward force through the handle, and vibration travels back up that loaded path into the hands, wrists, arms and joints, producing discomfort, fatigue and a risk of injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles reduce some of the vibration reaching the operator, but they do so by absorbing mechanical energy that would otherwise have gone into the covering element, so the tool is made kinder to the operator by being made worse at its job. The two problems are coupled: firmer coupling to the covering element is obtained by pressing harder, and pressing harder is exactly what increases the vibration dose to the operator.

What is needed is a way to hold a vibration device against a covering element with a force that does not come from the operator's arms, to conduct the vibration into the covering element without passing it through any compliant member, and to allow the device to be moved from area to area over the covering element without ever giving up that hold.
<!-- Abstract - body text only, no heading line. -->

A vibration device for bedding covering elements into thinset, mortar or adhesive has a rigid base carrying a vibration motor and an air-extraction mechanism on its first side and a chamber on its second side. A rigid perimeter member surrounds the chamber and ends in a bearing face of low-friction material such as plastic or PTFE. It is not a seal: a clearance remains against the exposed face of the covering element, and ambient air enters the chamber continuously. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air fast enough to keep the chamber below atmospheric pressure while air keeps entering, and the pressure differential presses the device onto the covering element without downward force from the operator. Every member between the motor and the covering element is rigid, so vibration transfers with little damping, and the bearing face lets the device slide to successive areas without releasing the hold.

content.text:
The figure briefs are repaired and the whole package re-checked. Summary of what I did:

**Endpoint targets made broad (no arbitrary exact placement anywhere in `figures/`)**
- FIG. 1: base **12** now targets the whole front band of the slab, not a face qualified by an invented thickness; the pump housing **20** targets its front face rather than a "broad" face.
- FIG. 2: first side **14** now reads "anywhere along its length" on the upper edge line instead of "the long stretch clear of both ends"; covering element **36** is simply "well inside its hatching".
- FIG. 3: perimeter member **24** is "well inside that band" instead of "deep inside … far from" both rectangles; second side **16** is "well inside that field, clear of the band".
- FIG. 4: the three bands drop the sheet-edge qualifiers; bearing face **26** and exposed face **38** keep full-boundary targets ("anywhere along its length").
- FIG. 5: covering element **36** targets the exposed tile surface without the "much larger than the machine" proportion.

**Renderer-control artefacts removed**: "drawn deep/large/thick/very broad", square-corner and single-thin-line stipulations in FIG. 3, "a single run of parallel lines" in FIG. 4, and the two label-room demands (open paper above the slab in FIG. 2, a gap sized so a point can stand in the FIG. 3 band). The two open spaces that remain, chamber **22** in FIG. 2 and clearance **34** in FIG. 4, stay because they are disclosed structure, not label room.

**Ordinals**: the only surviving "first"/"second" are the canonical part names *first side 14*, *second side 16* and the title of the second-embodiment sheet. Shape references use outermost/innermost, upper/middle/lower, left/right.

Nothing in `draft/` changed. Counts verified: 16 numerals in the table, the same 16 across the five sheets, at most 7 per sheet, every brief ≤ 2,542 characters, no notes, placeholders or em dashes.

input.summary: Repaired all five figure briefs for the new preflight: every numeral endpoint is now a broad visible interior or a full boundary, and every arbitrary placement, proportion, corner-shape and line-count instruction that existed only to steer the renderer has been removed. The application text, claims and numeral table are untouched. The one review finding was an HTTP 529 provider outage, not a defect in the draft, so nothing was changed on its account.
reasoning: The reviewer's single finding, 'Source fidelity is clean before rendering (fail): API Error: 529 Overloaded', is an infrastructure failure with no substantive content. I re-verified source fidelity by hand instead of editing text to appease it: every numbered part (10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 34, 36, 38, 40, 42, 44, 46) traces to an affirmative sentence in input/disclosure.md, and the features the earlier corrective messages listed for deletion (PTFE facing as a separate body, through-base duct, exhaust to atmosphere, battery or cord, integral one-piece loop, plural chambers, vertical-surface use, bail geometry) are absent from draft/ and from figures/. No text change was warranted, so I made none.

The preflight this turn bans exact endpoint instructions. The offenders were FIG. 2's first side 14 ('the long stretch clear of both ends of the slab and far from every edge of the sheet') and covering element 36 ('clear of its upper and lower edge lines and well away from the left and right edges'), and FIG. 3's perimeter member 24 ('deep inside that band, far from the outermost rectangle and far from the innermost'). Each became a broad interior or a whole-boundary target: numeral 14 now says 'anywhere along its length' on the upper edge line, which is the correct kind of target for a face seen edge on.

I removed the renderer-control geometry that the disclosure does not support: 'drawn thick' on base 12, 'drawn deep' on the FIG. 2 slab and band and the FIG. 4 bands, 'drawn very broad' on the FIG. 4 column, 'drawn large' on the FIG. 3 inner field, 'square corners' and 'one closed thin line' in FIG. 3, 'a single run of parallel lines' in FIG. 4, and 'drawn much larger than the machine' in FIG. 5. None of these proportions is in the inventor's words; keeping them would have let generated pixels dictate invented geometry.

Two label-room demands went as well: FIG. 2's 'leaving open white paper above the slab' plus the wide left and right margins tied to slab length, and FIG. 3's requirement that the band be wide enough for 'a point to stand in open paper' inside it. I kept the two open regions that are disclosed structure rather than drafting convenience: chamber 22, the space between the legs in FIG. 2, and clearance 34, the gap under the bearing face in FIG. 4. Those exist because the inventor says the chamber sits on the second side and the perimeter deliberately does not seal.

On the ordinal ban I drew a line: 'first side 14', 'second side 16' and the FIG. 5 title 'Second embodiment' are canonical part names and a figure caption fixed by the numeral table and by claim language, not ambiguous shape references, so they stay. What the gate is aimed at, ordinals used to pick out one of several identical shapes, is already gone: FIG. 3 uses outermost and innermost rectangle, FIG. 4 uses upper, middle and lower band, FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 use left and right, and FIG. 2 uses the right-hand leg to pick one of the two legs.

Claim 1 is unchanged and still turns on three things read together: a rigid perimeter member ending in a low-friction bearing face that leaves a clearance through which ambient air enters continuously; an extraction rate sufficient to keep the chamber below atmospheric while that ingress continues; and an all-rigid transmission path from motor to bearing face with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed, the bearing face being slidable while the differential is maintained. The description supports each limitation in the same words.

Nothing was added to claim 1 that the art does not force. Motor type, pump capacity, dimensions, power source, handle form and attachment point of the pulling element are all absent, because the disclosure fixes none of them and each would be scope surrendered for no return. The handle and the pulling element sit in dependent claims 8 and 9 and in the separate system claim 10, where the decoupled-control relationship is what is being protected.

input.prior_art_strategy: Claim 1 clears US-11408462-B2 and US-4934475-A on the perimeter itself. Both hold their body to the surface with an elastic seal: US-11408462-B2 recites first and second partitions each formed of an elastic member, with a rigid restricting member added only to stop the elastomer being sucked inward, and US-4934475-A recites a seal member cooperating with the wall to define a pressure reduction space. Claim 1 instead recites a rigid perimeter member terminating in a low-friction bearing face with a clearance remaining along at least part of it, through which ambient air enters continuously, and an extraction rate sufficient to hold the chamber below atmospheric under that continuous ingress. A deliberately leaking rigid rim is the opposite design choice from a conforming seal, and the specification explains why it is made: compliance in the load path is what damps the vibration the tool exists to deliver, so the clearance is described as the condition the device works in rather than a defect. US-4934475-A is further away in purpose than in structure: its vibration generator imparts a lifting force that reduces the adhering force in order to walk the body along, whereas here the vibration is the payload delivered into the covering element and the holding force is deliberately held constant while the device slides. US-11247858-B2 and DE-202021002652-U1 are lifting and laying equipment for panels, gripping a slab to move it, with no vibration delivered into a bedded element and no translation of the gripper over the gripped face while suction is maintained. US-10001245-B2 couples an end effector to a structure; its interest is in attaching and holding a tool at a location, not in sliding across a work face under a continuously replenished pressure differential. The second limitation that no reference supplies is the wholly rigid transmission path: claim 1 requires each member from motor to bearing face to be rigid with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed anywhere along it. US-11408462-B2 necessarily places elastomer in that path, and none of the references gives a reason to remove every compliant member from between a vibration source and the work. Even combined, a vacuum gripper and a tile vibrator do not teach a rim that restricts rather than closes the air path, nor an extraction rate specified against continuous ingress rather than against a sealed volume. System claim 10 adds the decoupled-control relationship, position set by tension on a flexible pulling element while contact force is supplied independently by the pressure differential, which no reference discloses. Method claim 14 recites translation over the exposed face while the differential is maintained, with claim 15 requiring holding and sliding to be simultaneous rather than alternatives.

The application text, claims and numeral table are untouched. The one review finding was an HTTP 529 provider outage, not a defect in the draft, so nothing was changed on its account.
reasoning: The reviewer's single finding, 'Source fidelity is clean before rendering (fail): API Error: 529 Overloaded', is an infrastructure failure with no substantive content. No text change was warranted, so I made none.

The preflight this turn bans exact endpoint instructions. The offenders were FIG. 2's first side 14 ('the long stretch clear of both ends of the slab and far from every edge of the sheet') and covering element 36 ('clear of its upper and lower edge lines and well away from the left and right edges'), and FIG. 3's perimeter member 24 ('deep inside that band, far from the outermost rectangle and far from the innermost'). None of those proportions is in the inventor's words, and keeping them lets generated pixels dictate invented geometry.

Two label-room demands went as well: FIG. 2's open white paper above the slab plus the margins tied to slab length, and FIG. 3's requirement that the band be wide enough for a point to stand in open paper inside it. I kept the two open regions that are disclosed structure rather than drafting convenience: chamber 22 between the legs in FIG. 2, and clearance 34 under the bearing face in FIG. 4. Those exist because the inventor says the chamber sits on the second side and the rigid perimeter deliberately does not seal.

On the ordinal ban I drew a line. Every limitation appears in the detailed description in the same words.

Nothing was added to claim 1 that the art does not force. Motor type, pump capacity, dimensions, power source, handle form and the attachment point of the pulling element stay out, because the disclosure fixes none of them and each would be scope surrendered for nothing. The handle and the pulling element sit in dependent claims 8 and 9 and in system claim 10, where the decoupled-control relationship is what is being protected.

<!-- Summary - body text only, no heading line. -->

A vibration device is disclosed for bedding a covering element into thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material. The device has a rigid base with a first side and a second side. A vibration motor is coupled to the first side. An air-extraction mechanism is coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side. A perimeter member extends from the second side around the chamber and terminates in a bearing face that rests on the exposed face of the covering element. The perimeter member is rigid and its bearing face is of a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials.

The perimeter member is not a seal and is not asked to behave like one. When the bearing face rests on the exposed face, a clearance remains along at least part of the perimeter member through which ambient air passes continuously into the chamber. The perimeter member restricts that flow without stopping it. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance. The resulting pressure differential acts over the area of the chamber and presses the device against the covering element.

Two consequences follow, and they are the point of the arrangement. First, the force holding the device down is supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator, so the operator does not have to press the device against the covering element and the loaded, vibrating path from tool to hand is removed rather than damped. Second, every member in the path from the vibration motor to the covering element, namely the base, the perimeter member and the bearing face, is rigid, with no elastomeric or foam element interposed, so the vibration crosses into the covering element without being absorbed on the way. The device is thus coupled harder and held down harder than a pressed-on sliding base, while the operator's hands carry less.

Because the member that touches the covering element is a rigid low-friction bearing face rather than a gripping cup, the device can be translated across the exposed face while the pressure differential is being maintained. Holding and sliding are not alternative modes to be switched between: the same continuously running extraction keeps the device down while it is moved, so vibration can be delivered at successive positions over the covering element without the hold ever being released and without the vibration amplitude falling away with distance from a fixed attachment point.

In one embodiment the device carries one or more handles, which serve to guide and steer the device rather than to press it down. In another embodiment a flexible pulling element such as a rope, wire or cable is attached to the device, and the operator moves the device by pulling on that element. This gives decoupled control: the position of the device is set by a small pulling force applied by the operator, while the force holding the device against the covering element, and with it the quality of the vibration coupling, is set independently and constantly by the pressure differential.

A method of bedding a covering element using the device, and a system comprising the device together with the flexible pulling element, are also disclosed.
