structured_output.summary: Fixed all eleven findings: the unsourced clearance magnitude and the exclusive clearance-here/contact-elsewhere geometry are out of the description, the absolute operator-force statements are permissive in the description, claim 17, the Summary and the Abstract, claim 6 now matches the description's continuous-extraction condition, the invented housing shapes, spacing, base overhang, even-thickness base and the handle on the pulling-element sheet are out of the briefs, the rectangular loop is now stated in the description as an example only, the FIG. 2 omission list and the wetting mechanism are corrected, and the process scaffolding is removed from numerals.md and from the nine section files.
reasoning: The clearance magnitude was the most dangerous item, because a stated dimensional fact about the gap is a limitation a reader can hold the application to and the inventor never gave any size. The description now says only that the clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity, which is a drawing convention rather than an assertion about the device, and the FIG. 4 brief no longer justifies its gap by the invented smallness of the real one; it asks for an open space sized so the clearance is visible. I also removed 'greatly' from the FIG. 4 view line and 'tall' from the bearing face bullet, since both carried the same unsourced premise.

The clearance geometry paragraph had drifted into asserting a partition of the interface: gap along part of the loop, hard contact over the remainder, vibration crossing at the contact and not at the gap. The disclosure affirms air entering beneath the perimeter and rigid contact with the tile, but not where each occurs. The paragraph now says the bearing face bears rigidly on the exposed face and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact, and that the clearance, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits air without a compliant member separating the faces. That keeps literal, in-the-same-words support for the 'along at least part of the perimeter member' recital in claims 1, 10 and 14 while dropping the exclusive version.

The operator-force item was both a fidelity and a scope defect, so I fixed it in every place it appeared rather than only the two cited. Claim 17 recited the absolute as a positive method limitation and now recites that the pressure differential holds the device without a downward force being required from the operator, which is the construction claims 5 and 13 already used. The description's 'hands carry no part of the contact load', 'the operator applies no downward force' and 'the only force the operator supplies' are now permissive, and I made the same correction in the method-of-use paragraph, which carried the identical phrasing and would otherwise have contradicted the amended claim.

For the invented figure geometry I recast structure as depiction convention rather than deleting the bodies. The motor and the air-extraction mechanism are now simply the two bodies carried on the top face of the base, each shown as a simple housing, with no rectangular shape, no left-or-right assignment, no non-touching requirement and no base overhang. The overhang mattered most because it existed to manufacture a labelling target; the base 12 endpoint is now 'well inside the visible part of its top face', which is a broad interior on the intended part and does not require the slab to run past anything.

On the handle in the pulling-element embodiment I took the narrower option the reviewer identified as source-safest: numeral 44 and the grip are gone from FIG. 5, the Brief Description no longer says the device again carries a handle, and the description points the handle to FIG. 1 alone. Handle 44 is still labelled on FIG. 1, so no numeral lost its sheet and no part or definition was deleted. The alternative would have required the specification to assert a both-at-once configuration the disclosure presents as separate embodiments.

Claim 6 recited a relationship neither the description nor the source states, tying continuous extraction to motor operation. It now reads 'continuously while the vibration device is in use', word for word with the description. This is a narrowing of nothing: the disclosure's continuity statement is about the device in use, and claim 1 already carries the extraction-rate limitation that does the work against the art.

The rectangular loop is a case where the drawings had to show some shape while the text was shape-neutral. I fixed it in the description, adding that the rectangular plan outline is shown by way of example only and that the perimeter member 24 may follow any closed outline around the chamber at the perimeter of the second side. That keeps claim 2's closed-loop recital broad rather than being read down to a rectangle, and it let the FIG. 3 geometry stand unchanged. I did remove the stray 'rectangular' from the perimeter band in FIG. 1 and FIG. 5, where it added nothing.

Two small reconciliations: the FIG. 2 entry now lists the handle with the motor and the air-extraction mechanism as omitted for clarity, matching a brief that omits everything carried on the first side; and the overview sentence now says the vibration increases the area of contact between covering element 36 and bonding material 40 and strengthens the bond, which are the effects the disclosure lists, instead of a wetting mechanism it does not give.

The process scaffolding is gone from numerals.md, leaving the heading and the sixteen-row table, and I also stripped the template comment from the head of each of the nine section files rather than leaving them to a render step, since the standing rule is that no instruction may appear anywhere in draft/.

Nothing in claim 1, claim 10 or claim 14 changed. The distinguishing combination is untouched: a rigid perimeter member ending in a low-friction bearing face with a clearance along at least part of it admitting ambient air continuously, an extraction rate holding the chamber below atmospheric under that ingress, and an all-rigid motor-to-bearing-face path with the face slidable while the differential is maintained. The edits removed unsourced description gloss around those limitations and aligned two dependent claims to the description, which strengthens written-description support rather than narrowing scope.

FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 show the extraction mechanism as a housing on the base with no connection to the chamber; FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 expressly state the route is not depicted; FIG. 4 is a fragmentary detail. The Brief Description tells the reader outright that the relationship is not shown. Under 37 CFR 1.83(a) the drawings must show every feature specified in the claims, so this invites an examiner objection. The connection itself is inventor-supported ("is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base"); only its routing and structure are not, which is why a schematic connection is the correct fix rather than a duct or opening.

No lettering, wording or marking is drawn as part of the artwork, and no border; the only characters on the sheet are the reference numerals listed below and their leader lines."

The briefs render each as a "simple housing" and the base as a "slab." These are acceptable depiction conventions in substance - they add no function, connection or proportion, and the claims and description stay shape-neutral - but neither brief nor the Brief Description of the Drawings labels them as schematic, so as filed the sheets read as asserting particular block-form bodies. This is a labeling gap only; no shape or embodiment should be added to the specification to justify the outlines.

The parallel apparatus and system claims use the correct indefinite form ("an operator"), so the definite article in claim 17 is an isolated slip that invites a 35 U.S.C. 112(b) indefiniteness rejection.

1. A vibration device for bedding a covering element into a bonding material, the vibration device comprising:

a base that is rigid and has a first side and a second side opposite the first side;

a vibration motor coupled to the first side;

a perimeter member extending from the second side and surrounding a chamber located on the second side, the perimeter member being rigid and terminating, remote from the base, in a bearing face of a low-friction material, the chamber being bounded by the second side, the perimeter member and, when the bearing face is placed in contact with an exposed face of the covering element, by the exposed face, and a clearance remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member, between the bearing face and the exposed face, through which clearance ambient air enters the chamber; and

an air-extraction mechanism coupled to the first side and in fluid communication with the chamber, the air-extraction mechanism being operable to withdraw air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while the ambient air continues to enter the chamber through the clearance, a resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device against the covering element;

wherein a vibration transmission path from the vibration motor to the bearing face passes through the base and the perimeter member, each member of the vibration transmission path is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed in the vibration transmission path; and

wherein the bearing face is slidable over the exposed face while the pressure differential is maintained.

2. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the perimeter member is a closed loop that runs around the chamber at a perimeter of the second side.

3. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the low-friction material of the bearing face is plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials.

4. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the perimeter member is free of rubber, elastomer and foam, and makes rigid contact with the exposed face.

5. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the pressure differential produces a holding force sufficient to hold the vibration device against the exposed face without a downward force being applied by an operator.

6. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the air-extraction mechanism is operable to withdraw air from the chamber continuously while the vibration device is in use.

7. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the air-extraction mechanism is a vacuum pump.

8. The vibration device of claim 1, further comprising a handle arranged to guide the vibration device over the exposed face while the pressure differential holds the vibration device against the covering element.

9. The vibration device of claim 1, further comprising a flexible pulling element connected to the vibration device, the vibration device being translatable over the exposed face by tension applied to the flexible pulling element while the pressure differential is maintained.

10. A system for bedding a covering element into a bonding material, the system comprising:

a vibration device comprising a base that is rigid and has a first side and a second side opposite the first side, a vibration motor coupled to the first side, a perimeter member extending from the second side and surrounding a chamber located on the second side, and an air-extraction mechanism coupled to the first side and in fluid communication with the chamber,

the perimeter member being rigid and terminating, remote from the base, in a bearing face of a low-friction material, the chamber being bounded by the second side, the perimeter member and, when the bearing face is placed in contact with an exposed face of the covering element, by the exposed face, and a clearance remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member, between the bearing face and the exposed face, through which clearance ambient air enters the chamber,

the air-extraction mechanism being operable to withdraw air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while the ambient air continues to enter the chamber through the clearance, a resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device against the covering element,

and a vibration transmission path from the vibration motor to the bearing face passing through the base and the perimeter member, each member of the vibration transmission path being rigid and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount being interposed in the vibration transmission path; and

a flexible pulling element connected to the vibration device, the flexible pulling element being arranged to move the vibration device across the exposed face when tension is applied to it,

whereby a position of the vibration device over the exposed face is controlled by tension applied to the flexible pulling element while a force holding the vibration device against the covering element is supplied independently of the flexible pulling element by the pressure differential.

11. The system of claim 10, wherein the flexible pulling element is a rope, a wire or a cable.

12. The system of claim 10, wherein the low-friction material of the bearing face is plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials.

13. The system of claim 10, wherein the perimeter member is free of rubber, elastomer and foam, and wherein the pressure differential produces a holding force sufficient to hold the vibration device against the exposed face without a downward force being applied by an operator.

14. A method of bedding a covering element into a bonding material, the method comprising:

placing a vibration device on an exposed face of the covering element that has been laid on the bonding material, the vibration device comprising a base that is rigid and has a first side and a second side, a vibration motor coupled to the first side, a rigid perimeter member extending from the second side and surrounding a chamber located on the second side and terminating in a bearing face of a low-friction material, and an air-extraction mechanism coupled to the first side and in fluid communication with the chamber, whereby the bearing face is brought into contact with the exposed face so that the chamber is bounded by the second side, the perimeter member and the exposed face, with a clearance remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member, between the bearing face and the exposed face;

operating the air-extraction mechanism to withdraw air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber through the clearance, and holding the vibration device against the covering element by a resulting pressure differential;

operating the vibration motor and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor to the covering element along a vibration transmission path passing through the base, the perimeter member and the bearing face, each member of the vibration transmission path being rigid and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount being interposed in the vibration transmission path; and

translating the vibration device across the exposed face, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face over the exposed face, so that the vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element.

15. The method of claim 14, wherein the pressure differential is maintained continuously while the vibration device is translated across the exposed face, so that the vibration device is held against the covering element and slid over the exposed face at the same time.

16. The method of claim 14, wherein the vibration device is translated across the exposed face by applying tension to a flexible pulling element connected to the vibration device.

17. The method of claim 14, wherein the vibration device is translated across the exposed face by guiding the vibration device with a handle, and wherein the pressure differential holds the vibration device against the covering element without a downward force being required from the operator.

18. The method of claim 14, wherein the low-friction material of the bearing face is polytetrafluoroethylene.

In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.

Overview

FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.

The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 does not deflect enough to absorb an appreciable fraction of the vibration energy, and it transmits that energy to the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22, and the chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The vibration motor

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 may be of any type that produces mechanical vibration in the base 12. What matters to the arrangement described here is not the mechanism by which the vibration is generated but the path by which it leaves the vibration device 10, which is dealt with below.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

The perimeter member and the chamber

A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The closed loop is shown in the drawings with a rectangular plan outline by way of example only; the perimeter member 24 may follow any closed outline that runs around the chamber 22 at the perimeter of the second side 16. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The bearing face 26 is a low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 is shown in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.

A property of this arrangement should be noted, because it is what the arrangement is for.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. It is not used to press the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36, and it need not be dimensioned or damped as though it were, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought into contact with the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12, the perimeter member 24 and the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.

# FIG. 1 - Perspective view of the vibration device in use

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, onto the covering element 36, drawn as one large plain tile. Outline line work, no shading or hatching. Every body has flat faces and straight edges. No lettering, wording or marking is drawn as part of the artwork, and no border; the only characters on the sheet are the reference numerals listed below and their leader lines.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The covering element 36, drawn as one large plain tile, fills the lower part of the sheet. A machine stands on it. Two bodies are carried on the top face of the base 12, shown schematically, the base 12 being shown as a slab, and a grip is carried on the machine.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole machine, the base 12 with every body carried on it, drawn with one continuous outer silhouette. Identified on that silhouette.
- The base 12 is the slab that carries the other bodies, the only slab on the sheet; its top face remains visible where no body stands on it. Identified well inside the visible part of its top face, clear of every bounding line.
- The perimeter member 24 is a shallow band standing under the base 12 and running round its underside at its edge, so the base 12 is held clear of the covering element 36 by that band; its outward-facing front and left surfaces are visible below the base 12, and it is the only part of the vibration device 10 that touches the covering element 36. Identified well inside its visible front surface.
- The vibration motor 18 is one of the two bodies carried on the top face of the base 12, shown schematically as a simple housing, with no body in front of it. Identified well inside its front face.
- The air-extraction mechanism 20 is the other body carried on the top face of the base 12, shown schematically as a separate simple housing. Identified well inside its front face.
- The handle 44 is a grip carried on the vibration device 10, standing clear of the two bodies on the top face of the base 12. Identified well inside its outline.
- The covering element 36 is the large plain tile on which the vibration device 10 stands. Identified well inside its exposed upper surface, clear of the vibration device 10.
- The chamber 22 is the space that the perimeter member 24 encloses beneath the base 12, which this view does not look into. A broken line, shown schematically, runs from the air-extraction mechanism 20 to the chamber 22 beneath the base 12 to indicate the fluid communication between them; no passage, opening or duct structure is drawn. Identified on that broken line where it runs below the base 12.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 10, 12, 18, 20, 22, 24, 36, 44

# FIG. 4 - Enlarged section of the perimeter member end

**View:** Enlarged fragmentary section through the lower end of a perimeter member of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the perimeter member where the clearance is present, with the bedded layers beneath. Outline line work, hatching on cut material. No lettering, wording or marking is drawn as part of the artwork, and no border; the only characters on the sheet are the reference numerals listed below and their leader lines.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The sheet shows the perimeter member 24, drawn as one upright hatched column, and three hatched bands beneath it, and nothing else. The column is a plain upright rectangle in outline, with no step, notch or cutout, standing in the right part of the sheet. Its straight parallel sides run unbroken from the top edge of the sheet, where the column is broken off, down to the horizontal line that closes its bottom. The column is one body of one material, hatched throughout, and no horizontal line crosses it between its top and the line that closes its bottom.

Three hatched bands lie one above another across the lower part of the sheet, each spanning the full width, each meeting the next along a straight horizontal boundary: the upper band is the covering element 36, the middle band is the bonding material 40, and the lower band is the substrate 42. The gap between the column and the upper band is shown as an open space, the bottom line of the column standing above the unbroken top edge line of the upper band, so that the clearance is clearly visible. Each of the three bands is identified well inside its own hatching.

- The perimeter member 24 is the whole hatched column. Identified well inside the hatching of that column, clear of the line that closes its bottom.
- The bearing face 26 is the flat lower end face of the column, seen edge on as the horizontal line that closes the bottom of the column and bounds the open gap from above. Identified on that bottom line, anywhere along its length.
- The clearance 34 is the open white gap between the bottom of the column and the top edge of the upper band, the two nowhere touching. Identified well inside that gap, clear of the lines bounding it.
- The covering element 36 is the upper band. Identified well inside its hatching.
- The exposed face 38 is the upper face of the upper band, seen edge on as its top edge line, running unbroken across the sheet. Identified on that top edge line, anywhere along its length.
- The bonding material 40 is the middle band. Identified well inside its hatching.
- The substrate 42 is the lower band. Identified well inside its hatching.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 24, 26, 34, 36, 38, 40, 42

- 24

- 38
- 40

content.text:
All five findings are fixed.

**Drawings (37 CFR 1.83(a) exposure)**: FIG. 1 now shows the claimed fluid communication. A broken line, shown schematically, runs from air-extraction mechanism 20 to chamber 22 beneath base 12, with no passage, opening or duct structure drawn. Numeral 22 is added to that sheet, bringing it to eight, and numeral 22 is identified on the broken line where it runs below the base. The FIG. 1 entry in the Brief Description says so, and the description's air-extraction paragraph now adds that the communication is indicated schematically in FIG. 1 by a broken line, no particular route being shown. FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 are otherwise unchanged.

**Text/numeral contradiction**: all five View lines now bar lettering, wording or marking drawn as part of the artwork and state that the only characters on the sheet are the listed reference numerals and their leader lines.

**FIG. 4 View line**: now reads as an enlargement of a perimeter member of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the perimeter member where the clearance is present, which reconciles it with FIG. 2's contact with no gap.

**Schematic designation**: the motor and pump are "shown schematically as a simple housing" on FIG. 1 and "the housings being shown schematically" on FIG. 5, the FIG. 1 geometry paragraph designates the two bodies as schematic with the base shown as a slab, and both the FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 entries in the Brief Description add "the vibration motor and the air-extraction mechanism being shown schematically".

**Claim 17**: "from the operator" is now "from an operator", matching claims 5 and 13.

Two briefs crossed the 2,800-character limit once the required clauses were added, so I removed a redundant sentence from each: the flat-faces-and-straight-edges constraint on FIG. 1 and a duplicate band-target sentence on FIG. 4. All five are now between 1,736 and 2,756 characters, the 16 numerals still match the table, and no sheet carries more than eight.

input.summary: Fixed all five findings: FIG. 1 now depicts the claimed fluid communication schematically by a broken line and carries numeral 22, all five View lines except the reference numerals from the no-lettering rule, the FIG. 4 View line carries the clearance-location qualifier, the motor and pump housings are designated as shown schematically in the briefs and in the Brief Description, and claim 17 now recites "an operator". The invention, numeral definitions and claim substance are otherwise unchanged.
reasoning: The 1.83(a) exposure was the finding with the most substance: every independent claim recites the air-extraction mechanism in fluid communication with the chamber, and no sheet showed it. The connection itself is inventor-supported; only its route and structure are not. So FIG. 1 now carries a broken line running from air-extraction mechanism 20 to chamber 22 beneath base 12, expressly shown schematically, with no passage, opening or duct drawn. That is the narrowest thing that satisfies the rule without reintroducing the through-base duct that an earlier corrective message deleted as unsupported.

Adding chamber 22 to FIG. 1 needed an endpoint that does not invent geometry, because the chamber is under the base and this view does not look into it. The numeral is identified on the broken line where it runs below the base 12, which is a target on the schematic indicator itself rather than on a hidden volume the sheet cannot show. That takes FIG. 1 to eight numerals, at the limit but within it, so no redistribution or extra sheet was needed.

I added one sentence to the description's air-extraction paragraph recording that the communication is indicated schematically in FIG. 1 by a broken line, no particular route being shown. Without it the text and the sheet would be out of step for a newly labelled numeral. The sentence describes the drawing convention only; it adds no route, no opening and no structure to the invention.

The text prohibition genuinely contradicted the numeral lists in the same file: a brief cannot both forbid all digits on the sheet and require reference numerals on it. Every View line now bars lettering, wording and marking drawn as part of the artwork and states that the only characters on the sheet are the listed reference numerals and their leader lines. That preserves the real intent, which is to stop the image model from drawing labels of its own, while leaving the annotation step free to place the numerals.

The FIG. 4 View line read as an enlargement of a perimeter member of FIG. 2 with no qualifier, so standing alone it contradicted FIG. 2, where the legs meet the covering element with no gap. It now says it is taken at a place along the perimeter member where the clearance is present, matching the qualifier already carried by the Brief Description and the detailed description. This is the same reconciliation those two documents already used, so nothing new is asserted about where the clearance lies.

The schematic designation is a labelling fix and I kept it that way. The motor and pump are shown schematically as simple housings and the base as a slab, in both perspective briefs and in the FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 entries of the Brief Description. I did not add any shape, block form or proportion to the specification to justify the outlines; the description stays shape-neutral, saying the vibration motor 18 may be of any type that produces mechanical vibration in the base 12.

Claim 17's definite article was an isolated slip against claim 14, which never introduces an operator. It now reads 'from an operator', the indefinite form claims 5 and 13 already use. No scope moved.

Adding the required clauses pushed two briefs over the 2,800-character limit, so I removed the least load-bearing sentence from each rather than trimming disclosed geometry: the flat-faces-and-straight-edges constraint on FIG. 1, which was an invented rendering constraint anyway and is now covered by the schematic designation, and the duplicate band-target sentence on FIG. 4, whose content is already in the three band bullets.

figures/FIG-2-...CHAMBER.md: View line replaced with the numeral-excepting form.
figures/FIG-3-...VIEW.md: View line replaced with the numeral-excepting form; brief otherwise unchanged.

figures/FIG-4-...END.md: View line now reads 'through the lower end of a perimeter member of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the perimeter member where the clearance is present' and carries the numeral-excepting form; the duplicate sentence identifying each of the three bands inside its own hatching removed, the three band bullets already carrying those targets.

figures/FIG-5-...PULLING-ELEMENT.md: View line replaced with the numeral-excepting form; the vibration device 10 bullet now reads 'two separate simple housings carried on it, the housings being shown schematically'.

draft/06-drawings.md: FIG. 1 entry now adds 'the vibration motor and the air-extraction mechanism being shown schematically and the fluid communication between the air-extraction mechanism and the chamber being shown schematically by a broken line'; FIG. 5 entry now adds 'the vibration motor and the air-extraction mechanism being shown schematically'; FIG. 2, FIG. 3 and FIG. 4 entries unchanged.

draft/07-detailed-description.md: the air-extraction paragraph now adds 'The fluid communication between the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the chamber 22 is indicated schematically in FIG. 1 by a broken line, no particular route being shown.'
draft/08-claims.md: claim 17 now recites 'without a downward force being required from an operator'.
draft/numerals.md and the remaining sections: unchanged.
input.prior_art_strategy: Claim 1, claim 10 and claim 14 are unchanged and clear the references on the same combination. US-11408462-B2 holds its body down with partitions expressly formed of elastic members, rigidity appearing only as a restricting frame that stops the elastomer being pulled into the decompression space, and US-4934475-A recites a seal member cooperating with the wall to define the pressure reduction space. Claim 1 recites the opposite: a rigid perimeter member terminating in a low-friction bearing face with a clearance remaining along at least part of it through which ambient air enters continuously, and an extraction rate sufficient to hold the chamber below atmospheric while that ingress continues, together with an all-rigid path from motor to bearing face carrying no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount, the bearing face being slidable while the differential is maintained. This turn's drawing work strengthens the file without touching that position: showing the fluid communication schematically satisfies the requirement that the drawings show every claimed feature, while the express statement that no passage, opening or duct is drawn keeps the application from acquiring a routing structure the inventor never described and that could later be read into the claims. Designating the motor and pump as schematic serves the same end, since the disclosure gives them no external form and the description remains shape-neutral, so nothing in the sheets can be used to narrow the motor or the extraction mechanism to a block-form housing. US-4934475-A also points away in purpose, its vibration generator imparting a lifting force that reduces the adhering force so the body can walk along, whereas here the vibration is the payload and the hold is kept constant while the device slides. US-11247858-B2 and DE-202021002652-U1 are panel lifting and laying equipment with no vibration delivered into a bedded element and no translation of the gripper across the gripped face under maintained suction. US-10001245-B2 concerns coupling an end effector to a structure rather than sliding across a work face under a continuously replenished differential. Correcting claim 17 to the indefinite article removes an indefiniteness exposure on the one dependent claim that ties guiding by handle to the operator-free hold.

tool_use_result.originalFile:
A vibration device is disclosed for bedding a covering element into thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material. The device has a rigid base with a first side and a second side. A vibration motor is coupled to the first side. An air-extraction mechanism is coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side. A perimeter member extends from the second side around the chamber and terminates in a bearing face that rests on the exposed face of the covering element. The perimeter member is rigid and its bearing face is of a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials.

The perimeter member is not a seal and is not asked to behave like one. When the bearing face rests on the exposed face, a clearance remains along at least part of the perimeter member through which ambient air passes continuously into the chamber. The perimeter member restricts that flow without stopping it. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance. The resulting pressure differential acts over the area of the chamber and presses the device against the covering element.

Two consequences follow, and they are the point of the arrangement. First, the force holding the device down is supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator, so the operator need not press the device against the covering element, and the loaded, vibrating path from tool to hand is avoided rather than damped. Second, every member in the path from the vibration motor to the covering element, namely the base, the perimeter member and the bearing face, is rigid, with no elastomeric or foam element interposed, so the vibration crosses into the covering element without being absorbed on the way. The device is thus coupled to the covering element without an intervening compliant member or air film, while the operator's hands carry less.

Because the member that touches the covering element is a rigid low-friction bearing face rather than a gripping cup, the device can be translated across the exposed face while the pressure differential is being maintained. Holding and sliding are not alternative modes to be switched between: the same continuously running extraction keeps the device down while it is moved, so vibration can be delivered at successive positions over the covering element without the hold ever being released and without the vibration amplitude falling away with distance from a fixed attachment point.

In one embodiment the device carries one or more handles, which serve to guide and steer the device rather than to press it down. In another embodiment a flexible pulling element such as a rope, wire or cable is attached to the device, and the operator moves the device by pulling on that element. This gives decoupled control: the position of the device is set by a small pulling force applied by the operator, while the force holding the device against the covering element, and with it the quality of the vibration coupling, is set independently and constantly by the pressure differential.

A method of bedding a covering element using the device, and a system comprising the device together with the flexible pulling element, are also disclosed.

In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.

Overview

FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.

The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 does not deflect enough to absorb an appreciable fraction of the vibration energy, and it transmits that energy to the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22, and the chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The vibration motor

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 may be of any type that produces mechanical vibration in the base 12. What matters to the arrangement described here is not the mechanism by which the vibration is generated but the path by which it leaves the vibration device 10, which is dealt with below.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12. The fluid communication between the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the chamber 22 is indicated schematically in FIG. 1 by a broken line, no particular route being shown.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

The perimeter member and the chamber

A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The closed loop is shown in the drawings with a rectangular plan outline by way of example only; the perimeter member 24 may follow any closed outline that runs around the chamber 22 at the perimeter of the second side 16. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The bearing face 26 is a low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 is shown in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.

A property of this arrangement should be noted, because it is what the arrangement is for.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. It is not used to press the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36, and it need not be dimensioned or damped as though it were, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought into contact with the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12, the perimeter member 24 and the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.

draft/05-summary.md:5:Two consequences follow, and they are the point of the arrangement. First, the force holding the device down is supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator, so the operator need not press the device against the covering element, and the loaded, vibrating path from tool to hand is avoided rather than damped. Second, every member in the path from the vibration motor to the covering element, namely the base and the perimeter member terminating in the bearing face, is rigid, with no elastomeric or foam element interposed, so the vibration crosses into the covering element without being absorbed on the way. The device is thus coupled to the covering element without an intervening compliant member or air film, while the operator's hands carry less.
draft/07-detailed-description.md:47:The vibration transmission path
draft/07-detailed-description.md:49:The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.
draft/07-detailed-description.md:69:A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought into contact with the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.

**Geometry to be drawn**

content.text:
All four findings are fixed.

**View legends**: all five briefs now read "apart from the view legend and the sheet number, the only characters on the sheet are the reference numerals listed below and their leader lines", each followed by its own legend sentence naming FIG. 1 through FIG. 5, placed below the drawing clear of line work and leaders. The no-lettering rule still applies to the artwork itself.

**Chamber 22 on FIG. 1**: the enclosed space beneath the base is now indicated in broken line, hidden behind the band of perimeter member 24, and numeral 22 is identified well inside that broken outline, clear of the schematic broken line. The fluid-communication indicator is a separate broken line running from air-extraction mechanism 20 to that space, still with no passage, opening or duct drawn, so 22 designates the same space on FIG. 1 as on FIG. 2.

**Schematic designation on FIGS. 2, 3 and 4**: FIG. 2 shows the base schematically as a horizontal slab with the legs shown schematically; FIG. 3 opens with the closed loop shown schematically with a rectangular plan outline by way of example only; FIG. 4 shows the column schematically as a plain upright rectangle. The FIG. 3 entry in the Brief Description carries the same qualifier. No shape, proportion or alternative embodiment was added to the Summary, description or claims.

**Transmission path**: the Summary, claim 14 and the method paragraph now describe two members with the bearing face as the end of the perimeter member, matching claim 1, claim 10 and the transmission-path paragraph, so nothing reads as a discrete facing part.

Adding the required clauses pushed FIG. 1 and FIG. 4 past 2,800 characters, so I removed redundant wording from each rather than disclosed geometry. All five briefs now run 1,978 to 2,797 characters, FIG. 1 carries eight numerals, and the 16 numerals still match the table.

input.summary: Fixed all four findings: every brief now permits the view legend and sheet number alongside the reference numerals and names its own legend, FIG. 1 shows the chamber space in broken line and targets numeral 22 inside that outline instead of on the fluid-communication indicator, the generic outlines in FIGS. 2, 3 and 4 are designated as shown schematically or example-only, and the Summary, claim 14 and the method paragraph now enumerate the transmission path as the base and the perimeter member terminating in the bearing face, matching claims 1 and 10.
reasoning: The earlier no-text fix had swapped an absolute prohibition for an exhaustive one, and an exhaustive list that stops at the reference numerals excludes the FIG. n legend and the sheet number that a five-view application must carry. Each View paragraph now excepts both and states the legend for that sheet, while the clause barring lettering drawn as part of the artwork stays, so the geometry stage is still told not to invent labels and the annotation stage is free to place the legend, the numerals and the leaders.

The chamber 22 endpoint was the substantive drawing defect. A leader terminating on the broken line that indicates fluid communication would have made 22 name the connection on FIG. 1 and the enclosed space on FIG. 2, one numeral for two things. The space itself is disclosed as a chamber located on the second side and bounded by the perimeter member, so it can be shown in hidden line without adding structure. FIG. 1 now draws that space in broken line behind the band of perimeter member 24, keeps the fluid-communication indicator as a separate schematic broken line with no passage, opening or duct, and puts numeral 22 well inside the broken outline of the space, clear of the indicator.

The schematic designations are a labelling cure only. The disclosure gives the loop, the base and the perimeter member's section no outline, so FIG. 3's rectangular plan, FIG. 2's slab and legs and FIG. 4's plain column are depiction choices of the same class as the housings already designated on FIG. 1 and FIG. 5. Each brief now says so in its own words, and the FIG. 3 entry in the Brief Description repeats the example-only qualifier that the detailed description already carries for the plan outline. I added no shape, proportion or optional embodiment to the Summary, the description or the claims to justify any outline.

The transmission-path enumeration was the one item that could have cost scope. Listing the base, the perimeter member and the bearing face as three items and then applying 'each member of the vibration transmission path being rigid' to that list characterises the bearing face as a member in its own right, which implies a discrete facing fixed to the end of the perimeter member, the exact structure earlier removed as untraced. The Summary, claim 14 and the method paragraph now read as two members with the bearing face as the end face of the perimeter member, so all three independent claims and the description describe the same path the same way, and the disclosure's single sentence about the perimeter being formed as a rigid loop of low-friction material supports it literally.

Adding the legend clauses pushed FIG. 1 to 3,082 characters and FIG. 4 past the limit, so I cut wording that carried no disclosed content rather than trimming geometry or relationships: on FIG. 1 the duplicated sentence about the enclosed space, 'the only slab on the sheet', and a few redundant qualifiers on the endpoint targets; on FIG. 4 'straight parallel' on the column sides, 'white' on the gap, and the repetition of the bottom-line description in the bearing face bullet. Every disclosed relationship on both sheets survives, including the rim as the sole contact, the single-material column and the clearance.

structured_output.summary: Fixed all four findings: every brief now permits the view legend and sheet number alongside the reference numerals and names its own legend, FIG. 1 shows the chamber space in broken line and targets numeral 22 inside that outline instead of on the fluid-communication indicator, the generic outlines in FIGS. 2, 3 and 4 are designated as shown schematically or example-only, and the Summary, claim 14 and the method paragraph now enumerate the transmission path as the base and the perimeter member terminating in the bearing face, matching claims 1 and 10.
reasoning: The earlier no-text fix had swapped an absolute prohibition for an exhaustive one, and an exhaustive list that stops at the reference numerals excludes the FIG. n legend and the sheet number that a five-view application must carry. Each View paragraph now excepts both and states the legend for that sheet, while the clause barring lettering drawn as part of the artwork stays, so the geometry stage is still told not to invent labels and the annotation stage is free to place the legend, the numerals and the leaders.

The chamber 22 endpoint was the substantive drawing defect. A leader terminating on the broken line that indicates fluid communication would have made 22 name the connection on FIG. 1 and the enclosed space on FIG. 2, one numeral for two things. The space itself is disclosed as a chamber located on the second side and bounded by the perimeter member, so it can be shown in hidden line without adding structure. FIG. 1 now draws that space in broken line behind the band of perimeter member 24, keeps the fluid-communication indicator as a separate schematic broken line with no passage, opening or duct, and puts numeral 22 well inside the broken outline of the space, clear of the indicator.

The schematic designations are a labelling cure only. The disclosure gives the loop, the base and the perimeter member's section no outline, so FIG. 3's rectangular plan, FIG. 2's slab and legs and FIG. 4's plain column are depiction choices of the same class as the housings already designated on FIG. 1 and FIG. 5. Each brief now says so in its own words, and the FIG. 3 entry in the Brief Description repeats the example-only qualifier that the detailed description already carries for the plan outline. I added no shape, proportion or optional embodiment to the Summary, the description or the claims to justify any outline.

The transmission-path enumeration was the one item that could have cost scope. Listing the base, the perimeter member and the bearing face as three items and then applying 'each member of the vibration transmission path being rigid' to that list characterises the bearing face as a member in its own right, which implies a discrete facing fixed to the end of the perimeter member, the exact structure earlier removed as untraced. The Summary, claim 14 and the method paragraph now read as two members with the bearing face as the end face of the perimeter member, so all three independent claims and the description describe the same path the same way, and the disclosure's single sentence about the perimeter being formed as a rigid loop of low-friction material supports it literally.

Adding the legend clauses pushed FIG. 1 to 3,082 characters and FIG. 4 past the limit, so I cut wording that carried no disclosed content rather than trimming geometry or relationships: on FIG. 1 the duplicated sentence about the enclosed space, 'the only slab on the sheet', and a few redundant qualifiers on the endpoint targets; on FIG. 4 'straight parallel' on the column sides, 'white' on the gap, and the repetition of the bottom-line description in the bearing face bullet. Every disclosed relationship on both sheets survives, including the rim as the sole contact, the single-material column and the clearance.
