1. A vibration device for bedding a covering element into a bonding material, the vibration device comprising:

a base that is rigid and has a first side and a second side opposite the first side;

a vibration motor coupled to the first side;

a perimeter member extending from the second side and surrounding a chamber located on the second side, the perimeter member being rigid and terminating, remote from the base, in a bearing face of a low-friction material, the chamber being bounded by the second side, the perimeter member and, when the bearing face is placed in contact with an exposed face of the covering element, by the exposed face, and a clearance remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member, between the bearing face and the exposed face, through which clearance ambient air enters the chamber; and

an air-extraction mechanism coupled to the first side and in fluid communication with the chamber, the air-extraction mechanism being operable to withdraw air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while the ambient air continues to enter the chamber through the clearance, a resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device against the covering element;

wherein a vibration transmission path from the vibration motor to the bearing face passes through the base and the perimeter member, each member of the vibration transmission path is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed in the vibration transmission path; and

wherein the bearing face is slidable over the exposed face while the pressure differential is maintained.

2. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the perimeter member is a closed loop that runs around the chamber at a perimeter of the second side.

3. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the low-friction material of the bearing face is plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials.

4. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the perimeter member is free of rubber, elastomer and foam, and makes rigid contact with the exposed face.

5. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the pressure differential produces a holding force sufficient to hold the vibration device against the exposed face without a downward force being applied by an operator.

6. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the air-extraction mechanism is operable to withdraw air from the chamber continuously while the vibration device is in use.

7. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the air-extraction mechanism is a vacuum pump.

8. The vibration device of claim 1, further comprising a handle arranged to guide the vibration device over the exposed face while the pressure differential holds the vibration device against the covering element.

9. The vibration device of claim 1, further comprising a flexible pulling element connected to the vibration device, the vibration device being translatable over the exposed face by tension applied to the flexible pulling element while the pressure differential is maintained.

10. A system for bedding a covering element into a bonding material, the system comprising:

a vibration device comprising a base that is rigid and has a first side and a second side opposite the first side, a vibration motor coupled to the first side, a perimeter member extending from the second side and surrounding a chamber located on the second side, and an air-extraction mechanism coupled to the first side and in fluid communication with the chamber,

the perimeter member being rigid and terminating, remote from the base, in a bearing face of a low-friction material, the chamber being bounded by the second side, the perimeter member and, when the bearing face is placed in contact with an exposed face of the covering element, by the exposed face, and a clearance remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member, between the bearing face and the exposed face, through which clearance ambient air enters the chamber,

the air-extraction mechanism being operable to withdraw air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while the ambient air continues to enter the chamber through the clearance, a resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device against the covering element,

and a vibration transmission path from the vibration motor to the bearing face passing through the base and the perimeter member, each member of the vibration transmission path being rigid and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount being interposed in the vibration transmission path; and

a flexible pulling element connected to the vibration device, the flexible pulling element being arranged to move the vibration device across the exposed face when tension is applied to it,

whereby a position of the vibration device over the exposed face is controlled by tension applied to the flexible pulling element while a force holding the vibration device against the covering element is supplied independently of the flexible pulling element by the pressure differential.

11. The system of claim 10, wherein the flexible pulling element is a rope, a wire or a cable.

12. The system of claim 10, wherein the low-friction material of the bearing face is plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials.

13. The system of claim 10, wherein the perimeter member is free of rubber, elastomer and foam, and wherein the pressure differential produces a holding force sufficient to hold the vibration device against the exposed face without a downward force being applied by an operator.

14. A method of bedding a covering element into a bonding material, the method comprising:

placing a vibration device on an exposed face of the covering element that has been laid on the bonding material, the vibration device comprising a base that is rigid and has a first side and a second side, a vibration motor coupled to the first side, a rigid perimeter member extending from the second side and surrounding a chamber located on the second side and terminating in a bearing face of a low-friction material, and an air-extraction mechanism coupled to the first side and in fluid communication with the chamber, whereby the bearing face is brought into contact with the exposed face so that the chamber is bounded by the second side, the perimeter member and the exposed face, with a clearance remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member, between the bearing face and the exposed face;

operating the air-extraction mechanism to withdraw air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber through the clearance, and holding the vibration device against the covering element by a resulting pressure differential;

operating the vibration motor and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor to the covering element along a vibration transmission path passing through the base and the perimeter member to the bearing face, each member of the vibration transmission path being rigid and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount being interposed in the vibration transmission path; and

translating the vibration device across the exposed face, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face over the exposed face, so that the vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element.

15. The method of claim 14, wherein the pressure differential is maintained continuously while the vibration device is translated across the exposed face, so that the vibration device is held against the covering element and slid over the exposed face at the same time.

16. The method of claim 14, wherein the vibration device is translated across the exposed face by applying tension to a flexible pulling element connected to the vibration device.

17. The method of claim 14, wherein the vibration device is translated across the exposed face by guiding the vibration device with a handle, and wherein the pressure differential holds the vibration device against the covering element without a downward force being required from an operator.

18. The method of claim 14, wherein the low-friction material of the bearing face is polytetrafluoroethylene.

draft/09-abstract.md:1:A vibration device for bedding covering elements into thinset, mortar or adhesive has a rigid base carrying a vibration motor and an air-extraction mechanism on its first side and a chamber on its second side. A rigid perimeter member surrounds the chamber and ends in a bearing face of low-friction material such as plastic or PTFE. It is not a seal: a clearance remains against the exposed face of the covering element, and ambient air enters the chamber continuously. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air fast enough to keep the chamber below atmospheric pressure while air keeps entering, and the pressure differential presses the device onto the covering element without downward force being required from the operator. Every member between the motor and the covering element is rigid, so vibration transfers with little damping, and the bearing face lets the device slide to successive areas without releasing the hold.

The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member.
draft/07-detailed-description.md:45:The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

A vibration device is disclosed for bedding a covering element into thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material. The device has a rigid base with a first side and a second side. A vibration motor is coupled to the first side. An air-extraction mechanism is coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side. A perimeter member extends from the second side around the chamber and terminates in a bearing face that rests on the exposed face of the covering element. The perimeter member is rigid and its bearing face is of a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials.

The perimeter member is not a seal and is not asked to behave like one. When the bearing face rests on the exposed face, a clearance remains along at least part of the perimeter member through which ambient air passes continuously into the chamber. The perimeter member restricts that flow without stopping it. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance. The resulting pressure differential acts over the area of the chamber and presses the device against the covering element.

Two consequences follow, and they are the point of the arrangement. First, the force holding the device down is supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator, so the operator need not press the device against the covering element, and the loaded, vibrating path from tool to hand is avoided rather than damped. Second, every member in the path from the vibration motor to the covering element, namely the base and the perimeter member terminating in the bearing face, is rigid, with no elastomeric or foam element interposed, so the vibration crosses into the covering element without being absorbed on the way. The device is thus coupled to the covering element without an intervening compliant member or air film, while the operator's hands carry less.

Because the member that touches the covering element is a rigid low-friction bearing face rather than a gripping cup, the device can be translated across the exposed face while the pressure differential is being maintained. Holding and sliding are not alternative modes to be switched between: the same continuously running extraction keeps the device down while it is moved, so vibration can be delivered at successive positions over the covering element without the hold ever being released and without the vibration amplitude falling away with distance from a fixed attachment point.

In one embodiment the device carries one or more handles, which serve to guide and steer the device rather than to press it down. In another embodiment a flexible pulling element such as a rope, wire or cable is attached to the device, and the operator moves the device by pulling on that element. This gives decoupled control: the position of the device is set by a small pulling force applied by the operator, while the force holding the device against the covering element, and with it the quality of the vibration coupling, is set independently and constantly by the pressure differential.

A method of bedding a covering element using the device, and a system comprising the device together with the flexible pulling element, are also disclosed.

**Schematic qualifier on FIG. 1 and FIG. 5**: FIG. 1's geometry paragraph now reads "the bodies and the base 12 being shown schematically, the base 12 being shown as a slab", so the qualifier no longer attaches only to the two housings, and perimeter member 24 is "the loop or skirt, shown schematically as a shallow band". FIG. 5 carries the same two corrections: "the base being shown schematically as a slab and the housings being shown schematically", and the perimeter member as the loop or skirt shown schematically as a shallow band. All five sheets now designate every generic outline, and nothing about form or proportion was added to the specification.

**Low-friction material in the independent claims**: claims 1 and 10 now recite "the perimeter member being rigid and of a low-friction material and terminating, remote from the base, in a bearing face that is an end face of the perimeter member", and claim 14 recites "a rigid perimeter member of a low-friction material ... terminating in a bearing face that is an end face of the perimeter member". That is the disclosure's own arrangement and matches the description sentence "The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member", so no claim reaches a separate low-friction facing on a perimeter member that is not itself low-friction. Claims 3, 12 and 18 are unchanged.

I made two consequential alignments so the specification does not state the relationship the amended claims now reject: the Summary sentence and the corresponding Abstract sentence now put the low-friction material in the perimeter member with the bearing face as its end face. Reworking the Abstract sentence took it to 153 words, so I tightened it to "surrounds the chamber, its end face forming a bearing face", bringing it to 149.

All five briefs remain between 1,978 and 2,797 characters, the 16 numerals still match the table, and FIG. 1 carries eight.

input.summary: Fixed both findings: FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 now designate the base and the perimeter member as shown schematically, matching FIGS. 2, 3 and 4, and claims 1, 10 and 14 now put the low-friction material in the perimeter member with the bearing face as its end face, as the disclosure and the description state. The Summary and Abstract sentences on the same point were aligned so the specification and the claims describe one arrangement.
reasoning: The schematic qualifier was a labelling gap, not a geometry problem, so I fixed it only in the briefs. On FIG. 1 the words 'shown schematically' attached grammatically to the two bodies, leaving the slab base and the shallow band reading as asserted form; the paragraph now says the bodies and the base 12 are shown schematically. On both perspective sheets the perimeter member is now 'the loop or skirt, shown schematically as a shallow band', which is the disclosure's own noun with the drawn form marked as a convention. Every generic outline across the five sheets is now designated, and no shape or proportion was added to the Summary, description or claims to justify any of them.

The claim item was the one with real consequences. Reciting only 'a bearing face of a low-friction material' reads on a low-friction facing carried on a perimeter member that is not itself low-friction, which is the separate-facing construction the record removed as untraced and which FIG. 4 deliberately excludes by drawing the column as one body of one material. Claims 1, 10 and 14 now recite the perimeter member as being of a low-friction material with the bearing face as its end face, which is exactly what the disclosure says and what the description already carried, so the claims no longer reach a construction the specification does not describe.

Claims 3, 12 and 18 stay as they are. With the independent claims amended, 'the low-friction material of the bearing face' resolves unambiguously to the material of the perimeter member, and the material list in those dependents still traces to the disclosure's plastic, metal, PTFE, combination-of-rigid-materials wording.

I made two consequential alignments beyond the listed fixes, because leaving them would have created a fresh mismatch between the amended claims and the specification. The Summary said the perimeter member is rigid and its bearing face is of a low-friction material, and the Abstract said the member ends in a bearing face of low-friction material; both now place the material in the perimeter member with the bearing face as its end face. That wording is fully supported by the disclosure sentence about the perimeter being formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material.

Reworking the Abstract sentence pushed it to 153 words, over the 150-word limit, so I tightened the same sentence to 'surrounds the chamber, its end face forming a bearing face', bringing the Abstract to 149 words without dropping any of the content it already carried.

Adding the schematic qualifiers lengthened FIG. 1, so I trimmed wording that carried no disclosed content: redundant repetitions of 'carried on' in the two housing bullets, 'held clear ... by that band' shortened to 'stands clear', and duplicate phrasing in the chamber bullet. The disclosed relationships on that sheet all survive, including the rim as the sole contact with the covering element, the hidden-line chamber and the schematic fluid-communication indicator.

figures/FIG-5-...PULLING-ELEMENT.md: the vibration device 10 bullet now reads 'the base and two separate simple housings carried on it, the base being shown schematically as a slab and the housings being shown schematically'; perimeter member 24 is now 'the loop or skirt, shown schematically as a shallow band'.

draft/08-claims.md: claim 1 and claim 10 now recite 'the perimeter member being rigid and of a low-friction material and terminating, remote from the base, in a bearing face that is an end face of the perimeter member'; claim 14 now recites 'a rigid perimeter member of a low-friction material extending from the second side and surrounding a chamber located on the second side and terminating in a bearing face that is an end face of the perimeter member'; claims 3, 12 and 18 unchanged.

draft/05-summary.md: 'The perimeter member is rigid and its bearing face is of a low-friction material such as ...' now reads 'The perimeter member is rigid and of a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials, and the bearing face is the end face of that member.'

draft/09-abstract.md: the corresponding sentence now reads 'A rigid perimeter member of low-friction material such as plastic or PTFE surrounds the chamber, its end face forming a bearing face.', keeping the Abstract at 149 words.
draft/06-drawings.md, draft/07-detailed-description.md, draft/numerals.md, figures/FIG-2, figures/FIG-3 and figures/FIG-4: unchanged.
input.prior_art_strategy: The claim amendment tracks the disclosure and does not give up the ground that clears the art; if anything it tightens it. Claim 1 still turns on the same combination: a rigid perimeter member terminating in a bearing face with a clearance remaining along at least part of it through which ambient air enters continuously, an extraction rate sufficient to hold the chamber below atmospheric under that continuous ingress, and a transmission path from motor to bearing face through the base and the perimeter member with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed. Moving the low-friction material from the bearing face to the perimeter member itself puts the claim on the inventor's actual structure, a rigid loop or skirt made of a low-friction material, and forecloses a reading in which a compliant or dissimilar facing sits at the end of the member, which is the very thing US-11408462-B2 teaches in elastomeric form with its first and second partitions and its rigid restricting frame. US-4934475-A likewise works through a seal member cooperating with the wall, and its vibration generator imparts a lifting force to reduce the adhering force so the body can walk along, the opposite of delivering vibration into the work while holding the coupling constant. Neither reference, alone or together, teaches a rim deliberately left unsealed with the extraction rate specified against continuous ingress rather than against a sealed volume. US-11247858-B2 and DE-202021002652-U1 are panel lifting and laying equipment with no vibration delivered into a bedded element and no sliding of the gripper over the gripped face under maintained suction. US-10001245-B2 concerns coupling an end effector to a structure rather than translating across a work face under a continuously replenished differential. Designating the base and the perimeter member as shown schematically on FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 keeps claim 2's closed-loop recital and the shape-neutral description from being read down to the slab and shallow band the sheets happen to show.

Every generic outline on all five sheets is therefore marked as a depiction convention, and no shape or proportion was added to the specification to justify one. Claims 1 and 10 now recite the perimeter member as being rigid and of a low-friction material and terminating, remote from the base, in a bearing face that is an end face of the perimeter member, and claim 14 recites a rigid perimeter member of a low-friction material terminating in a bearing face that is an end face of the perimeter member, so no independent claim reads on a separate low-friction facing carried on a member that is not itself of that material. Claims 3, 12 and 18 are left as they stand, and 'the low-friction material of the bearing face' now resolves unambiguously to the material of the perimeter member. So that the specification does not state the arrangement the amended claims exclude, the corresponding sentences in the Summary and the Abstract now put the low-friction material in the perimeter member with the bearing face as its end face; that rewording took the Abstract to 153 words, so I tightened the same sentence and it now stands at 149. All five briefs remain between 1,978 and 2,797 characters, FIG. 1 carries eight numerals and no sheet carries more, the sixteen numerals still match the table and the description, and no note, placeholder, question, human-directed instruction or em dash remains in draft/ or figures/.

1	# Previous review - verdict: fail
2	
3	Full source-ledger trace of draft/01-09, draft/numerals.md and the five figure briefs against input/disclosure.md and the single substantive USER passage in input/conversation.md (all later USER messages are process/corrective instructions and were not treated as inventor support). Every claim limitation, numbered part, material, relationship, operating condition, and both variants (handle; flexible pulling element) trace to an exact affirmative disclosure passage; no untraced invented structure was found, and the features previously identified for deletion (PTFE facing, through-base opening/duct, support column, fasteners, exhaust, no-valve limitation, cord/battery, one-piece loop, attachment formation, plural chambers, vertical-surface use, bail geometry) are all absent. Claims and description use identical relationships and terms; each of the 16 numerals denotes one part in every view; no note, placeholder, question, alternative, or instruction to a person remains. Three minor defects remain: an antecedent-basis mismatch in claims 3/12/18, and two FIG. 1 desynchronizations between the filed Brief Description of the Drawings and the figure brief (handle depiction not designated schematic; a second, undeclared broken-line convention).
4	
5	## Mechanical checks that did not pass
6	
7	- **Source fidelity is clean before rendering** (fail): Full source-ledger trace of draft/01-09, draft/numerals.md and the five figure briefs against input/disclosure.md and the single substantive USER passage in input/conversation.md (all later USER messages are process/corrective instructions and were not treated as inventor support). Every claim limitation, numbered part, material, relationship, operating condition, and both variants (handle; flexible pulling element) trace to an exact affirmative disclosure passage; no untraced invented structure was found, and the features previously identified for deletion (PTFE facing, through-base opening/duct, support column, fasteners, exhaust, no-valve limitation, cord/battery, one-piece loop, attachment formation, plural chambers, vertical-surface use, bail geometry) are all absent. Claims and description use identical relationships and terms; each of the 16 numerals denotes one part in every view; no note, placeholder, question, alternative, or instruction to a person remains. Three minor defects remain: an antecedent-basis mismatch in claims 3/12/18, and two FIG. 1 desynchronizations between the filed Brief Description of the Drawings and the figure brief (handle depiction not designated schematic; a second, undeclared broken-line convention).
8	  - Claims 3, 12 and 18 recite "the low-friction material of the bearing face" without antecedent basis
9	  - FIG. 1 handle 44 is given a drawn shape and placement that is neither disclosed nor designated "shown schematically"
10	  - FIG. 1 uses broken line for two different meanings, only one of which the Brief Description of the Drawings declares
11	
12	## Reviewer findings
13	
14	- **[minor] Claims 3, 12 and 18 recite "the low-friction material of the bearing face" without antecedent basis** (draft/08-claims.md claims 3, 12, 18 (relative to claims 1, 10, 14)) - Independent claims 1, 10 and 14 recite the low-friction material only as a property of the perimeter member ("the perimeter member being rigid and of a low-friction material"; "a rigid perimeter member of a low-friction material"). None of them recites a low-friction material of the bearing face. Dependent claims 3, 12 and 18 then refer back to "the low-friction material of the bearing face", which has no antecedent in any parent claim. The substance is source-supported (disclosure: "formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials"), so this is a pure antecedent defect, not a fidelity defect. The description already states both readings ("The bearing face 26 is a low-friction material" and "The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member"), so the fix does not disturb support.
15	  - Suggested fix: In draft/08-claims.md, replace "the low-friction material of the bearing face" with "the low-friction material of the perimeter member" in claims 3, 12 and 18, so claim 3 reads "3. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the low-friction material of the perimeter member is plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials.", claim 12 reads "12. The system of claim 10, wherein the low-friction material of the perimeter member is plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials.", and claim 18 reads "18. The method of claim 14, wherein the low-friction material of the perimeter member is polytetrafluoroethylene."
16	- **[minor] FIG. 1 handle 44 is given a drawn shape and placement that is neither disclosed nor designated "shown schematically"** (figures/FIG-1-PERSPECTIVE-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE-IN-USE.md ("Geometry to be drawn", handle 44 bullet and lead-in p) - The disclosure gives the handle's existence and purpose only: "The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface." No shape, form, count beyond "one or more", or mounting location is disclosed, and draft/07 line 59 is correspondingly shape-neutral. The FIG. 1 brief nonetheless directs a specific drawn grip at a specific location on the assembly. Every other generic body on this sheet is expressly neutralised as a depiction convention ("the bodies and the base 12 being shown schematically", "shown schematically as a simple housing", "shown schematically as a shallow band"), and draft/06-drawings.md tags the motor and the air-extraction mechanism as schematic, but neither the brief nor the Brief Description of the Drawings applies that tag to the handle. As drawn, the handle outline and its stated position therefore read as an invention assertion rather than a convention.
17	  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-1-...md, change the lead-in to "...the base 12 being shown as a slab, and a grip is carried on the machine, shown schematically." and change the handle bullet to "The handle 44 is shown schematically as a simple grip carried on the vibration device 10, clear of the two bodies on the base 12; no particular handle form or mounting is shown. Identified well inside its outline." # Previous review - verdict: fail

Full source-ledger trace of draft/01-09, draft/numerals.md and the five figure briefs against input/disclosure.md and the single substantive USER passage in input/conversation.md (all later USER messages are process/corrective instructions and were not treated as inventor support). Every claim limitation, numbered part, material, relationship, operating condition, and both variants (handle; flexible pulling element) trace to an exact affirmative disclosure passage; no untraced invented structure was found, and the features previously identified for deletion (PTFE facing, through-base opening/duct, support column, fasteners, exhaust, no-valve limitation, cord/battery, one-piece loop, attachment formation, plural chambers, vertical-surface use, bail geometry) are all absent. Claims and description use identical relationships and terms; each of the 16 numerals denotes one part in every view; no note, placeholder, question, alternative, or instruction to a person remains. Three minor defects remain: an antecedent-basis mismatch in claims 3/12/18, and two FIG. 1 desynchronizations between the filed Brief Description of the Drawings and the figure brief (handle depiction not designated schematic; a second, undeclared broken-line convention).

## Mechanical checks that did not pass

- **Source fidelity is clean before rendering** (fail): Full source-ledger trace of draft/01-09, draft/numerals.md and the five figure briefs against input/disclosure.md and the single substantive USER passage in input/conversation.md (all later USER messages are process/corrective instructions and were not treated as inventor support). Every claim limitation, numbered part, material, relationship, operating condition, and both variants (handle; flexible pulling element) trace to an exact affirmative disclosure passage; no untraced invented structure was found, and the features previously identified for deletion (PTFE facing, through-base opening/duct, support column, fasteners, exhaust, no-valve limitation, cord/battery, one-piece loop, attachment formation, plural chambers, vertical-surface use, bail geometry) are all absent. Claims and description use identical relationships and terms; each of the 16 numerals denotes one part in every view; no note, placeholder, question, alternative, or instruction to a person remains. Three minor defects remain: an antecedent-basis mismatch in claims 3/12/18, and two FIG. 1 desynchronizations between the filed Brief Description of the Drawings and the figure brief (handle depiction not designated schematic; a second, undeclared broken-line convention).
  - Claims 3, 12 and 18 recite "the low-friction material of the bearing face" without antecedent basis
  - FIG. 1 handle 44 is given a drawn shape and placement that is neither disclosed nor designated "shown schematically"
  - FIG. 1 uses broken line for two different meanings, only one of which the Brief Description of the Drawings declares

## Reviewer findings

- **[minor] Claims 3, 12 and 18 recite "the low-friction material of the bearing face" without antecedent basis** (draft/08-claims.md claims 3, 12, 18 (relative to claims 1, 10, 14)) - Independent claims 1, 10 and 14 recite the low-friction material only as a property of the perimeter member ("the perimeter member being rigid and of a low-friction material"; "a rigid perimeter member of a low-friction material"). None of them recites a low-friction material of the bearing face. Dependent claims 3, 12 and 18 then refer back to "the low-friction material of the bearing face", which has no antecedent in any parent claim. The substance is source-supported (disclosure: "formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials"), so this is a pure antecedent defect, not a fidelity defect. The description already states both readings ("The bearing face 26 is a low-friction material" and "The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member"), so the fix does not disturb support.
  - Suggested fix: In draft/08-claims.md, replace "the low-friction material of the bearing face" with "the low-friction material of the perimeter member" in claims 3, 12 and 18, so claim 3 reads "3. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the low-friction material of the perimeter member is plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials.", claim 12 reads "12. The system of claim 10, wherein the low-friction material of the perimeter member is plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials.", and claim 18 reads "18. The method of claim 14, wherein the low-friction material of the perimeter member is polytetrafluoroethylene."
- **[minor] FIG. 1 handle 44 is given a drawn shape and placement that is neither disclosed nor designated "shown schematically"** (figures/FIG-1-PERSPECTIVE-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE-IN-USE.md ("Geometry to be drawn", handle 44 bullet and lead-in p) - The disclosure gives the handle's existence and purpose only: "The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface." No shape, form, count beyond "one or more", or mounting location is disclosed, and draft/07 line 59 is correspondingly shape-neutral. The FIG. 1 brief nonetheless directs a specific drawn grip at a specific location on the assembly. Every other generic body on this sheet is expressly neutralised as a depiction convention ("the bodies and the base 12 being shown schematically", "shown schematically as a simple housing", "shown schematically as a shallow band"), and draft/06-drawings.md tags the motor and the air-extraction mechanism as schematic, but neither the brief nor the Brief Description of the Drawings applies that tag to the handle. As drawn, the handle outline and its stated position therefore read as an invention assertion rather than a convention.
  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-1-...md, change the lead-in to "...the base 12 being shown as a slab, and a grip is carried on the machine, shown schematically." and change the handle bullet to "The handle 44 is shown schematically as a simple grip carried on the vibration device 10, clear of the two bodies on the base 12; no particular handle form or mounting is shown. 1. A vibration device for bedding a covering element into a bonding material, the vibration device comprising:

a base that is rigid and has a first side and a second side opposite the first side;

a vibration motor coupled to the first side;

a perimeter member extending from the second side and surrounding a chamber located on the second side, the perimeter member being rigid and of a low-friction material and terminating, remote from the base, in a bearing face that is an end face of the perimeter member, the chamber being bounded by the second side, the perimeter member and, when the bearing face is placed in contact with an exposed face of the covering element, by the exposed face, and a clearance remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member, between the bearing face and the exposed face, through which clearance ambient air enters the chamber; and

an air-extraction mechanism coupled to the first side and in fluid communication with the chamber, the air-extraction mechanism being operable to withdraw air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while the ambient air continues to enter the chamber through the clearance, a resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device against the covering element;

wherein a vibration transmission path from the vibration motor to the bearing face passes through the base and the perimeter member, each member of the vibration transmission path is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed in the vibration transmission path; and

wherein the bearing face is slidable over the exposed face while the pressure differential is maintained.

placing a vibration device on an exposed face of the covering element that has been laid on the bonding material, the vibration device comprising a base that is rigid and has a first side and a second side, a vibration motor coupled to the first side, a rigid perimeter member of a low-friction material extending from the second side and surrounding a chamber located on the second side and terminating in a bearing face that is an end face of the perimeter member, and an air-extraction mechanism coupled to the first side and in fluid communication with the chamber, whereby the bearing face is brought into contact with the exposed face so that the chamber is bounded by the second side, the perimeter member and the exposed face, with a clearance remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member, between the bearing face and the exposed face;

operating the air-extraction mechanism to withdraw air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber through the clearance, and holding the vibration device against the covering element by a resulting pressure differential;

operating the vibration motor and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor to the covering element along a vibration transmission path passing through the base and the perimeter member to the bearing face, each member of the vibration transmission path being rigid and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount being interposed in the vibration transmission path; and

All three findings are fixed.

**Antecedent basis**: claims 3, 12 and 18 now recite "the low-friction material of the perimeter member", which has its antecedent in claims 1, 10 and 14 respectively, each of which recites the perimeter member as being of a low-friction material. The material lists in those dependents are unchanged.

**Handle designation on FIG. 1**: the lead-in now ends "and a grip is carried on the machine, shown schematically", and the handle bullet reads "The handle 44 is shown schematically as a simple grip carried on the vibration device 10, clear of the two bodies on the base 12; no particular handle form or mounting is shown." The FIG. 1 entry in the Brief Description now tags the handle along with the motor and the air-extraction mechanism. No handle shape or mounting language went into the description or the claims.

**Broken-line conventions**: the FIG. 1 entry now declares both, stating that the chamber is indicated in broken line as hidden beneath the base and that the fluid communication between the air-extraction mechanism and the chamber is shown schematically by a separate broken line, so the convention carrying numeral 22 is declared in the filed text.

Adding the handle designation took FIG. 1 to 2,819 characters, so I trimmed wording that carried no disclosed content: "outward-facing" and a wordier clause in the perimeter member bullet, and repetition in the chamber bullet and the lead-in. FIG. 1 is now 2,794 characters, all five briefs run between 1,978 and 2,797, the 16 numerals still match the table, FIG. 1 carries eight, and the abstract stands at 149 words.

input.summary: Fixed all three findings: claims 3, 12 and 18 now refer to the low-friction material of the perimeter member, which has antecedent basis in claims 1, 10 and 14; the FIG. 1 brief and the Brief Description now designate handle 44 as shown schematically with no particular form or mounting; and the FIG. 1 entry now declares both broken-line conventions, the hidden chamber outline and the separate schematic fluid-communication line.
reasoning: The antecedent defect came from last turn's amendment: once the independent claims placed the low-friction material in the perimeter member, the dependents' reference to the low-friction material of the bearing face had nothing to point back to. Redirecting claims 3, 12 and 18 to the perimeter member restores the chain without touching what those claims cover, since the material list and the PTFE species are the disclosure's own and the bearing face remains the end face of that same member.

The handle was the last generic body on FIG. 1 still reading as asserted structure. The disclosure gives its existence and purpose only, and the description is deliberately silent on form and mounting, so the sheet needed the same neutralising tag every other generic body already carried. The brief now shows it schematically as a simple grip and states outright that no particular handle form or mounting is shown, and the Brief Description tags it alongside the motor and the air-extraction mechanism. I put nothing about handle shape or attachment into the description or the claims, which is what would have converted a drawing convention into an embodiment.

The two broken-line meanings on FIG. 1 needed declaring rather than redrawing. The sheet legitimately carries both: a hidden outline delimiting the chamber and a separate schematic line indicating the fluid communication that every independent claim recites. Numeral 22 sits inside the hidden outline, so a reader told only about the fluid-communication convention would have no basis for reading the outline that carries the numeral. The FIG. 1 entry now declares both, and the figure brief needed no change because it already distinguished them.

Adding the handle designation pushed FIG. 1 to 2,819 characters. I took the excess out of wording that carries no disclosed content: 'outward-facing' and a longer relative clause in the perimeter member bullet, a repeated reference to the perimeter member in the chamber bullet, and 'being shown' in the lead-in. Every disclosed relationship on the sheet survives, including the loop running round the underside at the edge of the base, the rim as the sole contact with the covering element, and the two broken-line elements.

Nothing moved in the description, the numeral table or the other four briefs. The claim edits are formal, restoring antecedent basis rather than changing scope, so the independent claims still recite the combination that carries the application: a rigid low-friction perimeter member with a clearance admitting ambient air continuously, an extraction rate holding the chamber below atmospheric under that ingress, and an all-rigid path from motor to bearing face.

input.prior_art_strategy: The independent claims are untouched this turn and still clear the references on one combination: a rigid perimeter member of a low-friction material terminating in a bearing face that is its end face, with a clearance remaining along at least part of the member through which ambient air enters continuously, an air-extraction mechanism whose extraction rate holds the chamber below atmospheric while that ingress continues, and a transmission path from motor to bearing face through the base and the perimeter member carrying no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount, the bearing face being slidable while the differential is maintained. US-11408462-B2 depends on elastic partitions, adding rigidity only as a restricting frame that stops the elastomer being pulled into the decompression space, and US-4934475-A works through a seal member cooperating with the wall while its vibration generator imparts a lifting force that reduces the adhering force so the body can walk along, the opposite of holding a constant coupling while vibration is delivered into the work. Repointing claims 3, 12 and 18 to the perimeter member keeps the plastic, metal, PTFE and combination-of-rigid-materials fallbacks attached to the member that the art forms from elastomer, which is where the fallback is worth having. US-11247858-B2 and DE-202021002652-U1 are panel lifting and laying equipment with no vibration delivered into a bedded element and no sliding of the gripper over the gripped face under maintained suction. US-10001245-B2 concerns coupling an end effector to a structure rather than translating across a work face under a continuously replenished differential. Designating the handle as schematic prevents the drawn grip from being read as a disclosed handle form, and declaring the hidden chamber outline in the filed text keeps the sheet that depicts the claimed fluid communication readable without importing any routing structure.

In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.

Overview

FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.

The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 does not deflect enough to absorb an appreciable fraction of the vibration energy, and it transmits that energy to the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22, and the chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The vibration motor

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 may be of any type that produces mechanical vibration in the base 12. What matters to the arrangement described here is not the mechanism by which the vibration is generated but the path by which it leaves the vibration device 10, which is dealt with below.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12. The fluid communication between the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the chamber 22 is indicated schematically in FIG. 1 by a broken line, no particular route being shown.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

The perimeter member and the chamber

A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The closed loop is shown in the drawings with a rectangular plan outline by way of example only; the perimeter member 24 may follow any closed outline that runs around the chamber 22 at the perimeter of the second side 16. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The bearing face 26 is a low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 is shown in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.

A property of this arrangement should be noted, because it is what the arrangement is for.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. It is not used to press the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36, and it need not be dimensioned or damped as though it were, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought into contact with the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.

lines: A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The closed loop is shown in the drawings with a rectangular plan outline by way of example only; the perimeter member 24 may follow any closed outline that runs around the chamber 22 at the perimeter of the second side 16. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.

-The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The bearing face 26 is a low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member.

+The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

The single finding is fixed.

**Description, "The perimeter member and the chamber"**: the paragraph no longer opens by calling the bearing face a material. It now reads that the perimeter member 24 terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38, that the perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material with the bearing face 26 being the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face is of that low-friction material, followed by the material list. The attribution now matches claims 1, 10 and 14, which recite the material as a property of the perimeter member, and claims 3, 12 and 18, which recite "the low-friction material of the perimeter member". It also matches FIG. 4, whose column is one body of one material with no horizontal line crossing it, so nothing reads as a separate facing at the end of the member.

No change was made to the claims, the Summary, the numeral table or any figure brief. All five briefs remain between 1,978 and 2,797 characters, the 16 numerals still match the table and the description, FIG. 1 carries eight, and the abstract stands at 149 words.

input.summary: Fixed the single finding: the detailed description no longer states that the bearing face is a low-friction material. The paragraph now attributes the material to the perimeter member and identifies the bearing face as that member's end face, matching claims 1, 10 and 14 and the amended claims 3, 12 and 18. Nothing else changed.
reasoning: The sentence 'The bearing face 26 is a low-friction material' treated a surface as a body of material, which is the reading that lets a separate low-friction facing be imported at the end of the perimeter member. That construction was removed from this application as untraced, FIG. 4 excludes it by drawing the column as one body of one material with no horizontal line crossing it, and the claims as amended attribute the material only to the perimeter member. Leaving the sentence would have given an examiner a description passage contradicting both the claims and the drawing.

The repair is wording only, so I used the reviewer's own construction: the perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, and the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is therefore of that low-friction material. That last clause preserves what the original sentence was trying to convey, that the surface in contact with the covering element is low-friction, without positing a separate body. The material list follows unchanged and still traces to the disclosure's plastic, metal, PTFE, combination-of-rigid-materials wording.

I left the later sentence describing the bearing face 26 as being of a low-friction material and slidable over the exposed face 38. It is now consistent rather than contradictory, because the paragraph has just established that the end face is of the member's material, and it is the sentence that supports the slidable-while-held limitation in claim 1.

No claim, summary, abstract, numeral or figure brief was touched. The reviewer confirmed the rest of the package traces cleanly, and changing anything else would have risked reopening items already closed.

input.prior_art_strategy: The claims are untouched and still clear the references on one combination stated the same way in the claims, the description and the drawings: a rigid perimeter member of a low-friction material terminating in a bearing face that is its end face, with a clearance remaining along at least part of the member through which ambient air enters continuously, an extraction rate sufficient to hold the chamber below atmospheric while that ingress continues, and a transmission path from motor to bearing face through the base and the perimeter member carrying no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount, the bearing face being slidable while the differential is maintained. This turn's edit matters to that position because a description sentence implying a separate low-friction facing would have opened the door to reading the claimed member as a rigid frame carrying a distinct contact layer, which is structurally close to US-11408462-B2, where elastic partitions do the sealing and a rigid restricting member merely stops the elastomer being drawn into the decompression space. With the material attributed to the member itself, the claimed rim is a single rigid low-friction body, which neither that reference nor US-4934475-A, whose seal member cooperates with the wall and whose vibration generator imparts a lifting force to reduce the adhering force, teaches or suggests. US-11247858-B2 and DE-202021002652-U1 remain panel lifting and laying equipment with no vibration delivered into a bedded element and no sliding of the gripper over the gripped face under maintained suction, and US-10001245-B2 concerns coupling an end effector to a structure rather than translating across a work face under a continuously replenished differential.
